papers.title: REAP: Learning General Rearrangement Heuristics from Motion-Planner Feedback
papers.summary: Robotic rearrangement tasks require planning sequences of actions that fulfill high-level specifications while also being geometrically feasible. Symbolic abstractions make the combinatorial structure of rearrangement tasks tractable, but they usually do not fully capture the geometric constraints that determine which actions a robot can actually realize. These constraints are hard to express in the symbolic model. We propose REAP (Rearrangement with Elicited Action Preconditions), a framework in which a relational graph neural network heuristic is learned over a simple symbolic abstraction. A motion planner serves as a supervisor that elicits the hidden geometric preconditions of the problem during training. Deployed with greedy best-first search, the learned heuristic generalizes out-of-distribution along object count, plan length, and object arrangement, and can be trained jointly on several domains. Compared to classical heuristic search and learning-based baselines, REAP solves more problems, requires roughly an order of magnitude fewer motion-planner queries than comparable methods, and the action it ranks first is geometrically feasible in 94% of sampled states, against 22% for a random choice.

papers.title: How Much Can We Prune? Exploring the Performance Limits of Visual Token Pruning
papers.summary: Visual token pruning is increasingly used to reduce the memory and inference costs of vision-language models. Existing work has largely focused on designing method-specific selectors and demonstrating incremental improvements over prior methods at selected token budgets. It remains unclear whether the resulting performance reflects an inherent limit of visual token pruning or the limitations of current token-selection algorithms. We take a complementary perspective and ask: \emph{how well can visual token pruning perform when offline search cost is not the primary constraint?} We formulate pruning for general image understanding as selecting, under a fixed budget, one shared visual-token subset that supports a broad distribution of questions about an image. We approximate this utility with a finite auxiliary QA set generated by a frontier VLM and optimize a teacher-forced answer-probability objective with the evaluated model frozen. Motivated by the conceptual monotonicity and diminishing returns of adding visual evidence, we construct nested subsets greedily and introduce \emph{QA mini-batch greedy} (QA-MBG), which estimates token marginal gains from randomly sampled QA components at each step. Empirically, QA-MBG is both cheaper and more effective than full greedy. With one frontier-VLM call and approximately $0.5$ H100 GPU-hours per image, it produces a nested subset trajectory covering keep ratios up to $0.3$. Across Qwen3-VL-4B and Gemma~4 E4B on $900$ images from nine benchmarks, we find significant headroom over evaluated pruning baselines on held-out QA and image-grounded long-form generation, while the searched subsets substantially narrow the gap to full-token inference.

papers.title: LLM Evolutionary Search Strategies Should be Compared by Tokens
papers.summary: LLM evolutionary search is currently evaluated by counting proposals (candidate programs). We demonstrate this metric hides the true cost of search, and redo the comparison using tokens. By replaying 600 logged runs across 5 tasks and 3 methods, we show that proposal costs vary wildly from 16k to 39k tokens. In equal-proposal comparisons, this silently grants some methods up to 1.9x the compute of others, and gives evolution roughly 6x the budget of independent sampling. When we match token budgets, giving sampling six times more attempts, and remove scorer exploits, the evolutionary advantage largely vanishes. Evolution beats independent sampling by 5% or less on 12 of 15 task-method pairs, retaining a 23 to 28% margin on only 3, all on one task. A replication with Claude Haiku 4.5 reproduces this split, though a third backbone shows its size depends on the model too. The performance margin justifying these systems is often an accounting artifact. Reporting tokens, not proposals and not model calls, fixes this and costs nothing, as the logs already hold them.

papers.title: SituHOI: Scalable Capture of Scene-Situated Full-Body Human-Object Interaction
papers.summary: Modeling human-object interaction (HOI) in real environments requires jointly representing whole-body motion, manipulated objects, and scene geometry, yet existing datasets trade off scalable capture against structured, scene-aligned supervision. We introduce SituHOI, a large-scale RGB-D dataset containing 18,429 annotated clips across 16 indoor rooms and approximately 86 hours of quality-screened activity. It pairs recordings from a single moving RGB-D camera with static scene scans, object geometry, language descriptions, and estimated human and object trajectories. Using the scans as persistent references, our pipeline combines camera localization and depth-based metric alignment with human mesh recovery, object tracking, and temporal refinement to register all geometric annotations in a shared floor-aligned frame. These data support FlexHOI-Bench, a goal-conditioned joint motion prediction benchmark with variable observation and prediction durations. Given observed histories, scene and object geometry, and a terminal object pose, models predict future human and object motion. We provide SharedHOI as a reference predictor and evaluate world-space accuracy and human-object coordination. On a MoCap subset, our pipeline reduces human G-MPJPE from 195.4 to 68.3 mm and object translation error from 43.0 to 28.7 mm. SharedHOI leads four adapted baselines on all three aggregate FlexHOI-Bench metrics. Data will be released upon acceptance. An anonymized code repository is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/iclr2027-anonymous-code-1DFB.

papers.title: RL Teaches VLMs Where to Attend but Not How to Perceive
papers.summary: Although reinforcement learning (RL) effectively trains Vision-Language Model (VLM) agents, the mechanisms behind these capability gains are poorly understood. Across four diverse agent environments, we investigate whether the task-success gains from multi-turn RL are accompanied by improved grounded visual question answering about the environment. To assess this, we design environment-specific grounded VQA tasks that reveal improvements in grounded visual understanding. Representational probing shows that vision-encoder probe accuracy remains relatively stable, while LLM-layer probe accuracy improves. Attention analysis further reveals that LLM layers pay more attention to visual tokens during RL training. To test whether increased attention to visual tokens contributes to VQA gains, we introduce a lightweight plug-and-play intervention using a fixed attention bias. Without updating model parameters or computing gradients, this intervention partially restores VQA gains on the untrained model. These results reveal better utilization of visual information as a key mechanism behind the gains from RL.

papers.title: IWOO: Wave Optics Optimizer Improved with Hybrid Strategies for Numerical Optimization and Engineering Applications
papers.summary: The Wave Optics Optimizer (WOO) incorporates optical diffraction and interference into numerical optimization and has shown competitive performance in benchmarks and engineering applications. However, it can converge slowly, become trapped in local optima, and lose search effectiveness in later iterations. This paper proposes an Improved Wave Optics Optimizer (IWOO) that integrates four complementary strategies. First, a good point set and opposition-based learning are combined in GPS--OBL initialization to improve population quality and diversity. Second, an E-DM nonlinear perturbation mechanism is embedded in temporary triangle-based search to develop the TriEDM multi-path strategy and enhance search capability. Third, Correlation-Guided Groupwise Orthogonal Learning (CGOL) leverages relationships among decision variables to improve search efficiency while reducing computational overhead. Fourth, an adaptive stagnation-aware Runge--Kutta correction is introduced to mitigate premature convergence. IWOO is evaluated on the IEEE CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017 benchmark suites against representative and high-performing optimizers, with ablation studies assessing the contribution of each strategy. Within the representative algorithm group, IWOO achieves Friedman ranks of 1.8000, 1.5833, and 1.4483 on CEC2019, CEC2022, and CEC2017, respectively. Tests on six constrained engineering optimization problems further demonstrate its competitive accuracy, stability, and practical applicability.

papers.title: Agentic Interpretation: Harness-Governed Evidence Construction for Software Agents
papers.summary: Software agents answer behavioral questions about code, such as whether a patch passes tests or which lines caused a failure. These tasks require repository-wide evidence, yet most scaffolds leave intermediate findings in free-form trajectories, making them hard to reuse and easy to disconnect from final answers. We present Agentic Interpretation (AgInt), a framework for harness-governed evidence construction. The model proposes typed records, while a deterministic harness admits, grades, and persists them, reports unresolved requirements, and licenses answers under task-specific rules. The resulting certificate gives the model persistent external state and leaves an auditable decision record. Formally, append-only certificate states form a grounding lattice ordered by record inclusion, where each admitted record extends the state by union. We evaluate AgInt with four models on SWE-bench-Live and DeepSWE for patch acceptance and Defects4J and GitBug-Java for fault localization. AgInt outperforms the plain agent and Agentic Code Reasoning on all reported patch-acceptance metrics and ranks responsible lines higher while inspecting fewer irrelevant lines in fault localization. For GLM-5, reject-class F1 rises from 0.256 to 0.543 on SWE-bench-Live, All@1 rises from 0.140 to 0.400 on Defects4J, and wasted inspected lines fall from 31.5 to 11.7 on GitBug-Java. A matched-template control separates the mechanism: the persistent scaffold drives most fault-localization gains, while the certificate body and gate govern patch-acceptance calibration. With execution licensed, AgInt produces harness-reproduced witnesses for 293 of 475 null-dereference candidates versus 253 for a matched shell agent, and 62 of 117 resource-leak candidates versus 58. Across reported efficiency measurements, it uses 35% fewer executions and reduces cost per candidate by 59%.

papers.title: spora: A Unified Multimodal Dataset and Platform for Spatial Proteomics
papers.summary: Spatial proteomics (SP) captures the molecular composition and spatial organization of tissues at single-cell resolution, opening a direct view of the cellular ecosystems that drive disease. Protein panels, acquisition platforms, and tissue contexts differ from one cohort to the next, and a coherent picture of tissue biology can only emerge from models trained to bridge this heterogeneity. Foundation models offer the natural path forward, but their training depends on large, harmonized corpora that span platforms, panels, and cohorts. No public resource currently approaches that scale; available data sit in small, narrowly scoped releases with incompatible formats and conventions. We present $\texttt{spora}$, a large-scale multimodal SP dataset of 13,546 standardized multiplex images from 5,477 patients across 35 cohorts and five major SP technologies. Curated with biomedical experts, $\texttt{spora}$ provides model training-ready formats together with cell and tissue segmentations, structured clinical metadata, and, where available, paired H&E enabling the training of virtual staining models. It is complemented by $\texttt{spora [io]}$, a unified interface for tiling, sampling, and standardization across all cohorts and modalities, and $\texttt{spora [bench]}$, a benchmark suite spanning cell phenotyping, diagnostic and therapeutic prediction as well as virtual staining tasks across twelve cohorts that places current SP foundation models on common ground against task specific baselines.

papers.title: PACE: Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs
papers.summary: Native multimodal large language models (native MLLMs) jointly encode visual and linguistic sequences within a unified autoregressive Transformer, emerging as a promising paradigm for multimodal understanding. Unlike conventional ViT-based MLLMs relying on external vision encoders, ViT-free native MLLMs tokenize pixel patches directly, potentially suffering severe visual token redundancy. A pilot study confirms this: unlike ViT-based models that degrade under compression, ViT-free MLLMs tolerate aggressive compression with near-lossless or even improved performance. Yet existing compression methods target ViT-based settings, leaving native MLLMs, which stand to gain the most, unexplored. To close this gap, we introduce an analysis pipeline centered on token discriminability and cross-dimensional heterogeneous redundancy, revealing that (i) redundancy is distributed independently and heterogeneously along height and width axes, and (ii) early-layer visual tokens are indiscriminable and uniformly redundant. Guided by these findings, we propose PACE (Pareto-Adaptive Compression for Efficient Native MLLMs), the first visual token compression framework tailored for native MLLMs with Multimodal-RoPE. Leveraging dimensional decoupling of positional encoding, PACE decomposes attention into two orthogonal spatial saliency estimates along height and width, gated by a positional attention signal, yielding direction-aware importance with negligible overhead. It further casts token budget allocation as Pareto optimization over performance preservation, inference efficiency, and spatial coverage, jointly identifying optimal compression depths and retention ratios. Experiments show PACE maintains near-lossless performance at only 25%-50% visual token retention, even improving several benchmarks, while delivering over 2x FLOPs reduction.

papers.title: TWIN-MoE: Two-stage Intra-Expert Imputation Network for Incomplete Multimodal Learning
papers.summary: Recent Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) approaches address missing modalities either by routing each missingness pattern to a dedicated expert, which scales poorly as the number of modalities grows, or by imputing the missing modality from representations contributed by multiple experts, which requires a costly retrieval mechanism. We show that routing induces expert-conditioned representation neighborhoods and derive an imputation-error bound controlled by their local feature dispersion. When these expert-conditioned neighborhoods are more compact than the global representation space, intra-expert aggregation admits a tighter worst-case reconstruction bound than unconstrained global aggregation. Guided by this analysis, we propose TWIN, a two-stage intra-expert imputation framework. Pre-imputation generates a context-conditioned estimate in the encoder embedding space and radially soft-clips it using modality-specific statistics maintained in an observed FIFO queue, this ensures that the pre-imputed modality stays in empirically calibrated region of the target modality space. Post-imputation refines the missing representation after MoE by aggregating expert-conditioned observed representations within the same sample. Across four missing-modality benchmarks under natural, random, and asymmetric dropout protocols, TWIN achieves state-of-the-art performance while using substantially fewer parameters than competing MoE-based imputation methods.

papers.title: Analysis of Binary O-type Star Systems Using Recurrent Neural Networks
papers.summary: This work presents an initial analysis of the estimation of effective temperature and surface gravity for simulated O-type binary systems using a recurrent neural network. The proposed system uses 34 equivalent-width measurements from the optical region of a stellar spectrum. Two methods were applied to observed IACOB spectra before normalization: the addition of a blackbody continuum and the addition of a second observed spectrum. The first method produces only small differences in the normalized line profiles and in the estimated physical parameters over 3700-7000~\AA. In the second method, the secondary spectrum is added with contributions of 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, and 75 per cent, as defined relative to the original primary spectrum. The general comparison includes 192 simulated systems and 1152 modified spectra. For most of these spectra, the estimated effective temperature and surface gravity decrease as the contribution of the secondary component increases. Individual examples using HD14947, HD190429, HD48099, and HD206267 show that this behavior is not the same for every combination: some estimated effective temperatures fall below the estimates for both isolated spectra, and some surface gravity estimates increase. Comparisons with previously published values also depend on the physical parameter and reference considered. The results show that the proposed system is sensitive to the addition of a secondary spectrum, but do not establish a unique contribution for the secondary component of an observed binary.

papers.title: LLM Evolution in a Simple Simulated Market
papers.summary: Arguments that AI systems will evolve in harmful ways are largely made in the abstract. We provide a concrete empirical example. We simulate simple markets consisting of populations of twenty Large Language Model agents tasked with solving arithmetic problems. Agents differ only in their system prompt; those that go bankrupt are removed and replaced by mutated copies of the prompts of successful agents. Two market conditions select for opposite phenotypes: a market that rewards accuracy produces agents with high accuracy (94%) and high token use; a market that charges per token produces agents with low accuracy (10%) and low token use. In the second market, only tokens are incentivised yet we see a collapse in accuracy. Token use and accuracy are correlated traits such that selection on one also moves the other, and behaviour adapts along an unpriced dimension. A third neutral condition with no selection allows us to separate these effects from bias in the mutation operator. Adaptation occurs through a collective optimisation process that operates above the level of individual agents, who are never told the payment rule, do not receive feedback, and have no memory.

papers.title: Client-Aware Security Adaptive Early Exit Vision Transformers for Heterogeneous Federated Learning
papers.summary: Federated learning (FL) trains a shared model across data-owning clients without centralizing raw data, but client data difficulty and compute budgets can differ. We study local early-exit Vision Transformer (ViT) inference, where an intermediate classifier may return a prediction before the final Transformer stage. The proposed method replaces one global acceptance threshold with a client-specific base threshold from label entropy and shallow-exit confidence, then adjusts each input using predictive entropy, confidence, top-two class margin, and exit depth. Aggregation uses only clients that updated a parameter. Security-aware routing reaches 88.70% CIFAR-10 accuracy with 32.0% depth saving and 73.7% ImageNet-1K top-1 accuracy with 30\% saving. On matched six-client non-IID CIFAR-100, full-depth accuracy is 72.28% versus 68.20--71.80% for four heterogeneous-FL baselines; robustness-aware routing reaches 70.01% with 32.55% saving.

papers.title: The Window Is in the Reasoning: When LLM Agents Decide to Follow Prompt Injections
papers.summary: LLM agents that read untrusted content can be hijacked by prompt injections. Runtime monitors that try to catch a hijack before the agent acts, and benchmarks that score each task with a single run, share an assumption: whether an agent follows an injection is settled when the injection is read. We test this assumption with branching rollouts that replay an episode exactly up to the step at which the agent reads an injection and then resample the rest of the episode many times, splitting the outcome variance into a part fixed at read time and a part decided afterwards. Across four AgentDojo suites, a Qwen3 agent without thinking is largely decided at read time (0.91 of the outcome variance lies between states); with thinking on, this share drops to 0.62 (95% CI of the drop [-0.38, -0.22]), in the same direction for three attack templates and two success labels. How much is fixed at read time is a property of the model that the same measurement reveals, and thinking lowers the attack success rate of Qwen3 but raises it for two other models. Resampling from reasoning prefixes shows that the decision forms gradually as the agent reasons. Zero-shot chain-of-thought monitors built on cheaper models miss much of what is already decided, whereas stronger monitors, and a lookahead monitor that judges simulated next actions, come close to what the prefix determines. Finally, single-run labels of thinking agents disagree with a rerun up to 35% of the time, so benchmarks need repeated runs per task.

papers.title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
papers.summary: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

papers.title: OR-License: Evaluating LLM Agents as Real-World Operations Research Practitioners
papers.summary: Can large language model (LLM) agents deliver expert-level operations research (OR) solutions directly from original client materials, without prior expert reformulation? Existing OR benchmarks typically begin with self-contained descriptions or predefined optimization tasks, underrepresenting the translation of original business materials into professionally validated solutions. We introduce OR-License, an end-to-end benchmark of 31 instances across 10 industrial scenarios from paid OR engagements totaling USD 3.68 million. It preserves original requirements, input data, deliverable formats, and information boundaries after de-identification. To study information acquisition, we introduce ORSim, a controlled client simulator that discloses business facts without supplying OR expertise. Hidden evaluation checks feasibility and compares objective quality against original expert solutions accepted by clients before benchmark construction. Deployment-Adjusted Quality (DAQ) averages expert-relative quality across instances, assigning zero to infeasible deliveries. Across 11 frontier LLMs using coding-agent harnesses, several exceed the expert reference in conditional objective quality, but none matches its DAQ; the strongest primary Claude Code configuration achieves 88.39% strict feasibility and a DAQ of 0.87 against the expert reference of 1. Client information acquisition extends beyond clarification into solution development and validation, with some later stages showing higher confirmed issue-resolution proportions. Trajectory analysis identifies formulation and implementation failures, while task-equalized research-chain completion rates range from 24% to 45% across models on evaluable tasks. These findings motivate sustained information-gap resolution, faithful problem formulation, and evidence-linked self-improvement for reliable long-horizon agents.

papers.title: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
papers.summary: AI-assisted software development is evolving from interactive LLM assistance toward agentic systems that autonomously perform software engineering tasks, yet the effects of this shift remain insufficiently understood. We present an empirical study of 50 long-lived Java and Python open-source projects across three eras: pre-LLM, potentially LLM-assisted, and detected agentic development. Using snapshots from Software Heritage, we examine code similarity, software quality, and software evolution. Similarity is measured semantically through embedding-based cosine similarity and syntactically through CodeBLEU*. Quality is assessed with SonarQube metrics covering maintainability, complexity, reliability, and security. Evolution is characterized by annualized growth rates of LOC, functions, classes, files, and statements, and by commit activity in the three months preceding each snapshot. Results show no consistent evidence of increased similarity as semantic and syntactic similarity decreased significantly in Java for both the LLM and agentic eras relative to the pre-LLM era, while Python showed no significant differences. Software quality remained largely stable, although the agentic era showed significantly lower code-smell and SQALE index densities. Structural growth was generally lower in the agentic era, particularly for files, whereas development activity increased moderately in Java, especially in commits and added lines. These findings challenge the assumption that LLM- and agent-assisted development necessarily homogenizes code, degrades quality, or accelerates growth.

papers.title: BLANC: Adaptive Temporal Scheduling for Sign Language Production
papers.summary: Sign language production (SLP) aims to synthesize expressive signing motion from written text. Modeling signing motion presents two key temporal challenges. First, fine-grained hand articulations demand higher temporal resolution than relatively slower body movements. Second, signing events unfold over variable durations, calling for adaptive temporal scheduling during generation. To address these challenges, we first introduce a Multi-Rate Vector Quantizer (MRVQ), an articulation-decoupled motion tokenizer that represents the body and both hands as separate discrete streams at distinct temporal resolutions. Building on this representation, we propose BLANC (BLock-wise Adaptive diffusioN with Articulatory Clock), a gloss-free SLP framework that generates variable-duration motion blocks causally while denoising tokens in parallel within each block. At its core, a Latent Articulatory Clock (LAC) learns temporal structure from multi-scale motion-derived partitions to predict block durations and sequence termination during generation. We further introduce inference-time body-conditioned hand refinement to improve coordination across articulators. Extensive experiments on PHOENIX-2014T and CSL-Daily demonstrate that BLANC achieves state-of-the-art performance in sign language production.

papers.title: Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control for Stable Counterfactual Estimation under Donor Redundancy
papers.summary: Synthetic control methods estimate counterfactual outcomes by weighting untreated donor units to match a treated unit before treatment. In recent applications, however, the donor pool can be large, highly correlated, and short in pre-treatment history, yielding many near-equivalent solutions with unstable and difficult-to-interpret donor weights. We propose Graph-Regularized Synthetic Control (Graph-SC), a convex estimator that augments the classical pre-treatment matching objective with a graph Laplacian penalty. The graph encodes similarity among donor trajectories, encouraging coherent weights over structurally related donors while preserving the transparency of synthetic controls. We provide theoretical results characterizing the bias-variance tradeoff induced by graph regularization and establish efficient convergence guarantees with an accelerated proximal gradient method. Across a controlled simulation under donor redundancy, the California Proposition 99 benchmark, and observational counterfactual analyses on the Waymo Open Motion Dataset, Graph-SC improves weight stability, reduces sensitivity to redundant donor pools, and maintains competitive pre- and post-treatment accuracy relative to classical and regularized synthetic control baselines. Our results suggest that graph regularization is most valuable not as a universal accuracy booster, but as a principled mechanism for selecting stable and interpretable counterfactuals from near-equivalent synthetic controls with comparable pre-treatment fit.

papers.title: Prefix-Tuning for Arbitrary Output Sequences on Pretrained Transformers
papers.summary: Prefix-tuning is a parameter-efficient fine-tuning method for large language models (LLMs) that steers model outputs by prepending task-specific prefix representations to the input sequence. Despite its practical success, the theoretical understanding of the expressiveness of prefixes remains incomplete. In particular, the following question remains open: Given a pretrained autoregressive Transformer, for any input-output sequence pair $(\mathtt{x},\mathtt{y})$, does there always exist a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ such that prepending $\mathcal{S}$ to $\mathtt{x}$ induces the model to generate the target output $\mathtt{y}$? In this work, we prove that under the assumption that $\mathtt{y}$ is in the range of the pretrained Transformer, such a prefix $\mathcal{S}$ exists and can be explicitly computed by solving multiple linear systems. We further show that this assumption is necessary, in the sense that such a prefix may not exist when the assumption fails, thereby providing a complete answer to the above question. Our analysis is constructive and the obtained theoretical results hold under fairly general assumptions on model architecture. Extensive experiments on GPT-2 and Qwen3-4B demonstrate that our algorithm produces prefixes with strong control over model outputs.

papers.title: On the Selectivity of Generative Models in Structure-Based Drug Design
papers.summary: Designing small-molecule drugs that selectively bind to a target protein while avoiding unintended interactions with other proteins is essential for reducing side effects that contribute substantially to clinical attrition. Although structure-based drug design (SBDD) has advanced rapidly with deep learning, most generative models still optimize binding to a single target and disregard selectivity due to limited training data and unknown off-target interactions. Motivated by this gap, we introduce SELECTBENCH, a comprehensive benchmark assessing the selectivity of generative SBDD models. SELECTBENCH provides three curated evaluation tasks reflecting different real-world drug discovery scenarios: literature-based case studies, safety screening panels used in pharmaceutical development, and large-scale structure-based evaluation sets. We further introduce a suite of metrics to quantify selectivity and conduct a systematic evaluation of nine representative SBDD models, including methods explicitly trained for selectivity and widely-used inference-time guidance techniques. Our results show that even selectivity-trained models achieve only modest off-target discrimination and inference-time guidance provides limited gains, underscoring the need for method improvement. SELECTBENCH provides both a characterization of where current generative SBDD stands on selectivity and an open, extensible platform to accelerate progress. The benchmark is available at https://github.com/lovetaro/selectbench.

papers.title: The Weight of Teamwork: Does Communication Structure Help LLM Scientists Search for Scientific Laws?
papers.summary: Team performance is often reported as one delivered score, even though that score is produced in two stages: a system generates candidate answers and a selection rule returns one of them. We use symbolic regression as an observable scientific-search setting and compare fixed-budget LLM teams that differ in peer visibility and update timing, evaluating both their frozen candidate archives and the expressions selected from those archives. Distributing the call budget across more independent trajectories produced the largest measured gain, improving mean held-out fitting score Q by 0.70 at the widest tested allocation. Under a common archive-wide selector, the implemented Ring policy reduced mean Q by 0.33 relative to Independent, while Star and Complete remained unresolved. Holding the generated archives fixed, changing the delivery rule changed the measured architecture gaps, including the sign of the Complete point estimate. These results support reporting candidate generation and final selection as separate endpoints. They do not identify a communication mechanism or a universally preferred topology; rather, they show that an architecture ranking is not identified by communication structure alone when the rule that returns the final answer is left unspecified.

papers.title: From Spectrograms to Shallow Speech SSL: Audio-Frontend Design for Generator-Disjoint and Low-Latency Audio--Visual Deepfake Detection
papers.summary: Video-mediated conversational systems rely on synchronized speech and facial video, making audio--visual input integrity important for reliable perception. We study audio-frontend design in a fixed MRDF (Modality-Regularization-based DeepFake)-based pipeline with AV-HuBERT visual processing and an MSCT (multi-scale cross-modal transformer) fusion encoder. We compare spectrogram-style log-filterbank features with frozen wav2vec~2.0 and WavLM representations, dual-SSL fusion, executed depth, and shallow-layer aggregation. Across three training runs, full wav2vec~2.0 improves mean macro AUROC from $84.19\%$ to $87.19\%$ on generator-disjoint MMDF. Six-layer execution further improves detection, and learned non-uniform aggregation adds $2.53$ percentage points, reaching $90.61\%$. Shallow execution reduces measured inference latency relative to full-depth wav2vec~2.0 across the tested input durations; first-second evaluation reaches $86.85\%$ macro AUROC. In a single-run comparison, dual-SSL concatenation outperforms either single stream, while one-way cross-attention yields lower detection performance and higher latency than concatenation. Layer-weight analysis shows greater emphasis on early speech layers, while removing the selector's visual input has little effect on detection performance.

papers.title: lepidoptera: A Domain-Agnostic Engine for Causal Simulation with Mixed Variable Types, Vine Copula Dependence, and Individual-Level Counterfactual Propagation
papers.summary: lepidoptera is an open-source R and Python package for simulation from structural causal models with heterogeneous variable types. The package is built around a typed mechanism architecture, which separates the causal graph from the generating rule at each node and exposes each rule as an inspectable, serialisable object. A pre-built mechanism library covers all nine combinations of continuous, categorical, and ordinal parent and child types, removing the need for users to implement type-specific sampling from scratch. A vine copula mechanism estimates the full joint dependence structure from observed data using pair-copula constructions and the Rosenblatt conditional-simulation algorithm, supporting over twenty copula families. Individual-level counterfactual queries are supported through partial propagation, which freezes the random draws of unaffected nodes and replays only the downstream consequences of an intervention, thereby separating the individual treatment effect (ITE) estimand from the population-level average treatment effect (ATE) without additional model assumptions. An extension layer allows any pre-fitted predictive model to serve as a generative mechanism via a unified callable interface. Three worked illustrations spanning clinical trial planning, emergency-ward capacity analysis, and epidemiological mediation analysis demonstrate the package's scope.

papers.title: CoDA: A Human-LM Collaborative Codebook Development Assistant for Domain-Specific Text Annotation
papers.summary: We present CoDA, an open-source human-LM collaborative codebook development assistant that helps domain experts develop annotation guidelines for annotating new variables in unstructured text with language models. Existing language model annotation systems primarily focus on downstream classification performance, while assuming the availability of high-quality annotation guidelines, or codebooks. In practice, developing these codebooks is time-consuming and challenging, particularly for concepts that require expert knowledge. CoDA addresses this gap by collaborating with domain experts to iteratively develop codebooks through targeted review of incorrect language model predictions and incorporating expert feedback into the evolving codebook. We demonstrate CoDA on two real-world case studies: extracting health indicators from homelessness case management notes and classifying sentiment of wildlife trafficking posts on social media. Across both domains, CoDA produces codebooks that achieve downstream classification performance comparable to expert codebooks while reducing codebook development time from several weeks to two hours and requiring 5X fewer manually annotated examples. Applying CoDA to generate annotations at scale, we identified 2,410 case notes that contained health discussions or referrals and 10,196 social media posts expressing negative sentiment that may warrant investigation for potential wildlife trafficking. By accelerating codebook development, CoDA helps practitioners use language models to extract domain-specific insights from unstructured text at scale.

papers.title: Model Capacity Frontier: A Development Framework for LLM-Supported Social Simulation
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly incorporated into agent-based models (ABMs) on the premise that richer, context-sensitive human behavior can improve empirical fidelity. However, LLM-supported ABMs introduce an open-ended design space in which subtle modeling and configuration choices, such as prompt design and environment coupling, can substantially alter outcomes. Developing LLM-supported ABMs to simulate human collective behavior therefore requires navigating configuration sensitivity while identifying the limitations of the current model architecture. In this paper, we introduce the \textit{Model Capacity Frontier} (MCF), a framework that characterizes the empirical performance attainable by a specified architecture across its admissible configurations. In multi-objective settings, this capacity is represented by an estimated Pareto frontier obtained through systematic configuration exploration. We demonstrate MCF in crowd simulation of university commencement events with approximately 12,000 agents, using empirical movement data on temporal occupancy, spatial distribution, and flow direction. We first characterize the capacity of a conventional crowd model and then evaluate successive LLM-supported architectural extensions. In the process, MCF reveals which dimensions of attainable performance expand and which remain limited, providing empirical targets for refinement and re-evaluation. Initial LLM integration improves flow direction but degrades temporal occupancy and spatial distribution; subsequent architectural refinement of the LLM layer improves temporal occupancy and recovers spatial performance, while retaining much of the earlier gain in flow direction. Our case study shows how MCF guides the systematic architectural development of LLM-supported ABMs in configuration-sensitive, open-ended design spaces.

papers.title: Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree for Inference-time Search Under Sparse Reward
papers.summary: Tree-based samplers offer a compelling alternative for scalable inference-time search, bypassing the per-step reward and gradient dependencies that introduce systematic bias into SMC-style frameworks. Despite this advantage, contemporary tree samplers fail to achieve broad exploration. Their reliance on learned, DDPM-like transitions inherently couples neighbor states in a trajectory, thereby restricting child-parent feature divergence in the tree sampler. Consequently, these samplers suffer from restricted coverage of the target marginal distribution, severely hindering the exploration critical for efficient search under sparse reward. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a simple yet effective Bootstrap Stochastic Interpolant Tree (BSIT) sampler that decouples child node generation from explicit parent dependencies. By expanding the degrees of freedom during child node sampling, BSIT encourages diverse trajectory rollouts and unlocks broader path-space diversity-the exact catalyst needed for efficient exploration. Crucially, we show that BSIT's improved exploration accelerates convergence to the target distribution while achieving broader distributional coverage than samplers that rely on DDPM-like transitions for child-node generation, all without incurring additional function evaluations or reward feedback, thereby providing a highly efficient basis for rare target search. Extensive experiments across diverse search settings, including rare-species discovery and target-aligned molecule generation tasks, demonstrate BSIT's superior search efficiency over the baselines.

papers.title: Towards an Intelligent Decision Engine for Smart Contract Deployment
papers.summary: Layer 2 (L2) blockchain solutions emerged in recent years, predominantly in the Ethereum ecosystem, as a viable option for scaling a main blockchain network (L1). However, the selection of a L2 solution for deploying smart contracts backing blockchain applications is a decision that depends on many factors, such as costs, efficiency, popularity, and stability. We propose here a systematic methodology to help with this decision making process by using a set of relevant metrics and introducing user-defined profiles that capture different priorities among these metrics. We collect the major categories of smart contracts from a community-maintained data source, and we gather transactions for a six months period from three major L2 solutions: Arbitrum, Optimism, and Base. For each contract category and each blockchain, we compute a set of metrics and scores tailored to each user profile. By applying our methodology, we identify a clear bias in the classification, showing which L2 solutions are better suited for particular application types and user profiles.

papers.title: SWE-Bench Pro V2: A Cleaner, Harder-to-Game Coding Benchmark
papers.summary: SWE-Bench Pro is a widely used benchmark of long-horizon software engineering tasks for coding agents. As agents improve, they reach task issues earlier agents never touched and interact with the evaluation environment in ways the original harness did not anticipate. We present SWE-Bench Pro V2, a revised public split built to keep the benchmark accurate as capabilities advance. Agentic audits, expert adjudication and blind re-implementation repaired or retired 480 of the 731 tasks: 23 contracted engineers spent 404 hours, each working in a language they write professionally, and every revised instruction was verified by a second engineer solving the task from the text alone. A hardened protocol restricts network access to the model endpoint and re-grades every patch in a clean container, so agents cannot retrieve upstream fixes or get credit for changes outside their patch. On the 642 V2 tasks frontier agents resolve up to 99.4% while other systems stay clearly separated, and a 51-task Hard split spreads systems from 52.9% to 98.0%. We release the benchmark and distill lessons for maintaining agent benchmarks over time.

papers.title: Landmark-Free and Scale-Blind Multi-View Registration of Preoperative Liver Models to Intraoperative Surfaces
papers.summary: Augmented-reality guidance in laparoscopic liver resection requires aligning preoperative 3D liver models from CT/MRI with intraoperative surfaces. Monocular reconstruction in most cases cannot guarantee scale, albeit rigid-motion registration requires scale as an input. Our proposed framework ``SimCompose'' estimates the full similarity transformation $\Sim$, including scale, without relying on landmarks and applies the same transformation across multiple views with known relative geometry. However, reliable detection of registration failures remains challenging in surgical settings, where ground-truth alignment is generally unavailable. For this, we propose a geometry-based selector that evaluates candidate transformations without requiring ground truth. Large disagreement among these transformations is used to flag potentially unreliable registrations. Finally, we propose to use a non-rigid refinement based on a low-dimensional deformation model from Neo-Hookean simulations in the Simulation Open Framework Architecture (SOFA), without additional network training. SimCompose is trained exclusively on synthetic partial views. Its encoder processes point clouds normalised to a unit root-mean-square radius, without access to metric scale, and filters each view before multi-view fusion. Evaluation on unseen synthetic data (300 single-view pairs per run; 100 three-view registrations) shows that multi-view integration and candidate selection increase the success rate under stringent $\Sim$ accuracy criteria from 38.4% for a single-view, single-method configuration to 77%. Existing learning-based baselines do not satisfy these criteria even when provided with the exact scale. On five in-vivo patients with 92 keyframes, the rigid registration stage reduces surface error more than three-fold relative to learning-based baselines with external scale information.

papers.title: LoopHIL: Looping Hardware into LLM-assisted Agents for Wireless Embedded Systems
papers.summary: LLM agents are widely used for software development and debugging, but their adoption in embedded systems, especially for wireless tasks, remains limited. This is because embedded development requires hardware-in-the-loop testing. Agents cannot directly observe the spectrum, probe pins, or measure power, so they cannot verify wireless link functionality; currently, human engineers perform this verification. We systematically evaluate whether LLM agents can establish wireless links when provided with hardware access. We introduce LoopHIL, a framework that lets agents control a multi-device RF bench, monitor it with a spectrum analyzer, logic analyzer, and energy meter, and validate links against a verification ladder, all within code-enforced safety limits. Across four increasingly complex tasks, from generating a carrier to backscatter decoding by a commercial receiver, and using six models from two vendors, hardware-in-the-loop increases task completion rates from 54% to 79% and from 17% to 83% on the most challenging task. It also halves task time and output tokens. With debugging tools, agents decrease tag power consumption by up to 96%. However, small models often report unverified claims, so independent hardware checks remain necessary.

papers.title: Analyzing Repetition and Interference Effects in Memory-Constrained User Simulators
papers.summary: User simulators can help evaluate and train AI systems to interact with humans at scale. To do so, evaluation of user simulators must measure behavioral parity with people. We evaluate whether memory-constrained user simulators are sensitive to two factors known to affect human information retention: repetition of a fact and interference from competing information. We find that some simulators achieve human-like overall accuracy, and replicate the magnitude of repetition and interference effects, but none match people's accuracy on particular questions: while humans misremember facts, models forget them, leading to different error patterns. We release this data as a challenge benchmark for future work on user simulators.

papers.title: Who Plans, Who Edits? Verified, Cost-Aware Division of Labor for LLM-Driven Analog Layout Repair
papers.summary: Language-model agents can repair analog layouts when sign-off tools check every edit, but which model should plan a repair, which should edit it, and at what cost remain open questions. In our tool-grounded repair agent, models only choose bounded layout operators; sign-off tools rerun each task's contract checks after every edit, so failing layouts are never accepted. On layout-versus-schematic (LVS), design-rule checking (DRC), and post-layout repairs of three designs (a production high-voltage digital-to-analog converter (DAC), a 5-V oscillator, and a SKY130 operational transconductance amplifier (OTA)) with six tier-matched models from two vendors, 182 blind runs show that cheap models execute plans but rarely succeed alone (the cheapest model: 1 of 11 runs alone, 16 of 17 under a flagship planner; p < 0.001), cheap planners fail more often, and no fixed assignment is cheapest on every task. We propose a learning controller that selects models for each role and the escalation order from the first tool evaluation and updates Bayesian estimates after every attempt. With rules and initial estimates frozen before testing, the controller fixed 7 of 8 episodes on four sealed held-out tasks, matching the OpenAI flagship alone, at 15-40% of the flagship's spend per fix on three tasks but 8% higher spend overall. The cheapest mid-tier model alone fixed 6 of 8 at the lowest overall spend per fix but missed the hardest task. All 32 extracted DAC repairs match the human-guided LVS repair's integral nonlinearity (INL) within 0.005 least significant bits (LSB) at every code.

papers.title: Encoder-Free Multimodal LLMs Learn Implicit Encoders
papers.summary: We empirically analyze two recently proposed encoder-free multimodal LLMs, Gemma-4 12B and Inkling-Small. Unlike previous multimodal LLMs, these models do not use modality-specific encoders to extract tokenized embeddings representing audio and image input; instead, they directly feed windows of samples, pixels, or spectral features to the Transformer language model. We analyze whether the early layers of these models learn to function similarly to dedicated audio and visual encoders. We find that these early layers do in fact act as ``implicit encoders,'' encoding audio and visual inputs in a way that is largely invariant to their cross-modal context. Furthermore, when performing multimodal reasoning tasks, we show that independently encoding the modalities throughout these early model layers achieves the same accuracy as jointly encoding them from the first layer onwards. Finally, we use layer-wise probing to analyze the salient information captured by the implicit encoders and find their behavior to be similar to several popular encoder models.

papers.title: Towards Reinforcement Learning for Space Robotics: Fast Training and Reliable Real-World Transfer

papers.title: SPIDES: Information-Flow Control for Browser Agents
papers.summary: Browser agents automate complex workflows by reading and acting on arbitrary page content, but this flexibility exposes them to prompt injection attacks and unintended data exfiltration. Recent work argues that LLM-driven browser agents erode traditional web security boundaries such as the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) by acting across origins with the user's authority and no built-in isolation. We argue that restoring SOP is neither sufficient (a same-origin public sink can leak private data) nor necessary (legitimate tasks require authorized cross-origin flows) for protecting the security of users. We propose SPIDES, which instead enforces information-flow control by gating primitive browser actions such as typing, clicking and navigating on labels propagated from element-level HTML confidentiality and integrity annotations. Untrusted and confidential content is masked from the agent's context, while policies block unauthorized flows, providing security guarantees against both prompt injection and data exfiltration that hold independently of the model driving the agent. To evaluate SPIDES and baseline defenses under a common threat model, we build MicroNet, a closed ecosystem of 28 interlinked websites with element-level ground-truth labels and paired benign/adversarial tasks. SPIDES achieves 0% attack success rate by design while retaining high task completion rate and autonomy. Our findings demonstrate that information-flow control is an effective technique to extend web security to browser agents, gaining on autonomy and utility against state-of-the-art baselines. The source code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/SPIDES.

papers.title: Unbounded Losses, Unchecked Inputs: Measuring the Safeguards of LLM Options-Trading Agents
papers.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now place options orders at retail brokers, and developers publish open-source options agents faster than anyone has examined them. Prior security work on trading agents scored academic equities designs by whether an attacker can flip a buy-or-sell decision. We present the first measurement of the options agents that brokers and developers ship, scored by the safeguards they enforce and by the worst loss their documented order paths can reach. We screened 765 GitHub repositories, broker documentation, and the research literature and found 215 eligible repositories and 8 broker-native agent interfaces. We then scored 26 systems, including every broker interface and every open-source project with at least 20 stars, on seven robustness and eleven security safeguards with cell-level evidence. The ecosystem is new: 198 of the 215 repositories were created in 2026, and 129 (60.0%) appeared in the two weeks around one options-trading hackathon. Of the 22 systems that can place orders, 10 enforce a pre-trade limit outside the model, yet none of the 26 authenticate their text sources or cross-check market data. Of the 26, 17 can execute with no mandatory human step and 13 can reach unbounded loss, including 6 of the 8 broker interfaces. Because an attacker who writes the agent's inputs can move an order's strike, expiry, volatility, and legs while its direction stays correct, options agents need loss limits enforced at the order boundary.

papers.title: Learning Administrative Boundary-Aware Location Encoders via Reverse Geocoding
papers.summary: Location encoders learn compact representations of latitude--longitude coordinates for downstream geospatial prediction tasks. Existing approaches are pretrained using continuous or naturally occurring supervision, such as imagery, climate variables, or species distributions, and therefore do not explicitly capture administrative boundaries or place names, despite their strong influence on many real-world geospatial phenomena. We introduce, to our knowledge, the first method for learning administrative boundary-aware location encoders, using reverse-geocoded text as a self-supervised training signal. Our approach can be applied to existing location encoder architectures and consistently improves their downstream performance. We further introduce RevGeoRQ, a custom architecture tailored to reverse-geocoding supervision, which yields additional gains and exceeds contemporary location encoders on several downstream tasks. Finally, the use of human-interpretable reverse-geocoded strings and residual-quantized semantic IDs provides a more interpretable representation of geographic location than existing approaches. Code and model weights to be released soon.

papers.title: RATION: Towards Quantitative Risk-Based Access Control for AI Agents
papers.summary: AI agents increasingly interact with external environments to complete complex user tasks. These interactions can lead to unexpected behavior and expose agents to security threats such as indirect prompt injection. Current agent security systems largely protect agents by restricting their actions, which can result in a substantial security-utility trade-off for complex, open-ended tasks. To address this, we propose a quantitative risk-based approach to access control for AI agents that regulates measurable risks accumulated during task execution. As a concrete realization of this approach, we introduce RATION, a security framework that tracks measurable risks associated with agent actions and enforces quantitative constraints throughout execution. RATION first constructs a task-specific policy by combining explicit constraints derived from the user request with implicit risks calibrated from historical executions of similar tasks. During task execution, RATION continuously tracks the accumulated risks and applies different enforcement strategies depending on the type of risk. Extensive experiments on four security benchmarks show that RATION provides strong security while maintaining high task utility across diverse models and environments.

papers.title: Indirect Influences of Artificial Intelligence Advice on Complex Sepsis Treatment Decisions
papers.summary: Sepsis is a major public health concern, and many sepsis patients die due to ineffective hemodynamic management. Artificial intelligence could support hemodynamic decisions, particularly in complex cases where conflicting information and comorbidities drive uncertainty and practice variation. However, these systems' real-world value depends on not just accuracy, but how they influence the quality of clinician decisions. We first retrospectively evaluated an AI system's recommendations in 6,928 sepsis patients, finding that they improved upon the original providers' decisions overall but had significantly worse performance in complex cases. We then conducted a pre-registered experiment with 228 US critical care physicians to test their use of this imperfect advice in six complex treatment decisions, using one of three advice types designed to vary reasoning autonomy. Participants given simple model recommendations overcame poor advice, choosing optimal treatments in 56.3% of decisions compared to 31.8% if they had always followed the recommendations. They also made significantly better decisions than those receiving a less prescriptive advice type (42.9%). Physicians selectively adapted and improved weak advice, likely because it prompted them to reconsider their assessment. Our findings suggest that improving sepsis care decisions with AI may require accounting for these indirect influences resulting from human-AI collaborative reasoning.

papers.title: Morpheus-2.0: Multiscale Probabilistic Forecasting with Dual-Axis Attention
papers.summary: A universal forecaster is trained once and applied everywhere, so it must serve tasks whose schemas, forecast horizons, and temporal resolutions all differ. The number of targets and covariates changes from dataset to dataset, horizons vary by orders of magnitude, and sampling rates range from seconds to years. Existing time-series foundation models address these only in part, since they isolate each series or visit the two grid relations in separate blocks, and they fix the horizon and resolution before training begins. We introduce Morpheus-2.0, a compact encoder-only foundation model that represents targets and covariates on a single variable-time grid. Its dual-axis attention runs both relations side by side in every layer, one across variables at a timestep and one across time within a variable; a learned gate weights the two per layer, and an axis-aware rotary encoding preserves both grid coordinates. The forecast length is sampled during training, so one set of weights spans short to long horizons at no additional inference cost. Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale extends the model to several temporal resolutions at once, weighting them according to the series being forecast. Across GIFT-Eval, which spans several domains and frequencies, the two models give complementary operating points: Morpheus-2.0 attains 0.685 relative MASE with 81M parameters, while the larger Morpheus-2.0 Multiscale attains 0.646 relative MASE and 0.455 relative CRPS, the lowest of any published system on both metrics.

papers.title: VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research
papers.summary: Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self-authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the generated program and its checks share omissions or misinterpretations of task requirements, alongside incomplete verification coverage and ineffective optimization strategies. We propose VERAS, a verification-guided adaptive search harness for reliable OR that uses verification evidence to prioritize feasibility repair, constraint-coverage review, and solution-quality improvement. VERAS combines task-specific solution checkers with a separate verification agent to examine candidate solutions against the task requirements. It uses verification feedback to guide feasibility repair, additional constraint checking, and objective improvement, while candidate acceptance criteria screen revisions for deterioration in output validity or constraint satisfaction. On ORAgentBench, VERAS achieves a 42.99% pass rate, exceeding the reported 35.51% of Codex using the same LLM. Across two industrial-scale OR problems, VERAS reduces inter-datacenter peak bandwidth by 10.34% relative to native Codex and lowers annualized distribution network planning costs by 6.28% compared with expert-designed solutions. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/holimario/VERAS.

papers.title: What Matters for NVFP4 Training? A Comparative Study of Low-Precision Pretraining Recipes
papers.summary: Training large language models directly in 4-bit floating-point (FP) formats promises substantial improvements in throughput and energy efficiency. While some recipe design choices have been validated at scale, many promising approaches remain untested beyond small models and short token horizons, leaving open the question of which trends will hold. We present a systematic comparison of recent NVFP4 recipes at medium model scale, evaluating dense 8B and 30B-A3B MoE models trained for up to 1T tokens, with a focus on which ingredients are necessary for accuracy recovery. We propose a final recipe grounded in the principles behind established stable NVFP4 training at scale, incorporating state-of-the-art techniques such as unbiased gradient estimation with lower quantization error than stochastic rounding. To the best of our knowledge, this is the strongest FP4 training result demonstrated at this scale to date in loss gap to BF16. Through ablation studies, we find that: (i) each technique in the optimized recipe measurably improves loss trajectory, (ii) selective high-precision layers are necessary for recovering accuracy at scale, (iii) not all tensors in the backward pass benefit equally from de-biasing, leaving room to apply complementary error-reduction techniques to the remaining tensors.

papers.title: Koi: Evidence-Guided, Self-Calibrating Planning for Multi-Cloud, Heterogeneous LLM Inference Fleets
papers.summary: Deploying a large language model (LLM) requires choosing the right accelerator, parallelization strategy, engine configuration, and replica count amongst ~140 other variables across clouds, regions, and markets. These decisions are intertwined, and the best cluster-wide plan continually changes as jobs contend for shared capacity on shifting workloads. We present Koi, a self-calibrating cluster planner for heterogeneous, multi-cloud fleets. Koi uses a Recursive Language Model (RLM) hierarchy to propose hypotheses and reason over deployment while deterministic components predict serving behavior, score candidates, and control placement. It represents inference behavior as a fixed causal graph linking decisions (e.g., accelerator, parallelism), runtime mediators (e.g., KV-cache pressure, communication overhead), and outcomes (e.g., latency, throughput). Each deployment strengthens or weakens scoped causal relationships, building a comprehensive playbook for inference that the planner employs to guide future decisions. Job-wise configurations are composed into cluster-wide plans and evaluated against serving objectives, resource constraints, SLO risks, and cost. Across benchmarks, Koi achieves 1.18x greater goodput than the strongest baseline while reducing $/token by 20% in a real heterogeneous cluster. Ablations isolate the contribution of Koi's architecture: a pure language model attains a composite score of 35.3, the same model equipped with Koi's deterministic tools reaches 51.6, and the full Koi planner reaches 70.8.

papers.title: Tactix: Towards a Programmable Strategy Interface for Flexible SAT Solving
papers.summary: Modern SAT solvers combine a rich repertoire of proof rules with sophisticated strategies that determine when and how to apply them. Often, the internal implementations are tightly coupled to particular strategies, making it inconvenient to define new strategies without changing solver internals. We present Tactix, a proof-producing sequential CDCL solver that incorporates a wide range of techniques in state-of-the-art solvers with a clean separation of proof rules from solving strategies. This separation enables a public interface through which users can invoke particular techniques, observe their effects, and program a wide range of solving strategies. The default strategy of Tactix is programmable over this interface and outperforms state-of-the-art solvers on benchmarks from the 2024--2026 SAT Competitions. We also use the interface to develop novel strategies tailored to challenging benchmarks from two application domains, which led to performance gains over strong baselines. We intend Tactix to serve as an infrastructure for designing and evaluating novel solving strategies. Finally, we also present a self-study of the AI-assisted development process behind Tactix.

papers.title: ZeroDSS: Semantic Segmentation from Class Names Alone
papers.summary: Semantic segmentation depends heavily on real images with pixel-level annotations, making dense supervision a major obstacle to deployment in new domains. We study task-specific data-free semantic segmentation, where training uses generic pretrained generative priors but has access to no target-domain images, masks, or captions--only a predefined category set. We introduce Zero-Data Semantic Segmentation (ZeroDSS), a feedback-driven approach that treats synthetic supervision as an adaptively controllable training distribution rather than a direct surrogate for real data. ZeroDSS constructs a semantically structured prompt distribution through LLM-guided compositional generation and adaptive class rebalancing, then converts the prompts into image-mask pairs using diffusion attention. Its feedback-driven distribution refinement consists of a two-phase closed-loop training procedure with a single loop-back step. In Phase I, a segmenter is trained using confidence-weighted supervision and dual-scale consistency. In Phase II, model feedback is used to adaptively target underperforming categories and refine diffusion-derived masks using model predictions. After this refined initial training, a teacher-student framework is utilized in the final phase to iteratively improve the fused supervision and segmenter through exponential moving average (EMA) updates. Using synthetic training data only, ZeroDSS achieves 35.0% mIoU on MS COCO with DeepLabV3, and 66.3% and 63.5% mIoU on PASCAL VOC with DeepLabV3 and Mask2Former, respectively. These results show that explicitly constructing and iteratively refining the synthetic supervision distribution can substantially reduce the synthetic-to-real gap in dense prediction.

papers.title: Long Listening Thoughts: Eliciting Open Auditory Reasoning with Deliberative Perception and Cognitive Refinement
papers.summary: We introduce Long Listening Thoughts (LLT), a framework for constructing post-training datasets that improves audio reasoning by pairing deliberate perceptual grounding with explicit cognitive behaviors. On audio understanding and reasoning benchmarks, large audio-language models (LALMs) are limited primarily by perceptual errors, yet existing post-training datasets rely on audio descriptions of limited diversity. Through a four-stage pipeline, LLT (1) builds multi-aspect dense audio descriptions spanning semantic, acoustic, and temporal information, (2) generates more challenging questions, (3) synthesizes incorrect reasoning traces, and (4) extends short reasoning traces into long ones via a thought-continuation strategy that elicits cognitive behaviors such as verification and backtracking. Using LLT, we synthesize 1.6M reasoning traces and train Qwen2.5-Omni-7B with a two-stage pipeline of supervised fine-tuning (SFT) followed by direct preference optimization (DPO). This improves accuracy on MMAU Test-mini (71.5 to 78.2), MMAR (56.7 to 63.7), and MMSU (60.6 to 66.0).

papers.title: When Opposite Premises Translate Identically: A Source-Conditioned Diagnostic for Multilingual Commonsense Items
papers.summary: Multilingual reasoning comparisons depend on translated premises preserving the relations in their English sources. Automatic translation scores can rank source-target pairs, but an acceptance decision alone cannot certify a counterfactual benchmark field. We test a source-contrast diagnostic for ACCORD premises: reverse the English polarity, translate both arms independently, count identical target outputs, and score each arm against its own source. Across 71 matched question identities at two containing-item depths, five target languages, and three translation checkpoints, Swahili has 63, 113, and 67 exact collisions among 710 pairs per checkpoint. At a human-reference-calibrated threshold, round-trip NLI passes both arms of 3 of the 113 NLLB-3.3B collisions, while LaBSE passes 78. Each collision proves at least one unfaithful translation, but does not identify its arm. These controlled measurements do not establish screening accuracy on spontaneous translation errors or a language-by-hop reasoning effect; the study has no native equivalence labels or answer-model evaluation.

papers.title: Do 3D Large Language Models Really Use 3D Evidence?
papers.summary: Recent 3D Large Language Models (3D-LLMs) have shown strong performance on scene question answering with extensive post-training. Yet, existing benchmarks rarely evaluate how 3D-LLMs respond to referential ambiguity, insufficient scene evidence, or false presuppositions, obscuring whether their responses are grounded in 3D evidence. In this work, we introduce UNICORNS, a benchmark for evaluating the reliability of 3D-LLM responses across four evidence conditions. UNICORNS contains 11,387 questions across 557 ScanNet scans, covering eight challenge categories alongside answerable controls. A response passes only if it satisfies the required response behavior and contains no scene claim unsupported by the available evidence. Evaluation of six open-sourced 3D-LLMs reveals a pronounced performance gap: even the strongest zero-shot model achieves 61.22% accuracy on answerable controls, but only 40.94% across the eight challenge categories. To address this gap, we further propose HORN, an obligation-aware post-training method combining group-relative task rewards, leaf-conditioned obligation rewards, and supervised control replay. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HORN reaches $75.1 \pm 1.0\%$ across the challenge categories and $77.2 \pm 0.8\%$ overall, outperforming all baselines without degrading answerable-control accuracy. Our findings enable a systematic evaluation and improvement of evidence-grounded 3D reasoning for 3D-LLMs (code: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/unicorns-6B38/).

papers.title: HumanSkill-4D: Training-Free Language Querying of Animatable Gaussian Avatars in Space and Time
papers.summary: We introduce avatar referring segmentation, which selects regions of animatable Gaussian avatars from language queries. A query can also specify a pose or motion to select matching intervals. This lets users interact with avatars for local editing and motion inspection. However, making these selections with existing language Gaussian splatting methods poses two challenges: adjacent parts and garments are hard to separate and may be referred to indirectly (region ambiguity), while fine-grained motions can look alike in RGB (motion ambiguity). We address these challenges with HumanSkill-4D, a training-free framework that shares a multimodal large language model (MLLM) and geometric operators across avatars. For each avatar, a semantic memory links body-part and garment categories to persistent Gaussian regions and appearance descriptions. The MLLM uses category names and descriptions to select categories by appearance, relation, or function. To find matching intervals, it composes operators into programs that check query conditions on driving joint trajectories stored in a motion memory. These category choices and operator outputs make selections traceable, while composing or adding operators supports new motion conditions. To evaluate this task, we introduce three human-annotated benchmarks and show that HumanSkill-4D outperforms the baselines in part segmentation and 3D and 4D referring segmentation, with compact memories and only minutes of setup per avatar.

papers.title: Tree Plurality Veto: Voting in Few Rounds with Efficient Communication and Low Metric Distortion
papers.summary: We consider the metric distortion framework for voting, where $n$ voters and $m$ candidates are embedded in an unknown metric space. A voting rule selects a candidate using only voters' ordinal preferences, and its distortion is the worst-case ratio between the social cost of the selected candidate and the minimum social cost. We study how round complexity trades off against total communication in deterministic voting protocols with low distortion. Deterministic rules can achieve the optimal distortion of $3$ in one round by eliciting complete rankings using $\Theta(nm\log m)$ bits, while a direct sequential implementation of PluralityVeto achieves the same distortion using only $O(n\log m)$ bits but requires $\Theta(n)$ rounds. Our main result is TreePluralityVeto, a deterministic voting protocol that, for every $r\ge 2$, achieves distortion at most $2r-1$ using at most $r$ rounds and $O(n\log m+n s^{1/(r-1)}\log s)$ bits of total communication, where $s = \min\{n, m\}$. The protocol runs PluralityVeto on a hierarchical partition of the voters, collecting restricted rankings in parallel at each level. The branching factor controls the tradeoff between rounds and communication, and a matching-based analysis shows that each level increases the distortion bound by at most $2$.

papers.title: SENTRY: A Streaming Edge Network Trust Engine for Real-Time Audio Deepfake Detection
papers.summary: Real-time voice cloning has enabled large-scale streaming deepfake and vishing attacks, while existing Network Detection and Response (NDR) solutions rely on GPU-based post-processing that requires buffered audio and generalizes poorly to unseen speech synthesis models. This paper presents SENTRY, a hardware-oriented, streaming trust engine for inline deepfake detection at the network edge. SENTRY employs an integer lifting-wavelet front end together with a bank of multiplier-free transforms, including wavelet-packet envelopes, Walsh-Hadamard sequency profiles, waveform micro-statistics, and long-term spectral features, designed so that acoustic analysis needs only integer add, shift, compare and bitwise operations. A supervised gradient-boosted tree classifier is combined with an unsupervised Mahalanobis out-of-distribution detector trained solely on authentic speech, and their outputs are fused by a lightweight logistic layer to produce graduated LOG, CHALLENGE, or DROP actions. Under a closed-set protocol, SENTRY reaches 98.75% accuracy at a 1.25% equal-error rate (EER) on WaveFake, with perfect separation of HiFi-GAN and WaveGlow; its supervised track alone achieves an AUC of 0.9994 (fused: 0.9993). On ASVspoof 2019 LA (attacks A01-A06) over an 8 kHz mu-law telephony channel, it reaches 94.75% accuracy at a 5.05% EER, with a supervised-track AUC of 0.9948 (fused: 0.9884) and per-attack EERs below 7%. In our prototype, the feature front end runs as bit-exact integer code on one Arm Cortex-A53 core, and the classifier and fusion stage are synthesized for a Xilinx Zynq UltraScale+ MPSoC using no DSP slices, returning a decision 220 ns after a feature vector is ready. These results indicate that deepfake screening can be placed inline without GPUs or floating-point hardware; generalization to unseen generators is left to future work.
