papers.title: Fabric retrofit scenario analysis under uncertainty for an urban housing stock using machine learning
papers.summary: Fabric retrofit is central to decarbonising housing, and planning it depends on expected savings and their uncertainty. This study asks which upgrade saves most per dwelling and across a housing portfolio, how uncertain the savings are, and whether upgrade order matters. We propose an uncertainty-aware framework that converts predicted changes in energy performance certificate scores after wall, roof and window upgrades into standardised energy-cost savings and emission reductions. Six machine-learning models predict the 1-100 Standard Assessment Procedure (SAP) energy-cost and environmental impact (EI) emission scores from 17 certificate descriptors. Each model's errors on similar dwellings give calibrated prediction intervals. A global-best strategy applies the most accurate model throughout; a sample-specific strategy chooses each dwelling's model using these local errors. The analysis covers 103,414 officially registered dwellings in Westminster, London. CatBoost was the global-best model, with mean absolute errors of 3.487 SAP and 4.379 EI points on held-out dwellings. Both strategies projected similar savings; under global-best, roof insulation saved most per dwelling, GBP 203 annually (uncertainty range 176-229), and wall insulation most across the portfolio, GBP 6.09 million annually (uncertainty range 5.69-6.72). For 5,382 dwellings needing all three upgrades, every order delivered the same final package, yet installing roofs, walls, then windows a year apart accumulated 54% more projected cost savings over three years than the reverse order. Emission reductions followed the same pattern. Using only certificate data, the framework helps local authorities rank measures for dwellings and portfolios and sequence upgrades to bring savings forward.

papers.title: SIESTA-QCOMP: Bridging Classical and Quantum Computing for Strongly Correlated Systems
papers.summary: Density Functional Theory (DFT) is the established workhorse of computational materials science, yet it faces fundamental challenges with strongly correlated electrons, such as in transition metal complexes and bond-breaking processes. While quantum computing offers a theoretically exact path to resolve these problems, current hardware limitations prohibit fully quantum simulations of realistic material systems. To bridge this gap, we present SIESTA-QCOMP, a modular suite embedding quantum methodologies within DFT. Harnessing SIESTA's localised basis set, we implement a projection-based embedding scheme that treats the bulk environment classically while mapping the strongly correlated "impurity" subspace to a quantum processor. The architecture uses a socket-based driver to orchestrate workflows between the Fortran-based SIESTA engine and Python-based frameworks like Qiskit, ensuring high interoperability. We detail the hybrid workflow, currently utilising a Variational Quantum Eigensolver (VQE), and discuss the road map toward methods such as Sample-based Quantum Diagonalisation (SQD). We illustrate the framework on an hypothetical iron porphyrin calculation and argue that such hybrid architectures are not merely interim solutions but essential foundations for integrating quantum utility into materials design, as envisioned by our broader QCOMP4DFT initiative.

papers.title: UDL-RT: A unified differentiable all-sky microwave radiative transfer model with learnable parameterizations
papers.summary: Radiance-based retrievals and data assimilation require radiative transfer models (RTMs) to simulate radiances and quantify their sensitivities to atmospheric and surface conditions. Conventional RTMs often rely on separately maintained forward, tangent-linear, and adjoint codes, complicating model development and extension. Here, we present the Unified Differentiable and Learnable Radiative Transfer model (UDL-RT), a PyTorch-based framework for all-sky microwave radiative transfer that couples neural-network (NN) parameterizations of gaseous absorption, hydrometeor bulk scattering properties (BSPs), and ocean surface emissivity with an explicit radiative transfer solver in a unified differentiable computational graph. Automatic differentiation directly computes Jacobians with respect to input variables, reducing the model maintenance burden. The NN parameterizations offer flexible representations of complex nonlinear relationships. For example, the NN gas-absorption parameterization reduces the standard deviation of brightness-temperature (TB) errors by approximately 60-85% in the water-vapour channels compared with linear regression. Moreover, UDL-RT propagates loss gradients to trainable parameters to optimize physical parameterizations against observations, with GPU-accelerated batched computation supporting efficient iterative learning. Using Microwave Humidity Sounder-2 (MWHS-2) observations, we optimize the snow BSP parameterization through gradient-based learning. The optimized parameterization improves agreement between simulated and observed TB distributions and reduces the systematic bias and skewness of observation-minus-background (O-B) departures. Overall, UDL-RT integrates radiance simulation, sensitivity analysis, and parameterization optimization within a unified framework, supporting future remote sensing retrieval and data assimilation applications.

papers.title: Rovibrational dynamics in strongly-coupled gas-phase methane
papers.summary: Polaritons, the hybrid light-matter states formed when molecular transitions are strongly coupled to an optical cavity mode, appear to alter chemical dynamics, reactivity, and photophysics, though the mechanisms and reproducibility of these effects remain hotly debated. Nearly all reports in polariton chemistry rest on spectroscopic measurements of optical cavity transmission. Interpretation of these experiments therefore relies on understanding the linear and nonlinear spectroscopy of strongly-coupled systems. Working in the gas phase can dramatically simplify spectroscopic observables, as the intermolecular and environmental interactions that complicate the response of condensed-phase systems can be minimized. Our prior work introduced a platform for gas-phase molecular polaritons and demonstrated that linear cavity transmission spectra in the strong coupling regime are well described with classical Fabry-P\'erot cavity physics. Here, we extend this platform to the nonlinear spectroscopy of cavity-coupled rovibrational transitions of methane. We monitor transient changes in the cavity transmission spectrum following optical pumping of intracavity molecules via an axis orthogonal to the longitudinal cavity axis. We find that the classical Fabry-P\'erot cavity treatment quantitatively reproduces our transient spectra and allows for extraction of the collisional relaxation and transport timescales of intracavity molecules. We observe no difference in the dynamics of strongly-coupled methane versus free-space, non-cavity control experiments. This effort connects our gas-phase work to the much larger body of transient condensed-phase polariton spectroscopy and represents a step towards predictive understanding of molecular dynamics under strong coupling.

papers.title: Transient growth and Counter-propagating Rossby Waves in a sloped Eady problem
papers.summary: A mechanistic interpretation for baroclinic normal mode instability with exponential growth is the interaction arising from Counter-propagating Rossby Waves (CRWs), where pairs of CRWs phase-lock and interfere constructively. On the other hand, an arbitrary initial condition can lead to finite transient growth as long as there is constructive interference. The present work investigates the characteristics of finite time transient instabilities and its description in terms of CRWs in a baroclinic system with asymmetric interaction, in contrast to usual settings where there is an inherent symmetry that leads to equal and opposite CRWs. A sloped Eady problem on a $f$-plane is considered here, which has the benefit that there are only two CRWs in the system, and the presence of a bottom topographic slope can be formulated in a such a way that only one of the CRW is affected and controlled by a single parameter representing the asymmetry, via modifying the bottom background potential vorticity gradient. We derive conditions where the instantaneous growths have key CRW properties that are independent of the asymmetry parameter for a reasonably general family of norms, and that the instability characteristic in the total energy norm is entirely independent of the asymmetry parameter. For finite time transient growth, the optimal initial condition is in some sense counter to that of the exponential growing normal mode: where the bottom slope is such that it is strengthening the bottom CRW, the normal mode has a larger bottom CRW, but the finite time optimal initial condition wants the bottom CRW to be weak instead, and vice-versa. While the results presented here are for the sloped Eady problem, the same results were also found for an analogous Phillips problem, and we speculate the instability characteristics may have origins in the underlying symmetries that are common to those two problems.

papers.title: Charge-Selective Displacement of Spatiotemporal Optical Vortices at a Spatially Uniform Time Boundary
papers.summary: At a spatially uniform, in-plane-isotropic time boundary, the transverse displacement of a spatiotemporal optical vortex changes sign with its topological charge, despite a charge-independent conversion weight. Radial spectral filtering couples to the vortex phase while preserving identical converted spectral intensities for opposite charges. For a narrow scalar Gaussian spectrum, the displacement follows the logarithmic slope of the spectral weight and occurs with zero mean transverse momentum. In a finite pumped GaAs waveguide, unequal attenuation during extraction adds angular deflection. Independent Maxwell--Drude simulations test this extraction-induced response and give $\pm42$~mrad before detector filtering. Calculated centroid traces at multiple planes separate propagation-induced drift from position offsets.

papers.title: Realization of valley-controlled orbital angular momentum via inter-orbital coupling
papers.summary: Orbital angular momentum (OAM) represents a fundamental degree of freedom (DoF) for understanding novel phenomena in solids and synthetic lattices. However, the generation and control of OAM in lattice systems remain challenging. Here, we experimentally observe valley-controlled OAM states in inversion-symmetry-broken photonic honeycomb lattices consisting of s- and higher-orbital sublattices. These OAM states manifest as chiral vortex arrays in real space. By selectively exciting s-orbital modes carrying no initial OAM at either the K or K' valley, we observe higher-orbital OAM modes generated via inter-orbital coupling in neighboring sites. Specifically, s-p orbital coupling generates OAM states with topological charge l=+1 or l=-1, while s-d orbital coupling yields higher-charge OAM states with l=+2 or l=-2. The sign of the topological charge is determined by the valley DoF, enabling deterministic control of vortex chirality across the entire array. Our theory further reveals that a local vortex-chirality symmetry enforces the valley-dependent selection of vortex chirality at the K and K' valleys, establishing a direct connection between the valley DoF and real-space vortex chirality. These results establish a versatile platform for engineering chiral vortex arrays via orbital physics and exploring orbital- and topology-mediated phenomena in photonic systems and beyond.

papers.title: Boosting fluorescence and polarization with nanophotonics for single-molecule chiral sensing
papers.summary: Detecting chirality is essential in chemistry and biomedicine. Circular dichroism identifies chiral molecules through their differential absorption of circularly polarized light. However, its sensitivity is limited by vanishing absorption at low concentrations. Fluorescence-based methods have already enabled other optical techniques to reach the single-molecule limit and could, in principle, also extend chiral detection to reach this sensitivity regime. They are marred, however, by the combination of weak fluorescence signals and low polarization contrast. To overcome these limitations, we leverage high-index dielectric nanophotonics to simultaneously enhance both fluorescence and polarization for chiral sensing. We propose a reciprocity-based analytical framework for a chiral dipolar emitter coupled to a nanoantenna and reveal the different contributions and trade-offs governing the enhancement of circularly polarized fluorescence. Guided by this insight, we tailor achiral dielectric nanostructures to reach a 1000-fold enhancement of fluorescence intensity together with a 10-fold increase in polarization. Crucially, we show that accounting for extrinsic polarization effects in the angular emission patterns of nanophotonic structures is indispensable for reliable enantiomer discrimination. Our approach opens a realistic path for single-molecule chiral sensing.

papers.title: Strategic Origins of Network Structure
papers.summary: The structure and dynamics of complex networks are intimately linked. Despite immense progress in statistically characterizing these systems, a generalized mechanistic framework explaining why specific mesoscale structures emerge remains elusive. Here we introduce the game-graph equilibrium, the stable rest point of a payoff-driven partner-choice dynamic, analogous to a Nash equilibrium. This reveals network structure as the fossilized record of strategic interaction. We prove analytically that two-type games have exactly four network topologies, which are their exhaustive thermodynamic phases: assortative, disassortative, and two core-peripheries. This result generalizes to $K^K$ topological classes for $K$-type interactions. Furthermore, four distinct Nash equilibria produce core-periphery topologies, yet their payoffs reveal whether the underlying dynamic is cooperative or exploitative. To recover the generating dynamics from observed networks, we develop mechanistic inference by constraining a block model to lie on a low-dimensional, game-theoretic manifold. Applied to real-world networks, the model yields interpretable quantities, distinguishes states that look identical to conventional methods, predicts network topologies it has never seen without retraining, and controls its own complexity without hand-tuned penalties. Networks such as international trade are well described by the model despite the hard constraint, suggesting that real-world systems are organized by payoff-driven partner choice. Our framework resolves a foundational ambiguity by offering a precise, mechanistic definition of communities: strategic equivalence.

papers.title: Modeling the Coevolution of Human Skills and AI Adoption
papers.summary: The value of relying on generative AI depends on two quantities that evolve with its use: users' unaided skill, which may decline without practice, and the originality of AI-assisted work, which may decline as more people rely on similar tools. We model this process as a coevolutionary game in which individuals choose between autonomous and AI-assisted work, with autonomous practice strengthening their skills while reliance on AI gradually erodes them. When the reinforcing effect of skill erosion outweighs the crowding cost of lost originality, the population exhibits two alternative stable states: low AI adoption with high average skill, and high AI adoption with low average skill. Because skill is individual, autonomous workers remain more skilled than AI users, making autonomous work less vulnerable to population-wide skill decline. The strength of this effect is governed by a timescale ratio: the rate at which skills adapt relative to the rate at which individuals change strategy. The same ratio determines the full distribution of skills, which we derive analytically. Populations with identical AI adoption and average skill can differ sharply: when strategies change frequently, skills remain homogeneous and collective lock-in to high AI adoption is stronger; when strategies persist, lock-in weakens but the population can polarize into highly skilled autonomous workers and AI-dependent individuals. Modeling output overlap further shows that more diverse AI outputs can make widespread adoption harder to reverse. Together, these results expose tradeoffs between the benefits of widespread AI adoption and its long-run risks, making collective lock-in and skill polarization distinct intervention targets.

papers.title: Low-Field J-Coupling Spectroscopy Measured with a Diamond Nitrogen Vacancy Spectrometer
papers.summary: Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond (NVs) are point defects well suited to quantum sensing of magnetic fields. NV spin states can be initialized and read out optically with high spatial resolution, enabling detection of pL-scale volumes of nuclear spins. Using Coherently Averaged Synchronized Readout (CASR), standard NMR spectroscopy techniques such as free decay, spin echo, and PGSE have been performed with Hz-scale spectral resolution using NV-diamond sensors. However, using NV detection for conventional high-resolution NMR at multi-tesla fields is challenging due to the need to manipulate NV electronic spins at resonance frequencies 100 GHz or higher. Low-field J-coupling spectroscopy provides an alternative path to chemical resolution in a regime more easily accessible to NVs. Here, we demonstrate homonuclear and heteronuclear J-coupling spectroscopy using an NV-NMR spectrometer based on permanent magnets operating at $\sim$890 kHz proton Larmor frequency (bias magnetic field $\sim$21 mT). This field strength enables chemical characterization based on J-coupling using sequences such as Synchronized Echo (SyncE) and Spin-Echo Double Resonance (SEDOR), which do not require the strong chemical shift dispersion and pristine field homogeneity of high-field NMR. The frequency range is easily detected by NVs using standard XY dynamical decoupling sequences and is well-suited for applying Overhauser DNP, which can boost proton signal by two orders of magnitude. We acquire initial NV-NMR measurements of T$_1$, T$_2$, and Overhauser DNP in glycerol before advancing to SEDOR spectroscopy of methanol-$^{13}$C and a methanol-$^{13}$C/acetonitrile-2-$^{13}$C mixture at sample volumes $\sim$50 pL, in which we demonstrate measurement of $^1J_\text{CH}$ couplings and resolution between species. We also acquire a homonuclear J-coupling spectrum of a natural-abundance propylene carbonate sample.

papers.title: A general mechanism for collective foraging: percolating recruitment cascades coupled to a maximum-entropy
papers.summary: Foraging recruitment is a contagion: an agent finding a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade -- the model for rumour and adoption spread on social networks -- embedded in space. Because activation is degree-normalized, the same rule that spreads the cascade also stifles it as neighbourhoods crowd (density-dependent blocking), so the swarm aggregates on a resource, then releases to explore again. The cascade runs on the communication network, but acting on it moves agents in physical space, and that motion rewires the network: network and physical space are one coupled system, and this feedback -- not tuning -- makes the coordination self-limiting. Because recruitment chains along the graph rather than near neighbours alone, whether a discovery stays local or spans the swarm is a matter of percolation, and past a critical connectivity the swarm holds itself in a cascade window -- locally near-critical though globally subcritical, a self-organized, sandpile-like drive-avalanche cycle. Nothing is tuned, yet behaviours foraging biology documents separately emerge together -- recruitment, marginal-value patch-leaving, and Levy search with a switch to local exploitation. These are not coincidences but one least-committal principle: the resource field and the search both follow from maximum entropy -- Levy search matched to the field's sparsity, recruitment to its clustering, so active-matter order and optimal foraging are one system in two domains. The gains are real but conditional: up to 7.6x the harvest of solitary search when resources are sparse and clustered, shrinking to nothing when search is already easy. Percolating cascades yield a large return on minimal communication. And that sparse, clustered field is the generic one -- resources almost inevitably aggregate, and maximum entropy makes it the least-committal one once they do -- so one untuned rule should recur widely.

papers.title: Scaling laws for contamination traversal times during vacuum breaks in superconducting accelerators
papers.summary: A sudden loss of vacuum in a superconducting radio-frequency (SRF) accelerator drives warm gas into the evacuated beamline, where it propagates through interconnected SRF cavities cooled by liquid helium, causing surface contamination, intense heat deposition, and dangerous pressure buildup. Yet predicting how such a failure propagates through realistic multicell cavities has remained difficult because compressible gas dynamics, condensation and cryogenic heat transfer are strongly coupled. Here we develop and experimentally validate a multidimensional computational framework that resolves these processes, and apply it to a full-scale nine-cell SRF cavity. We find that the repeated cell geometry produces staircase-like gas-front propagation, as impingement, recirculation and localized cryopumping strongly retard the bulk flow within each cell. Across a broad range of breach sizes, the cavity traversal time follows a robust power-law scaling with leakage area, providing quantitative guidance for the response time of beamline isolation and protection systems. The simulations also reveal a geometry-confined Mach disk whose position and size track the advancing gas front, suggesting that its acoustic emission could potentially enable rapid, non-invasive detection and localization of vacuum failures. These findings pave the way for a new generation of predictive diagnostics and protection strategies to safeguard large-scale superconducting accelerators.

papers.title: Hidden Perturbative Structure in Attosecond Streaking
papers.summary: Attosecond streaking is inherently multiphoton, yet we uncover a hidden perturbative structure revealing the underlying continuum--continuum angular-momentum propensity. By filtering the inversion-odd response in helium streaking data at the IR fundamental, we isolate an angular distribution dominated by the $P_1$ and $P_3$ Legendre components, whose complex coefficients yield an effective $s/d$ two-photon amplitude ratio. Multichannel, two-electron time-dependent Schr\"odinger equation calculations demonstrate that the characteristic Fano propensity survives electron correlation. Incorporating the experimental XUV attochirp reproduces the measured emission-edge trend, while near-threshold calculations predict resonant amplitude and phase signatures associated with the bound He $np$ Rydberg series. This symmetry- and frequency-filtering approach offers a general spectroscopic framework with potential applications to atomic, molecular, and solid-state systems where attosecond streaking is established.

papers.title: Second-Order Correction for Statistical Bias in Monte Carlo Depletion Calculations
papers.summary: Depletion analyses are often driven by Monte Carlo neutron transport methods that introduce uncertainty into the transmutation matrix used to evolve a material composition. The nonlinearity of the matrix exponential applied to this transmutation matrix causes the uncertainty to introduce a systematic bias in the computed isotope vectors. This work derives a second-order correction for this bias that can be computed with quantities obtainable from typical Monte Carlo transport routines. An augmented Bateman system is formulated to evaluate these quantities and an adapted Chebyshev rational approximation method uses transmutation matrix factorizations for efficient evaluation of the second-order correction. Then, the correction is demonstrated using a ten-nuclide verification problem, an ITER port-plug activation problem, and a 9-pin boiling water reactor lattice containing self-shielded gadolinium-bearing fuel.

papers.title: Undulatory Swimming in Sand: Subsurface Locomotion of the Sandfish Lizard
papers.summary: The desert-dwelling sandfish (Scincus scincus) moves within dry sand, a material that displays solid and fluidlike behavior. High-speed x-ray imaging shows that below the surface, the lizard no longer uses limbs for propulsion but generates thrust to overcome drag by propagating an undulatory traveling wave down the body. Although viscous hydrodynamics can predict swimming speed in fluids such as water, an equivalent theory for granular drag is not available. To predict sandfish swimming speed, we developed an empirical model by measuring granular drag force on a small cylinder oriented at different angles relative to the displacement direction and summing these forces over the animal movement profile. The agreement between model and experiment implies that the noninertial swimming occurs in a frictional fluid.

papers.title: Large Language Model Steering of Acousto-Optic Tweezer Arrays
papers.summary: Controlling quantum hardware requires choosing and revising experimental strategies as nonlinear response, coupling, and drift limit calibration. We experimentally investigate a general-purpose large language model (LLM) as a human-in-the-loop strategy layer for a neutral-atom tweezer platform. Through step-by-step interaction with experimental feedback, the LLM guides a transition from multiplicative row--column correction to a drift-corrected local response-matrix method when separable feedback stalls. Deterministic software performs image analysis and numerical updates, while an experimentalist verifies and authorizes each waveform. For a $10\times10$ crossed-acousto-optic-deflector array, this workflow reduces the Gaussian-peak coefficient of variation from $20.30\%$ to $1.57\%$ in 30 candidate-update rounds. The experiment demonstrates feedback-informed strategy selection on a physical quantum-control subsystem, rather than direct generation of control parameters alone. These results highlight the potential of LLMs to guide control optimization across diverse quantum platforms by adaptively formulating and refining experimental strategies.

papers.title: Fast and High-Fidelity Motional-State-Preserving Transport in Optical Tweezers
papers.summary: Reconfigurable neutral-atom processors require rapid, high-fidelity transport of atoms between optical-tweezer sites. In finite-depth Gaussian traps, fast motion can leave residual motional excitation even when the atom reaches its destination. We develop a basis-parameterized gradient-ascent pulse-engineering (GRAPE) framework for one-dimensional transport of a single $^{87}$Rb atom. A shortcut-to-adiabaticity reference is refined using 17 trajectory parameters, with ten additional parameters providing bounded trap-depth modulation; depth affects both confinement and the inverse construction of the physical trap center. For a $12.6\,\mu$m transfer completed in only $30.5\,\mu$s, corresponding to approximately $2.75$ periods of the reference trap, the selected joint protocol achieves a ground-state infidelity of $2.41\times10^{-7}$. Because preparing an exactly pure motional ground state is experimentally challenging, we also optimize population-weighted transport for initial distributions with mean vibrational occupations $\nbar\simeq0.16$ and $1.87$, reaching same-state probabilities of about $0.99993$ and $0.9934$. Trap-depth fluctuations can further degrade transport fidelity. Robust optimization under a measurement-informed depth-noise model improves the mean error, worst sampled error, and fidelity dispersion for the specified noise realizations. Coordinated control of tweezer position and confinement thus offers a route to rapid transport with low residual excitation for flexible atom rearrangement and dynamic connectivity in neutral-atom processors.

papers.title: Dynamic Hotspot Migration and Self-Induced Resonances in Ultrafast Laser-Irradiated Silicon Thin Films
papers.summary: The spatial distribution of energy in silicon thin films under femtosecond laser irradiation is demonstrated to be influenced by the interaction between carrier-induced refractive index modulation and self-induced Fabry-P\'erot resonances. We resolve three characteristic excitation regions such as interface-localized, binodal and multi-nodal regimes considering the analysis of silicon-on-insulator (SOI) configurations across thicknesses of 100, 230, and 350 nm. We report a nonlinear hotspot migration effect where the transient reduction of the refractive index stretches the internal standing wave, translating intensity antinodes toward the film volume during the pulse. Numerical results demonstrate that at higher fluences, plasma-induced extinction suppresses internal reflections, triggering a transition from resonance-mediated absorption to plasma shielding. These findings establish a physical basis for depth-resolved modification in laser nanomanufacturing, providing a dual-capacity for simultaneous surface patterning and depth-resolved subsurface modification with direct applications in laser-assisted interfacial separation and 3D integrated photonic fabrication.

papers.title: Generative marginal learning for finite-size molecular simulation with application to stress calculation
papers.summary: We propose generative marginal learning (GML), a framework for equilibrium sampling and local observable estimation in molecular simulations. By training a conditional diffusion model on large-system simulations, GML learns the marginal distribution of a retained region, enabling configuration generation without explicitly simulating the surrounding environment or imposing periodic boundary conditions on the retained region. We derive a marginal effective potential and the associated conditional mean-force identity, which provide the basis for both denoising and force-alignment training. As an application, we estimate the spatially averaged Irving--Kirkwood stress near a vacancy defect. Numerical results demonstrate that GML substantially improves pair structure and local stress accuracy compared with small periodic molecular dynamics simulations, mitigating finite-size effects in calculating local molecular observables.

papers.title: Superradiant temporal transition radiation of a relativistic electron beam
papers.summary: A charge in uniform motion carries a bound field that does not radiate. Transition radiation releases part of it at a boundary in space. We propose and analyze the case of radiation emission due to a boundary in time: a relativistic electron bunch passes through an aperture in a semiconductor (silicon) wafer, and while its bound field occupies the wafer, a femtosecond laser switches the semiconductor into an electron-hole plasma. The field is a valid solution of the old medium and not of the new one, so it is handed to the plasma as an initial condition for radiation emission at the plasma frequency. Because in temporal transition radiation (t-TR) the wavevector is conserved, and the frequency is not, the emission can appear in a spectral band that the bunch's own field does not populate. Every electron contributes in phase to the initial condition at the switching moment, so the emitted energy scales as $N^2$. We derive the field energy conversion at the temporal boundary and the resultant measurable amplitude and frequency line-shape of the radiation taking into consideration plasma carriers collisional loss. The simplified analytical model of the process and its scaling laws are confirmed by use of FDTD numerical computations for a reference case based on the parameters of an existing 6.5 MeV photoinjector accelerator. For this case we predict wideband t-TR radiation emission at THz frequencies, where the emission center frequency, near the plasma frequency, is selectable across an octave, set by the laser fluence, and the intensity is governed by the beam charge. The predicted radiative energy is detectable in a single shot. The experimental considerations for observing it are given in a Supplement.

papers.title: Multigroup Implicit Monte Carlo Radiation Hydrodynamics on Moving Voronoi Meshes with STORM and RICH
papers.summary: We present and validate an Implicit Monte Carlo (IMC) radiation-transport solver in the open-source, mesh-agnostic storm library, coupled to the moving-mesh hydrodynamics code rich in three-dimensional Voronoi tessellations. The solver is multigroup, or continuous in frequency, throughout; it transforms photon packets exactly between the comoving and laboratory frames, books every exchange with the material as a laboratory four-momentum so that the IMC path conserves energy to roundoff, formulates the Fleck factor in the fluid's proper time, and accelerates optically thick cells with multigroup Discrete Diffusion Monte Carlo (DDMC) behind an emissivity-preserving interface. We tested the solver on a broad suite of benchmark problems, and it performed well on all of them. The solver is built on the MPI-parallel Monte Carlo framework of storm, which scales to 13,440 cores.

papers.title: The chair challenge: can mechanics really tell men from women? A centre-of-mass analysis of a viral party trick
papers.summary: In the "chair challenge" a person stands several foot lengths from a wall, bends forward until the head touches the wall, lifts a chair and tries to stand up. Online videos suggest that women can do this and men cannot, supposedly because women have a lower centre of mass or men have larger feet. We model the body as a planar chain of rigid segments with standard biomechanical parameters and search all postures allowed by the rules for the one that places the combined centre of mass of body and chair furthest back. As a rule of thumb, the largest toe-wall distance is roughly the trunk-plus-head length minus the distance from hip to centre of mass. For a slow, static rise this limit is 2.36 foot lengths for the male and 2.49 foot lengths for the female reference model, just short of the customary 2.5 foot lengths. The limit is set mainly by trunk-plus-head length relative to foot length, not by the height of the centre of mass; in centimetres the male model actually has more room. With the body proportions of 6068 participants in the 2012 US Army anthropometric survey, the sex difference shrinks from 0.13 to 0.03-0.05 foot lengths, half to one European shoe size. Individually, only 13% of men and 22% of women would pass statically, and predicting sex from the outcome is right in 54-68% of cases (for equal numbers of men and women), against 50% for a coin and 83% for a tape measure. Shoes, age and momentum matter more than the residual sex difference. The problem suits first-year undergraduate mechanics, combining static equilibrium of an articulated body, scaling and units, an inverted-pendulum estimate and a simple classification problem. The chair challenge is a fine demonstration of static equilibrium and a lousy sex predictor.

papers.title: Negative partisanship drives anti-frontrunner volatility in election dynamics
papers.summary: Negative partisanship---where voter mobilization is driven primarily by aversion toward an opposing candidate rather than positive alignment---profoundly reshapes modern electoral dynamics. Here, we formulate a two-dimensional piecewise map to model campaign opinion dynamics, where voter abstention arises endogenously from a latent spectrum of voter activation barriers. We show that cross-candidate rejection sensitivity triggers a non-smooth collapse of abstention, dividing the phase space into an under-mobilized regime and a fully mobilized campaign regime. In symmetric elections with radicalized voter bases, spontaneous symmetry breaking via a pitchfork bifurcation gives rise to asymmetric polling attractors partitioned by mirror-symmetric basins of attraction, where early public perceptions---encoded in initial campaign conditions---act as a deterministic catalyst selecting candidate lead lock-in long before election day. For elevated cross-rejection, the symmetric equilibrium destabilizes via a period-doubling flip bifurcation, driving persistent anti-frontrunner polling swings. Rather than predicting static candidate hegemony, our model reveals that high negative partisanship turns elections into time-sensitive dynamical systems, where final election outcomes reflect discrete sampling snapshots of an oscillating campaign trajectory.

papers.title: Construction of crystal-based light sources with LWFA electron beams
papers.summary: We discuss a possibility to construct a crystal-based light source (CLS) of gamma-rays using electron beams produce by Laser Wake Field Acceleration (LWFA). This state-of-the-art acceleration technique is capable of producing few-GeV, ultra-short (fs) electron beams. In the case studies presented, we demonstrate the feasibility of novel gamma-ray CLSs based on exposing single crystals to electron beams available at the ELI-ELBA. The results of rigorous numerical simulations are presented to characterise the radiation emitted emitted by 1 and 4 GeV electrons incident on a 200-micron-thick single silicon crystal along the (110) plane. The simulations were performed using the current divergence as well as a smaller value that is believed to be a realistic to achieve in the near future. We demonstrate that it is feasible to achieve a photon yield of $10^6-10^7$ photons/s in the photon energy range from 5 to 50 MeV. Looking further ahead, we also performed a similar analysis for a 4-GeV positron beam incident on much thicker targets, up to 2 mm oriented silicon crystal. In this case, the photon yield can be increased by an order of magnitude.

papers.title: Design and synthesis of laser inscribed flexible Bragg gratings containing silicon oxynitride-doped silicon thin film for authentication applications with the insights from X-Ray Absorption Spectroscopy and Quantum Mechanical Calculations
papers.summary: Silicon-on-insulator is mostly the main driving material system for the field of silicon photonics, including PICs, due to high index contrast and compatibility with current semiconductor manufacturing processes [1]. A recent example is silicon oxynitride-doped silicon [2] discovered recently by our group, offering to set a new position for the fields of silicon photonics with a precise control of refractive index from 2.1 to 2.5 together with the photosensitivity property at different wavelengths. In this study, we demonstrate that the synthesis of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon can be performed on a flexible substrate for the fabrication of Bragg gratings (BG) at low temperatures below 100 degrees Celsius that are emerging for advanced applications. Their use in preserving ultra-fast lasers inscribed micro-information has been demonstrated numerically and experimentally due to its multispectral reflection behaviour from the ultraviolet (UV) to the near-infrared (NIR) regions. The unique structural characteristics of silicon oxynitride-doped silicon were studied at the Si L, O K and N K edges using soft X-ray absorption studies. The quantum mechanical calculations provide the potential formation mechanism of SiON-doped Si, whereas the crystal structure prediction for bulk Si3N4-xOx was conducted using the particle swarm optimization method in combination with density functional theory (DFT).

papers.title: A Unified Interface Neural Network for Elliptic Interface Problems
papers.summary: We develop a Unified Interface Neural Network (UINN) framework for elliptic interface problems with discontinuous coefficients. A single shared network provides a unified representation of the solution in both subdomains, while a projection--correction construction embeds the solution and flux jump conditions directly into the neural trial space. This design aligns with the classical numerical principle of incorporating interfacial physics into the approximation basis to construct interface-unfitted numerical methods. The jump conditions are therefore satisfied exactly for any network parameters. Compared with methods based on separate phase networks and numerical formulations with interface penalty terms, UINN provides a unified representation with exact enforcement of interfacial jump conditions and interface-penalty-free optimization. Those features streamline the numerical formulations and can enhance training robustness. Numerical experiments on smooth interfaces at modestly large and high coefficient contrasts demonstrate UINN's solution accuracy, near-machine-precision satisfaction of the interface jump conditions, and enhanced robustness.

papers.title: Yielding-dependent Taylor dispersion in electrokinetic-magnetohydrodynamic Casson microflows
papers.summary: Longitudinal dispersion in a yielding fluid depends on the velocity distribution and on how the flow is maintained. We study a neutral tracer in pressure-assisted electrokinetic and magnetohydrodynamic flow of a Casson fluid through a slit microchannel. The nonlinear stress and velocity equations determine the yielded layers, the unyielded core and the axial flow. Mei's multiple-scale homogenization of the advection-diffusion equation then separates transverse relaxation, mean drift and longitudinal spreading, yielding the Taylor-Aris auxiliary problem and effective diffusivity. An exact pressure-driven solution gives cubic decay of the mean velocity and eighth-power decay of the dispersion enhancement near flow arrest. Under fixed pressure and electrical forcing, increasing the yield parameter from $Y=0$ to $0.7$ moves the optimum Hartmann number from $Ha_p=0.696$ to $2.634$, while the corresponding normalized diffusivity decreases from $D_T^{\mathrm C}=1.454$ to $1.015$. At fixed mean throughput and $Ha_p=1$, the trend reverses: $D_T^{\mathrm C}$ increases from $1.000433$ to $1.002311$. The homogenized energy identity traces this difference to the velocity departure from the sectional mean, including that within the unyielded core. Analytical limiting solutions, direct concentration calculations, numerical convergence studies and a coupled Casson shear test support the reduced-flow predictions. An electrolyte-based dimensional assessment identifies the magnetic optima as theoretical forcing states for representative aqueous microchannels. These results are relevant to predicting longitudinal tracer spreading in microchannels carrying fluids with a yield stress, whether pressure or throughput is controlled.

papers.title: Probing Flow-Induced Chain Scission in Shear-Banding Wormlike Micelles
papers.summary: We investigate the microstructural dynamics of wormlike micellar (WLM) solutions based on CPyCl/NaSal/D\(_2\)O under shear flow using spatially resolved rheo-diffusion NMR, velocity-compensated diffusion measurements, and rheo-optical imaging in a Taylor--Couette geometry. Two viscoelastic systems were examined: a non-shear-banding WLM with a molar salt-surfactant concentration ratio of \(R=0.4\) and a shear-banding WLM with \(R=0.53\). Rheo-optical and velocity measurements confirm homogeneous flow for the non-shear-banding system and the coexistence of low- and high-shear bands within the stress-plateau regime for the shear-banding system. Despite the pronounced heterogeneity in velocity and shear rate associated with shear banding, the local surfactant self-diffusivity remains spatially uniform across the gap and throughout the stress-plateau regime. Furthermore, analysis of the mean-squared-displacement scaling reveals no measurable difference between the high- and low-shear bands. These results demonstrate that the micellar microstructure remains largely unchanged despite the formation of shear bands and provide direct experimental evidence that flow-induced micellar chain scission is not a dominant mechanism governing shear banding in this WLM system.

papers.title: Rydberg Atomic Receiver for Wireless Physical Layer: A Survey
papers.summary: With the escalating development of the quantum information technologies, the Rydberg atomic receiver has been envisioned as a promising alternative to its classical electronic counterparts, attracting extensive attentions from both physics and electronic engineering disciplines. By exploiting the electrical acuteness of Alkali atoms with diverse Rydberg energy states for electromagnetic field measurement, Rydberg atomic receiver is capable of surmounting the inherent limitations on the operating bandwidth and detection sensitivity of the classical electronic counterparts. Against this background, this article provides an extensive overview of Rydberg atomic communication and sensing from fundamental theory, critical technologies to practical implementations. Firstly, the milestones of the Rydberg atomic receiver evolution was introduced. Then we provide a clear understanding of Rydberg atomic receiver mechanisms from the perspective of classical communication and sensing, and highlight the unprecedented advantages over traditional electronic receivers as well as the technical challenges. Afterwards, necessary fundamentals are presented including the Rydberg atoms, typical non-coherent/coherent structures, and explicit experimental configurations, followed by discussions on state-of-the-art development of the Rydberg atomic receiver. Specifically, advancements on electric-field detection methods for accurate measurement of amplitude, phase, frequency and polarization, are extensively investigated. Based on the established methodologies, recent innovations in Rydberg atomic communication and sensing are reviewed, ranging from waveform design and array-based signal processing to radar applications like localization, imaging and remote sensing, with practical experimental results presented. Finally, we summarize the promising research trends around Rydberg atomic receiver.

papers.title: Variational Principles for Hierarchical Systems of Equations
papers.summary: A unified construction of variational principles (VP) is applied to hierarchical systems of equations. The adjoint set of equations involved in this construction differ from the original hierarchy set in important ways. Notably, upward and downward nature of hierarchy are reversed between the two sets, as are boundary conditions and, most significantly, whether or not the equations are factorizable. These features may make for ease of solving one of the two sets and thereby for usefulness of the VP themselves that employ both.

papers.title: Connectivism as an Innovative Didactic Experience in Preservice Physics Teacher Education
papers.summary: This chapter examines the use of connectivism as a pedagogical approach in preservice physics teacher education through a classroom experience conducted in a Contemporary Physics course at the Universidad Pedag\'ogica y Tecnol\'ogica de Colombia (UPTC). The study involved 21 preservice teachers organized into four collaborative groups. Using a qualitative approach, students selected and discussed digital learning resources, interacted through WhatsApp, and prepared collaborative reports connecting contemporary physics concepts with scientific and technological applications. The analysis considered conceptual understanding, argumentation, questioning, critical thinking, relationships among concepts, and the use of digital resources. Students' reports and feedback indicated favorable perceptions of the collaborative activities and provided examples of conceptual connections, evidence-based explanations, and reflection on future teaching practices. The chapter discusses the possibilities of connectivist learning networks for physics teacher education, drawing on the findings of this particular classroom experience.

papers.title: A General Treatment of Coupled Cavity Resonators
papers.summary: Consider several cavity resonators whose resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields are known, and suppose that they are coupled through apertures. How can the resonant frequencies and resonant electromagnetic fields of the resulting coupled-cavity resonator be expressed in terms of the original resonant frequencies and electromagnetic fields? This is a problem frequently encountered in radio-frequency systems for accelerators. One example is a multicell cavity used in high-energy electron accelerators. In this note, the resonant frequencies and resonant electromagnetic fields of such coupled cavities are examined as generally as possible, based only on Maxwell's equations and boundary conditions. Specifically, the response function of a cavity as viewed from its coupling ports, namely, its admittance matrix, is derived, and a formulation is developed to express the coupled resonant electromagnetic fields using this matrix. The resulting formulation shows that the coupled resonant modes can be described in terms of overlap integrals between the resonant modes of the cavities and the waveguide modes at the coupling apertures. It also shows that the coupled resonant frequencies are given by the zeros of the determinant of a matrix constructed from the admittance matrices. The results thus obtained are applied to simple systems to confirm the validity of the formulation. Numerical calculations based on this formulation are also carried out for periodic systems in an attempt to derive dispersion relations.

papers.title: All-Dielectric Tight-Binding Photonics via a Band-Gap Vacuum
papers.summary: Tight-binding photonics bridges condensed-matter physics and optics, providing a powerful framework for engineering band structures and topological phases with light. For photons, however, the vacuum is gapless, so resonators in air carry radiative tails that produce spurious long-range couplings. Here we embed resonators in a photonic band-gap vacuum (BgV), a photonic crystal whose band gap plays for photons the role vacuum plays for bound electrons. The BgV localizes each resonance exponentially, so designed short-range couplings define the lattice Hamiltonian. We thereby experimentally realize a faithful Benalcazar-Bernevig-Hughes Hamiltonian in an all-dielectric photonic crystal, resolving corner resonances and their orbitals in microwave measurements. Unlike the vacuum surrounding electrons, the BgV is itself designable, controlling relative couplings and closed-loop interference through its band dispersion and Bloch modes. Full-wave calculations and extracted models show that uniformly modifying the BgV, with all resonators fixed, switches the quantized polarization of a two-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger lattice and converts a zero-flux lattice into a $\pi$-flux one. We also numerically realize three-dimensional pyrochlore and hyperhoneycomb lattices with space groups $R\bar{3}m$ and $C2/c$, the latter a nodal-loop semimetal with topological drumhead surface states. These results establish the BgV as a designable vacuum for all-dielectric tight-binding photonics in two and three dimensions.

papers.title: Reduced Molecular Plasma Kinetics with Non-Boltzmann Vibrational Distribution
papers.summary: Vibrational kinetics can strongly affect energy transfer, chemical kinetics, and discharge behavior in molecular plasmas, but resolving all internal states is often impractical for reactor-scale simulation. Compact, physics-based vibrational closures are particularly needed when complete state-to-state (StS) data are limited. Starting from a detailed $\mathrm{H}_2$ StS plasma-kinetics framework coupled to an electron-Boltzmann calculation, this work develops a reduced vibrational-kinetics formulation. The $\mathrm{H}_2$ vibrational ladder is reduced to two non-Boltzmann groups that evolve their population and internal energy. State-resolved reaction rates and associated energy-exchange terms are projected onto the groups for subsequent tabulation in reactor-scale plasma models. StS-informed samples of the reduced-model are propagated for pulsed RF $\mathrm{H}_2$ plasmas across a scan of pulse-averaged absorbed power and compared with the corresponding StS simulations. Predictions from the sampled models reproduce the bulk plasma response, including electron density, atomic-H density, and $\mathrm{H}_3^+$ density. Discrepancies in $\mathrm{H}^-$ production and the upper-energy-group vibrational temperature persist across the sampled reductions. This indicates a limitation of the present VDF reconstruction rather than the nominal parameter choice. Tail-sensitive processes therefore require a more accurate representation of the vibrational distribution.

papers.title: High-Efficiency Silicon-Lithium Niobate Grating Coupler enabled by Fully-Etched Subwavelength Structures
papers.summary: A new approach of silicon-lithium niobate (Si-LN) grating couplers (GCs) with a fully-etched structure is proposed. The coupling strength is engineered through subwavelength structures, allowing improved directionality. The adjoint-based inverse design method is simultaneously adopted to achieve efficient coupling between photonic circuits and fibers. Considering the birefringence of LN, the proposed Si-LN GCs are optimized and fabricated for TE mode along the crystallographic Z and Y directions. The experimentally measured coupling efficiencies are -3.3 dB and -3.9 dB along the crystallographic Z and Y directions, respectively. The measured 3-dB bandwidths are broader than 54 nm and the back reflections can be suppressed down to -15 dB over 50 nm for both directions. The proposed Si-LN GCs are realized by only single-step Si etching, offering a practical solution for fast device prototyping in Si-LN photonic integrated circuits.

papers.title: Pairwise assessment correlations predict cooperation of the Leading Eight under private assessment
papers.summary: Indirect reciprocity can sustain cooperation when individuals use reputations to decide whom to help. The Leading Eight norms sustain such cooperation under public assessment, where all individuals share the same assessments. Under private assessment, however, observers may disagree, yet their assessments remain correlated. Two quantities, the average fraction of good assessments $h$ and the conditional probability $h_{\mathrm G}$ that one observer assesses a player as good given that another does, are known to determine the stability of cooperation, but how $h_{\mathrm G}$ itself is determined has remained open. Within a pairwise approximation, we derive a closed equation for $h_{\mathrm G}$ that, together with that for $h$, determines both quantities for all eight norms, including third-order ones. This description substantially improves agreement with simulations over a mean-field approximation that neglects correlations, and recovers the known classification of the Leading Eight into three classes. The remaining discrepancies are largest for L2 and L5 at low error rates and decrease as assessment error increases. Relating $h_{\mathrm G}$ to the variance of individual goodness suggests that these discrepancies reflect information beyond the first two moments of the goodness distribution. Our framework provides a concise and analytically tractable tool for evaluating social norms under private assessment.

papers.title: Dual Reverse Time Migration: Efficient Least-squares Imaging with Multiple Scattering in Dual Space
papers.summary: Least-squares reverse time migration (LSRTM) estimates a broadband reflectivity image by iteratively minimizing the data misfit. Despite its superior imaging performance over conventional reverse time migration (RTM), LSRTM is fundamentally limited by the first-order Born approximation and incurs a high computational cost due to the iterative solution of a source-dependent model-space Hessian. We propose dual RTM, a seismic imaging framework that reformulates the inverse problem in the dual space, where the optimization variable is the scattering information of all orders, rather than being limited to the first-order scattering of the Born approximation. Unlike LSRTM, which directly estimates the reflectivity model, dual RTM reconstructs the missing scattering data (dual variable) through a fixed-point iteration governed by the full wave equation, enabling the recovery of higher-order scattering and multiple reflections without repeated background velocity updates. Furthermore, dual RTM replaces the source-dependent model-space Hessian with a source-independent data-space Hessian. A hybrid time--frequency formulation enables this Hessian to be assembled and inverted once in the Fourier domain as an offline preprocessing step, reducing the online computational cost of each dual iteration to that of a single RTM application. Numerical experiments on challenging synthetic benchmarks demonstrate that dual RTM suppresses acquisition footprints, improves amplitude fidelity, and enhances deep imaging where primary reflections alone provide insufficient illumination. These results establish dual RTM as an efficient bridge between conventional RTM/LSRTM and nonlinear waveform inversion for high-resolution large-scale seismic imaging.

papers.title: Effect of Physical Barriers on High-Harmonic Generation in Liquid-Phase
papers.summary: High-harmonic generation (HHG) in liquid-phase systems presents fundamental differences from gas and solid phases, notably a reduction in the harmonic cutoff, its apparent independence from laser parameters, and the appearance of a second plateau. In this work, we introduce a one-dimensional quantum model that incorporates physical boundaries to simulate the effect of solvation shells in liquid water by means of a complex absorbing potential (CAP). By systematically varying the position, width, and strength of the CAP, we explore how these physical constraints influence the HHG spectrum. Our findings confirm that spatial confinement, specifically the physical truncation of electron trajectories, is the primary factor governing the cutoff in liquid-phase HHG. This confinement leads to a cutoff that is independent of laser intensity and wavelength, aligning with experimental observations and existing hypotheses proposed by Mondal et al. in 2023 and 2026. Furthermore, by implementing a semi-transparent CAP, we successfully reproduce the less intense second plateau observed in liquid-phase HHG. Time-frequency analysis confirms that this characteristic spectral feature is driven by partial wave-packet transmission through the solvation shells, which allows a surviving fraction of electrons to undergo longer continuum excursions. Our one-dimensional approach successfully isolates the fundamental role of physical boundaries in liquid-phase HHG, providing a clear and intuitive understanding of the underlying physics.

papers.title: Fractal forcing of turbulence by settling particles
papers.summary: The settling of particles in a fluid medium can trigger complex collective dynamics, dramatically affecting the distribution of energy across flow scales. In this work we present the first fully-resolved observations of the turbulence induced by large particle structures, also known as cluster-induced-turbulence (CIT), obtained through particle-resolved direct numerical simulations at high volume fractions and density ratios in large domains. We find that particles arrange in macroscopic fractal structures, exciting turbulent fluctuations at scales much larger than the individual constituents. By virtue of their fractal nature, these clusters force the continuous-phase in a multiscale, self-similar way. We further show that these cluster-driven, vertically decorrelated fluctuations at large scales coexist with, but are fundamentally distinct from, the established particle-driven high-wavenumber scaling. Beyond unveiling a different form of clustering in particle-settling, these results highlight a naturally arising, self-assembling path to fractal-generated turbulence.

papers.title: Intermolecular Packing and Cooperative Stabilization in Nucleotide Monophosphate Crystals
papers.summary: We examine the known polymorphs of cytidine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate (CMP) using dispersion-corrected density functional theory. The monoclinic phase is predicted to be the most stable, lying 1.76 and 3.00 kcal/mol per molecular unit below the orthorhombic and triclinic forms, respectively. Monoclinic CMP contains a ribose-based H-bonding motif along the crystallographic $\vec{b}$ direction, comprising alternating intra- and intermolecular interactions, motivating an investigation of cooperative stabilization along this pathway. We employ chain-of-molecules (COM) and chain-of-slabs (COS) models to quantify the direction- and size-dependent stabilization and extend the analysis to the corresponding 5$^\prime$-monophosphates of thymidine, uridine, adenosine, and guanosine. Successive dimer-addition energies reveal the strongest size-dependent cooperative stabilization along the $\vec{b}$ direction, whereas growth along $\vec{a}$ and $\vec{c}$ exhibits substantially weaker size dependence. Among the nucleotides examined, adenosine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate shows the strongest chain-growth stabilization in the COM model, whereas the uridine variant shows the strongest stabilization in the COS model. Guanosine 5$^\prime$-monophosphate exhibits the weakest response in both models. Minimal-basis iterative stockholder (MBIS) analysis further supports molecular polarization along the growing assemblies. These results demonstrate how nucleobase identity and the surrounding crystal environment modulate direction-dependent cooperative stabilization associated with extended hydrogen-bond networks.

papers.title: Higher-Order Co-Infection on Hypergraphs
papers.summary: People encounter infections through overlapping groups, such as households, classrooms, and workplaces. Understanding how these shared contacts affect the spread of multiple pathogens is critical to determining what information epidemic models need to retain. We introduce HyCo-SIS (Higher-order Co-infection SIS), a discrete-time SIS model on hypergraphs with explicit reinforcement between overlapping active groups and pairwise transmission. We investigate how this reinforcement affects infection dynamics and whether simplified representations of hypergraphs preserve the resulting behavior. We derive an exact representation of overlap reinforcement as target-dependent four-person interactions and determine when a symmetric representation is possible. Numerical experiments examine reinforcement strength, contact structure, and susceptibility to secondary infection, as well as calibrated pairwise approximations. Our results demonstrate that redistributing overlap weights can substantially change finite-time co-infection even when every individual's total overlap coefficient is preserved. We further derive an exact five-person calculation and demonstrate why equal mean infection pressure does not necessarily produce equal acquisition probabilities. These findings identify how the allocation of higher-order interactions can influence contagion dynamics beyond their aggregate strength. Beyond epidemiology, this work contributes to the statistical physics of spreading processes by examining how the arrangement of many-body interactions shapes collective dynamics, and what information is lost when those interactions are simplified.

papers.title: LIDAR with Optically Amplified Thermal Light
papers.summary: Thermal light exhibits intensity fluctuations or photon bunching that has been used as a source of entropy or temporally correlated light. However, its low spectral density limits its use in practical applications like LIDAR. One method of remedying this is optical amplification to boost its brightness. In this paper, we show that the normalized second order coherence function $g^{(2)}(\tau)$ of a thermal light source is preserved after amplification. We then use amplified thermal light to demonstrate a LIDAR raster scan of a building at 1.3 km with a depth resolution of 2 cm.

papers.title: Experimental verification of the PRIORA Monte Carlo code for proton radiography
papers.summary: PRIORA (Proton Radiography Ion-Optical Ray-tracing Analysis) is a fast Monte Carlo model for high-energy proton radiography. It combines fitted proton-matter interaction tables with energy-dependent transfer maps of arbitrary order and simulates approximately $10^6$ protons/s through a complete ion-optical system on an 8-core laptop. We verify it with GSI data obtained with the Ta_bench target: fifteen precision slits in a 2 mm Ta plate between symmetric PMMA staircases. A single experimental image provides the image scale, spatial resolution as a function of chromatic load, signed focus in both planes, effective angular acceptance and multiple-scattering contrast. With identical processing of experiment and simulation and no physics adjustment, PRIORA reproduces the data obtained with 2 and 4 GeV protons. At 2 GeV, PRIORA also recovers sub-percent quadrupole trims consistent with the control-system records and determines a target-plane spatial resolution of $115\pm6\,\mu$m.

papers.title: Phonon-dominated thermal conductivity of a superconducting amorphous MoSi thin film
papers.summary: We use the differential 3{\omega} method to directly measure the temperature dependent thermal conductivity for about 90 nm Mo0.78Si0.22 thin films. The measurements are performed in a closed-cycle cryostat to access the temperature range between 50 K and 300 K. The MoSi thin films are capped with Al2O3 and probed with a Pt wire. The results show that the thermal conductivity does not satisfy the Wiedemann-Franz law. This implies that thermal transport in MoSi is not dominated by electrons but by phonon-like excitations, contrary to what is assumed in many electro-thermal models of superconducting devices. We argue that this property might be related to the weak localization visible in the resistivity as a function of temperature curves of the superconductor.

papers.title: Spatio-temporal precipitation downscaling at hourly resolution based on km-scale regional simulations
papers.summary: Effectively preparing for changes in extreme flooding requires understanding present and future rainfall extremes with return periods up to $\sim$100-1000 years, including changes in intensity, spatial structure at km-scale and sub-daily temporal variability. Conventional km-scale climate models give greatly increased realism compared to typical global climate models (GCMs) but are too computationally costly to allow enough simulations for robustly quantifying changes in extremes. This work presents an approach based on video diffusion to generate realistic precipitation at 8.8km-hourly resolution by spatially and temporally downscaling daily, GCM-scale atmospheric variables. The emulator is trained to produce similar output to a $4\times$-coarsening of the Met Office's 2.2km-resolution UK convection-permitting model. An application for such an emulator is to downscale large-ensemble GCM simulations to allow quantification of $\sim$100-1000-year return level rainfall, which in turn can be used to drive hydrological and flood models for improved projections of future changes in flood risk.

papers.title: The RUBIK satellite payload concept: a 3D-segmented plastic scintillation-based particle tracking detector
papers.summary: We present the design concept and first experimental results of RUBIK, a three-dimensional resolving plastic scintillation detector developed as a scientific payload for the Research and Observation in Medium Earth Orbit satellite mission of the Institute of Space Systems of the University of Stuttgart. The name RUBIK is inspired by the Rubik's Cube, a familiar example of a three-dimensional segmented structure, reflecting the 5x5x5 modular arrangement of the sensitive volume. The sensitive volume consists of 125 PVT-based plastic scintillator unit cubes, each penetrated by two perpendicularly aligned wavelength-shifting fibres, which guide scintillation photons to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), providing 50 independent readout channels. Custom readout electronics, comprising two discriminator boards with per-channel programmable thresholds, an FPGA-based data-acquisition board, and a dedicated power and bias distribution board, have been developed exclusively from commercial off-the-shelf components. A single-layer prototype with ten readout channels was used for concept validation through SiPM bias voltage and temperature characterisation, and a time-over-threshold based amplitude reconstruction method was validated against radioactive source and cosmic ray measurements. First hit-pattern measurements with 220 MeV protons at a clinical proton therapy facility confirmed that spatially resolved hit clusters consistent with the expected beam geometry were observable in the single-layer readout, demonstrating the capability to resolve particle-induced signal patterns as a first step towards 3D track reconstruction in the full instrument.

papers.title: How stagnation lines move, persist and break up in fluid flows
papers.summary: Stagnation curves of arbitrary shape (zeros of $\mathbf v(\mathbf x,t)$) are non-generic yet common; we derive their motion. Differentiating $\mathbf v=\mathbf0$ gives $\mathbf L\mathbf U=-\mathbf a$ ($\mathbf U$ curve velocity, $\mathbf a=\mathbf v_t$, $\mathbf L=\nabla\mathbf v$ kills tangent, acts on normal plane via $2\times2$ block $\mathbf K$); dynamics enters only via $\mathbf a$. Normal velocity: $-\mathbf K^{-1}$ times normal $\mathbf a$; tangential solvability: scalar condition $\Sigma=0$ per point ($\Sigma$: part of $\mathbf a$ outside range $\mathbf L$). Potential flow: $\mathbf K$ is strain rate, normal velocity pressure gradient over principal strain rate $\epsilon$, persistence needs uniform pressure on it. Stokes flow: tangential vorticity enters $\mathbf K$ (centre lines), $\Sigma$ involves normal vorticity. Navier-Stokes: $\Sigma$ set by instantaneous flow via nonlocal pressure, viscosity. If $\Sigma\ne0$, line becomes, to first order in $t$, isolated points at zeros of $\Sigma$ (critical points of $\varphi_t$ if potential; maybe none in Stokes flow: loops vanish). Symmetry (line an orbit of rigid-motion group, no velocity along it) suffices for persistence, not necessary: flows steady in rigidly moving frame have $\Sigma\equiv0$. Incompressibility enters via $\mathrm{tr}\mathbf K=0$; for inviscid irrotational homentropic compressible flow, line dilatation is $\varphi_{tt}/c^2$, so lines can be nodes, persistence needs uniform enthalpy, singular $\mathbf K$ arises at ordinary points, acoustic standing waves give exact examples (node line breaking into alternating sinks, saddles); also degenerate $\mathbf K$ (pairs born at distance $O(\sqrt t)$), curvature, torsion evolution, closure for moving-singularity-driven flows, helical and elliptically conical stagnation-point flow, exact Navier-Stokes example: saddle, centre lines split into four points per period.

papers.title: Demonstration of continuous non-invasive monitoring of plant metabolism using mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy
papers.summary: Life is a rhythmic process driven by cellular and physiological mechanisms that allow plants to respond and adapt to their environment. In addition to natural fluctuations, plants are increasingly exposed to environmental stresses, mainly caused by climate change and anthropogenic pollution. Multiple approaches across different biological scales (gene, cell, metabolite, and physiology) have shed light on acclimation mechanisms but generally lack sufficient temporal resolution. Establishing a non-invasive and high-temporal-resolution monitoring method to measure plant activity across different conditions is therefore needed to fully assess how plant metabolism changes under stress. Here, we established a novel approach to perform continuous and non-invasive mid-infrared photoacoustic spectroscopy on vascular plants, with the aim of identifying and monitoring the chemical composition of peripheral tissues, including sap, over periods ranging from a few minutes to several months. We describe an experimental setup, the physics underlying its operation, and present a multi-day acquisition. Compared with controls, data enabled to identify a diurnal pattern, with peaks of approximately equal duration, that recurred consistently over the experiment. Estimations of the impact of instrumental and environmental fluctuations indicate that the signal amplitude and trends cannot be explained by instrumental drifts. The experiment thus demonstrated the detection of a signal associated with plant physiological activity. While its origins remain to be clarified, this preliminary experiment demonstrates the feasibility of the measurements and provides a basis for future developments.

papers.title: Vibro-acoustic optimisation of sandwich panels using the wave/finite element method
papers.summary: This paper investigates the use of a wave-based method in the framework of structural optimisation of composite panels involving advanced components. The wave/finite element method (WFEM) is used to evaluate the influence of a core's geometry on the transition frequency of a sandwich panel involving composite skins. This transition occurs is a sandwich panel when the transverse shear stiffness has a significant influence on the flexural motion, compared to the bending stiffness. It follows that the modal density and the acoustic radiation will considerably increase above this frequency. The periodic waveguide is modelled at the mesoscopic scale using a 3D finite element model of the unit-cell. Therefore this method does not require an homogenisation of the core based on Gibson and Ashby formulations to provide the wave dispersion characteristics. Although the cellular cores compared in this study share the same mass-to-stiffness ratio, a significant alteration of the transition frequency and modal density can be observed compared to honeycomb cores. A periodic octagonal core is designed, providing up to 70 % increase of the transition frequency and a significant reduction of the modal density.

papers.title: Proton acceleration at interplanetary shocks: A numerical study for the HENON mission
papers.summary: The ESA-ASI HENON CubeSat mission will operate in a distant retrograde orbit about 0.08 au upstream of Earth to provide advance space-weather monitoring. Its instruments include an energetic particle detector measuring protons from 2 MeV to hundreds of MeV. Early detection of energetic particles is crucial for protecting technological infrastructure. To investigate proton acceleration at interplanetary shocks, we developed a test-particle numerical simulation in which protons move in the drift approximation around a parallel shock transition and gain energy through a first-order Fermi process at each crossing. They can propagate around the shock either diffusively or superdiffusively; particle transport affects shock acceleration. Protons were injected at the shock with an energy distribution of about 10 keV and scattered in pitch angle by a collision operator. We varied the pitch-angle scattering time, upstream and downstream plasma speeds, and the type of transport. In the superdiffusive case, a power-law distribution of scattering times was generated by mimicking a L\'evy walk. Multiple runs identify the parameter ranges that yield efficient acceleration and higher energies. For typical parameters, superdiffusive acceleration turns out to be somewhat faster than normal diffusive acceleration. We find that the main control parameter appears to be the upstream shock speed, and that energies in the range of 2-10 MeV can be reached for upstream speeds in the shock frame, $V_1$, of the order of 300 km/s or more. Conversely, for a speed of $V_1 \leq 150$ km/s the proton energy reaches only a few hundred keV. These results help explain why many interplanetary shocks accelerate ions only to moderate energies. They also suggest that when the HENON particle instrument is able to detect energetic protons above 2 MeV, the shock speed in the spacecraft frame is of the order of 800 km/s or more.

papers.title: How Much Does Auger Spectroscopy Add to XAS? A Fisher-information Analysis of Core-Hole Dynamics in $Ar^+$
papers.summary: X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) and resonant-Auger spectroscopy probe different stages of core-hole excitation and decay, but distinct spectra need not provide independent information about decay parameters. We quantify their complementarity for the $Ar^+$ $2p\to3d$ manifold using state-resolved atomic calculations and a two-parameter Fisher-information model. A common scale of primary autoionization rates $s_\Gamma$ and a selective spectator-$pp$ rescaling $\eta_{pp}$ both alter XAS linewidths. Their spectral responses are nearly collinear because the spectator-$pp$ fraction varies weakly among populated intermediate states. We compare XAS with an effective, scan-integrated, normalized Auger spectrum defined on a final-state-energy coordinate, with fixed excitation weights and final-state widths. Within this reduced observable, the common rate scale cancels from the normalized branching fractions, while $\eta_{pp}$ redistributes intensity among ionic final states. This cancellation is a property of the adopted model, not of photon-energy-resolved resonant-Auger spectroscopy generally. Under the reference count and resolution assumptions, XAS alone yields a Cram\'er-Rao lower bound (CRLB) corresponding to a 1.20% local fractional standard uncertainty in the excitation-weighted total natural width; adding Auger reduces this uncertainty by only 0.70%. In contrast, the uncertainty in the spectator-$pp$ branching fraction falls by 99.19%, with similarly large gains for partial-rate scales. A generalized Fisher comparison gives a 123.5-fold improvement on the standard-deviation scale along the most enhanced information mode. Thus, the principal benefit of the complementary Auger observable is to resolve a nearly degenerate decay-channel decomposition rather than substantially refine the total natural width.
