papers.title: Permafrost augmented simulation and forecast using hybrid modeling through spectral neural networks
papers.summary: Purpose - Global warming is impacting several crucial Earth systems, including the permafrost. This study investigates the possibility of performing fast and reliable simulation and forecasting of permafrost behavior, addressing a critical gap in the existing literature related to high computation times and energy costs of the simulations. Methodology - A numerical cryohydrogeological study on water and energy transfer in a forested, continuous permafrost site has been conducted using parallel high-performance computing to simulate the permafrost dynamics. The numerical results reasonably replicate the measured soil temperature profiles and the dynamics of infiltrated waters. This work uses a spectral network to achieve a fast, reliable, and stable surrogate model for the simulations to forecast over long periods of time. The surrogate is also enhanced by assimilating experimental data through the development of a hybrid modeling framework. Findings - The proposed approach improves the physical simulation while maintaining the stability of the dynamic model over long periods of time. The results reveal that the proposed hybrid modeling remains stable in integration and forecasting. The final hybrid solution demonstrates a significant improvement in simulation accuracy when tested against a test set of measurements. Predictions of the permafrost behavior in the coming decade are later made based on the CMIP6 climate change scenarios. Originality - This research offers a novel perspective on permafrost modeling that extends the current understanding of its behavior under different climate change scenarios. It shows a higher-than-expected temperature increase of the permafrost. Moreover, the stable forecasting of climate change effects is demonstrated.

papers.title: Epitaxial Displacement-etched GaAsSb Quantum Dots Emitting at Telecom Wavelengths
papers.summary: Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are essential components for integrated photonic and quantum information systems, yet current epitaxial growth techniques face significant limitations in complexity of growth, material selection, and density tunability. Here we report a displacement etch technique that enables controlled formation of GaAsSb QDs with emission at telecommunications wavelengths. Our approach uses arsenic molecular flux (As$_2$) to react with antimonide surfaces through thermodynamically favorable displacement reactions, creating three-dimensional quantum confined nanostructures without requiring strain-driven growth or complex droplet-based processes. Density functional theory shows the two competing As-for-Sb exchange pathways to be nearly equivalent in both reaction energy and activation barrier, which places morphological control in the subsequent adatom kinetics rather than in the surface reaction itself. A single process parameter, the As$_2$ exposure, sets the QD areal density across three orders of magnitude, from 10$^2$ to 10$^5$ $\mu m^{-2}$, covering both isolated emitters and dense gain media. Structural analysis reveals well-defined GaAsSb QDs with a mixed GaAs/GaSb composition and no extended defects. Temperature-dependent photoluminescence measurements confirm emission at 1550 nm (0.8 eV) within the telecommunications C-band, with characteristic QD-like temperature dependence. Because the QDs form on a lattice-matched GaSb surface in a single growth step, the technique offers a practical route to C-band emitters built into the GaSb/AlGaSb device family already used for mid-infrared sources and detectors.

papers.title: A 4-20 GHz Superconducting 90deg Hybrid Using Capacitively Loaded Coupled Lines for 2SB Heterodyne Receivers
papers.summary: We report the design and cryogenic characterisation of a broadband superconducting 90deg intermediate-frequency (IF) hybrid covering 4 to 20 GHz for sideband-separating (2SB) heterodyne receivers. The design supports the development of wide-instantaneous-bandwidth 2SB receivers for millimeter and submillimeter observatories, improving spectral grasp for broadband line surveys and high-redshift line searches.

papers.title: Frustration and topology in the phase behavior of solute-frustrated $q$-clock models
papers.summary: Frustration can enhance fluctuations and create new and interesting phase behavior. When combined with the ability to host topological defects, frustration can increase the complexity of a system's phase diagram through topological and frustrated topological transitions. To understand the interplay of frustration and topology on phase behavior, we introduce and study solute-frustrated $q$-clock (SF$q$C) models, in which solute sites are added to the $q$-clock model, a lattice model where each spin can take one of $q$ orientations. The $q$-clock model can exhibit spontaneous symmetry breaking and topological transitions, and the interaction between the spins and a solute frustrates the system, in essence by creating a fixed lower bound on the concentration of positive topological defects or vortices. We perform Monte Carlo simulations and develop theoretical descriptions of SF$q$C models with $q=4$ and $q=6$ to understand their phase behavior. We find that these systems exhibit rich phase diagrams that depend on the choice of parameters. In particular, SF$q$C models have a wide range of interesting low-temperature phases, including the presence of strongly frustrated domains and the absence of long-range order. We also find topological effects even at low temperatures; for instance, we find that topological defects can drive crystallization. We anticipate these results to guide the development of materials that take advantage of frustration and topology to tune phase behavior and fluctuations.

papers.title: Active rheology shapes collective flows in uniaxially compressed 3D spheroids
papers.summary: How compression changes both the magnitude and organization of cell motion remains unclear. Using a three-dimensional active vertex model, we examine how tissue state and active dynamics shape the response of confined spheroids to uniaxial compression. With polarity alignment switched off, compression enhances transverse motion in solid-like spheroids throughout the tested activity range, whereas the fluid-like response reverses from acceleration at low activity to slowing at high activity. Changes in contact persistence organize these responses along a common empirical trend. Passive five-cell calculations reveal how compression reshapes local rearrangement barriers: the response depends on geometry and loading direction, and a high-strain increase in the fluid-like mean coexists with many low-barrier paths. In a separate high-alignment regime, strong compression induces coherent rotation in solid-like spheroids, while fluid-like spheroids show no comparable collective rotation. The rotating solids have a higher contact-persistence index than the fluids and exhibit tangential peripheral cell organization. Controlled perturbations reveal compression-induced softening of a differential-twist mode and slower relaxation with activity. Together, these results identify an activity-dependent reversal of the motility response and compression-induced coherent rotation as two distinct outcomes of loading, linking them to contact persistence, local rearrangement costs, and active coordination.

papers.title: Strong Thermal Conductivity Suppression in Isotope Purified Single Crystal Diamond with Phonon Scatterings of Color Centers
papers.summary: The thermal conductivity of natural diamond can be further improved by ~50% by eliminating isotope impurity to obtain pure 12C diamond. However, unlike isolated point defects, how color centers scatter phonons and correspondingly limit the thermal conductivity remain poorly understood. Here, we report the thermal conductivities of two isotope-purified diamond with different Nitrogen-vacancy (NV) color center concentrations, confirmed by photoluminescence (PL) and secondary-ion mass spectrometry (SIMS). Results show ~ 3200 W m-1 K-1 and ~ 2100 W m-1 K-1 for two samples of low and high NV concentrations, respectively. Modified Callaway model analyses show that first-principles-derived scattering parameters can reproduce room-temperature thermal conductivity of the high NV concentration sample under a vacancy concentration assumption (~30% of the total Nitrogen concentration), but fail to reproduce its temperature dependence. Compared to PL and SIMS results, which show ~7.1-fold NV concentration and ~92-fold difference in total Nitrogen concentration between two samples, suggesting the assumed 30% vacancy fraction may be greatly overestimated. Taken together, these results suggest that NV-color-center defects may scatter phonons more strongly than models treating Nitrogen and vacancy as independent point defects, providing new insights into color-center-induced phonon-scattering mechanisms.

papers.title: HEXRD and HEXRDGUI: a flexible toolkit for X-ray diffraction analysis in dynamic compression experiments
papers.summary: This article describes the application of HEXRD, an open-source Python library for X-ray diffraction analysis, and HEXRDGUI, its companion graphical application, to dynamic compression experiments. Built on a generic multi-detector geometric model, the toolkit supports arbitrary instrument configurations with independently positioned planar or cylindrical detector panels, arbitrary beam directions, and multiple X-ray sources. It calibrates instruments from powder rings, Laue spots or the rings of an unknown phase, fits whole patterns by Le Bail or Rietveld refinement, and imports data from the TARDIS, FIDDLE and PXRDIP platforms at the National Ignition Facility (NIF) and OMEGA EP. Although originally developed for high-energy diffraction microscopy at synchrotron sources, HEXRD has been adopted as an analysis tool for dynamic compression X-ray diffraction experiments at facilities including the NIF, the Matter in Extreme Conditions end-station at the Linac Coherent Light Source, the Dynamic Compression Sector (DCS) at the Advanced Photon Source, OMEGA EP at the Laboratory for Laser Energetics, and the High Energy Density (HED) instrument at the European XFEL. Calibrated from the same ring positions on a single planar detector, HEXRD and the independent code pyFAI predict the same scattering angle 2$\theta$ to numerical precision. On a dual-source dataset from the NIF, calibrating the detectors against both X-ray sources at once fits the rings of both to an RMS of 0.18{\deg} in 2$\theta$, about one image-plate pixel, whereas a fit to either source alone, with the plate tilts held at their nominal values, fits its own rings nearly as well but mispredicts the other's by about 0.6{\deg}. papers.title: Spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior
papers.summary: Uncovering low-dimensional representations of brain-wide neural dynamics and their relationship to behavior remains a central challenge. Here, we show that spontaneous brain-wide rotational dynamics constrain cue-evoked behavior and learning. To systematically establish these findings, we developed a dimensionality-reduction technique called Rotational Component Analysis (RCA) that optimizes the detection of low-variance rotational modes even within individual trials. We applied RCA to motor-cortical spike-train data from monkeys and humans, mouse cortex-wide calcium imaging, and human functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and magnetoencephalography (MEG). In mice, a rotational mode identified from activity recorded at rest predicts cue-evoked behavior: the phase of rotation when a randomly timed cue arrives predicts whether the animal subsequently pulls the lever. We explain this surprisingly strong correlation using both a recurrent neural network (RNN) and a minimal two-dimensional model of response learning, in which the intrinsic rotational mode serves as a dynamical constraint on response and learning. We further identify double-rotation modes containing two centers of rotation that separate preparatory from task dynamics in both mouse and human data. Remarkably, corresponding modes also organize neural dynamics during a non-motor human task, and rotational irreversibility captures early psychosis even when principal component analysis shows no group difference. Our work establishes rotational dynamics as low-dimensional coordinates that constrain how ongoing brain states are converted into behavior. More broadly, RCA provides a versatile tool for detecting hidden nonreciprocal dynamics in biological and physical datasets.

papers.title: Photon production at Kepler escape threshold
papers.summary: We obtain an exact closed-form total photon count for a prescribed Newtonian Kepler parabola, with a fully relativistic treatment of its radiation. We also obtain closed expressions for the angularly resolved photon spectrum and elementary expressions for the total radiated energy and momenta. The count is finite, scale-independent, and analytic in subluminal speed at closest approach. At large maximum rapidity $\eta$, $N\sim(7\alpha/\sqrt6)\eta$, while $E\propto e^{3\eta}$ at fixed passage timescale: the radiation chiefly hardens. For slow motion at fixed coupling and closest distance, a nearby ellipse emits fewer photons but more energy and angular momentum per orbit. The hyperbolic photon count remains IR divergent arbitrarily close to threshold, while the count at the exact parabolic threshold is finite.

papers.title: Dependence of the acoustic propulsion of nano- and microcones on their orientation and aspect ratio
papers.summary: Recent research revealed the orientation-dependent propulsion of a cone-shaped colloidal particle that is exposed to a planar traveling ultrasound wave. Here, we extend the previous research by considering nano- and microcones with different aspect ratios and studying how the propulsion of a particle depends on its orientation and aspect ratio. We also study how the orientation-averaged propulsion of a cone-shaped particle, which corresponds to an isotropic ultrasound field, depends on its aspect ratio and identify an aspect ratio of 1/2 where the orientation-averaged propulsion is particularly strong. To make our simulation results easier reusable for follow-up research, we provide a corresponding simple analytic representation.

papers.title: Squeezing and Decoherence of Axion Dark Matter
papers.summary: Bosonic particles beyond the Standard Model, such as axions, are among the leading candidates for dark matter. If such particles have a small mass, they are usually described as a purely classical field. However, it was recently shown that this description is incomplete: their inherent gravitational self-interactions can squeeze the field, producing a quantum feature beyond the classical description. Here we analyze squeezing of light dark matter in the presence of decoherence. We show that squeezing is continuously generated, and rapidly enough to survive dissipation, and may also remain present under thermal fluctuations and dephasing. Our results demonstrate that dark matter might possess persistent quantum features and motivate further investigation of their implications for dark matter detection.

papers.title: \textit{In situ} certification of multiparticle indistinguishability in a generic interferometer
papers.summary: We propose a scalable and efficient \textit{in situ} method for assessing the multiparticle indistinguishability of identical bosons or fermions in quantum interference experiments on linear interferometers by harnessing quantum parallelism and the bunching/anti-bunching tendencies of these particles. The proposed certification method can be applied to any generic linear interferometer. For particles occupying distinct input ports of a Haar-random unitary interferometer, the number of experimental runs required to attain a prescribed statistical precision is polynomial in the number of particles, the interferometer size, and the inverse precision, with high probability. Our method is robust under losses: for uniform particle losses, the polynomial scaling is preserved when the inverse single-particle survival probability is polynomially bounded. Our scheme is especially suitable for certifying the indistinguishability of single photons in large-scale interference experiments, such as Boson Sampling in the regime of quantum advantage over classical computation.

papers.title: NEP-kappa 2.0: A unified framework for phonon transport and nonequilibrium thermalization with machine-learning interatomic potentials
papers.summary: We present NEP-kappa 2.0, a unified framework that integrates density-functional theory, material-specific machine-learning interatomic potentials, and pretrained force models for advanced phonon calculations. A common workflow enables harmonic lattice dynamics, quasi-harmonic and stochastic self-consistent phonon treatments, three- and four-phonon transport, Wigner population--coherence transport, and time-dependent phonon dynamics. Applications to 3C-SiC, BAs, and Cs$_2$AgInCl$_6$ demonstrate consistent force-model comparisons, finite-temperature renormalization, higher-order scattering, and intermode coherence. Beyond steady-state transport, mode-resolved simulations of selectively excited 3C-SiC reveal that half of the injected optical-phonon energy reaches acoustic modes within approximately 3.75 ps, primarily through one-optical--two-acoustic scattering. Acoustic branches exhibit response times differing by a factor of five, with competing scattering channels producing a transient energy overshoot. Channel-resolved entropy production and persistent nonthermal occupations distinguish interbranch energy redistribution from intrabranch thermalization. The framework connects equilibrium phonon transport with microscopic nonequilibrium energy dynamics.

papers.title: Multiplicative Noise in Nanolaser Amplification: From Discrete Emission Events to the Additive-Noise Limit
papers.summary: Laser amplification kicks off with just a few photons in the cavity, a regime where standard additive Langevin noise cannot capture the real fluctuations. To understand how this amplification begins, we map out a single-mode photon-carrier model that links macroscopic lasers directly into nanolasers. Stationary rate equations reveal that stimulated emission takes over across a tight pump window. In nanolasers, however, spontaneous processes coexist across a much broader range. Because steady-state averages miss the individual events that lead to the macroscopic photon number, we frame the stochastic dynamics around the actual discrete transitions, deriving a state-dependent diffusion approximation. The destruction of an excited carrier concurrent with the generation of a photon creates a negative photon-carrier cross-correlation. This unavoidably leads to a correlated, multiplicative Gaussian-noise framework. We track the resulting discrete dynamics with an established, event-based Laser Markov Chain (LMC) which stochastically samples pump, relaxation, emission, and cavity-loss events keeping all physical quantities as non-negative integers. Comparing its predictions to those of our multiplicative model proves that the latter reproduces excellently well the statistical behavior of photons and carrier, as long as a continuous diffusion description holds. Once the emission drops into the few-photon regime, however, the discrete model becomes indispensable. On the other hand, at large photon counts relative fluctuations shrink to a level where the state-dependence of the diffusion matrix can be ignored, to leading order, thus returning to the classic Langevin description of the system's stochastic dynamics.

papers.title: Measuring the Quantum Phase of Multiphoton Systems
papers.summary: The quantum phase of a multiparticle system has remained a long-standing mystery in quantum physics. The absence of a phase operator that faithfully represents this physical quantity has prevented the formulation of a meaningful uncertainty relation with particle number. Here, we resolve this problem by measuring, for the first time, the quantum phase of multiparticle systems containing up to fifteen particles. We achieve this through a new quantum state tomography scheme that combines homodyne interferometry with photon-number-resolving detection. This approach enables us to reconstruct complementary photon-number and phase representations and establish the corresponding number-phase uncertainty relation. Our measurements further provide access to the mutually unbiased basis of a multiparticle system, a fundamental resource for multiparticle quantum information processing. Furthermore, we report the spatially resolved characterization of the quantum phase. These results provide an operational framework for measuring quantum phase in multiparticle systems, with implications for fundamental quantum physics and scalable multiparticle quantum technologies.

papers.title: A Stress-Induced Tetragonal Distortion in K2OsCl6 under Pressure
papers.summary: The structural behaviour of cubic (Fm-3m) K2OsCl6 under compression was investigated to 35.4 GPa using angle-dispersive synchrotron powder X-ray diffraction. Upon increasing pressure, K2OsCl6 undergoes a sequence of structural transformations from the ambient-pressure cubic phase to a tetragonal (P4/mnc) phase above 9.5(3) GPa, followed by a transition to a monoclinic (P21/n) phase beginning at approximately 14.2 GPa. The tetragonal and monoclinic phases coexist over the pressure range 14.2-17.2 GPa, while the monoclinic phase is observed as the sole phase at 17.9 GPa and remains stable up to the maximum pressure investigated. Analysis of the diffraction profiles and unit-cell parameters indicates that the intermediate tetragonal structure is likely associated with stress-induced symmetry lowering rather than a distinct thermodynamic phase. This distortion, which is adequately described by the tetragonal P4/mnc space group, is attributed to non-hydrostatic deviatoric stresses arising from the pressure-transmitting medium. Equation-of-state analysis reveals a pronounced reduction in compressibility across the structural transitions, with the bulk modulus increasing from 26(2) GPa for the cubic phase to 71(3) GPa for the monoclinic phase. The pressure-induced structural sequence is analogous to that reported for related compounds such as K2IrCl6, although the transitions in K2OsCl6 occur at lower pressures. All structural transformations are reversible upon decompression.

papers.title: Effect of chirality on active elastomers and solids in three dimensions
papers.summary: We examine the effect of chiral activity on nematic and polar uniaxial elastomers and solids by constructing the general hydrodynamic equations for these phases. We start with the elastomer, which is not only invariant under rigid rotations but also under an independent rotation of the uniaxial direction, and show that this higher symmetry strongly constrains the effects of chiral activity. We then break the elastomeric symmetry by adding a symmetry-breaking term to the free energy but still retain invariance under rigid rotations. The resulting state has the symmetry of a uniaxial solid, and we show that in a fixed background medium chiral activity generically destabilises it. The force density responsible for this {{instability}} vanishes as the field that breaks the elastomeric symmetry goes to zero. Further, the presence of the symmetry-breaking field also allows for an additional odd elastic force density that generically destabilises momentum-conserved chiral and uniaxial solids in the inertial regime.

papers.title: Chirality destroys oriented active solids
papers.summary: We construct a hydrodynamic theory of the effect of chiral and active force densities on three-dimensional uniaxial solids. We show that in a fixed background medium active chiral force densities---that arise at lower order in gradients than odd elasticity---generically destabilise the solid state. We further show this active instability also affects isotropic chiral solids in an anisotropic medium, a situation that is relevant for cell clusters moving through the extracellular matrix. Interestingly, the instability is eliminated in a higher-symmetry solid, known as the polar elastomer; indeed, we show that chirality does not affect the leading-order mechanics of such materials. We further demonstrate that momentum-conserving polar active solids have two chiral odd elasticities in contrast to the one discussed for two-dimensional solids. However, we again find that the higher symmetry of polar elastomers eliminates one of these with the remaining one being equivalent to the two-dimensional odd elastic force density. Our results should apply to numerous biological and condensed matter systems.

papers.title: Time-resolved transient absorption spectroscopy with quantum light
papers.summary: We present a fully quantum theory of time-resolved transient absorption spectroscopy, providing a general framework for describing the linear response of a nonequilibrium target to quantum probe fields beyond the semiclassical approximation. We elucidate how quantum correlations between probe-field frequency modes couple to coherences in the target and derive a simple expression for computing the resulting spectroscopic signals. We identify conditions under which quantum light can modify transient absorption spectra beyond the limits achievable with classical fields. Our work establishes a theoretical foundation for exploiting quantum light in ultrafast spectroscopy and suggests new routes for resolving dynamics in matter on timescales shorter than the duration of the probe pulse.

papers.title: Gini coefficient of scientists and universities
papers.summary: Using the public database of Google Scholar article citations of scientists and universities we apply the algorithm for constructing Lorenz curves to the resulting citation distributions. Using Lorenz and Pareto curves, broadly used for economic analyses of wealth inequality across countries, we show that this approach gives a useful insight of citation distributions of world-leading scientists characterized by the Gini coefficient $G$ obtained from the Lorenz curves. For articles of 15 Nobel laureates (including A. Einstein and R. Feynman) we find the average $G=0.81$ with 50% of articles capturing only 2.7% of all citations and the top 10% (1%) of articles capturing 71% (30%) of all citations. Furthmore, we determine for world-leading universities the Gini coefficient via the citations of affiliated scientists. We show that about 65 percent of all citations belonging to a university (e.g. Princeton, Cambridge) are generated only by 10 percent of their university scientists while 50% of scientists produce only 3% of all university citations. The citation distributions are well described by the concept of Rayleigh-Jeans thermalization and condensation with similarities traced to the world wealth inequality.

papers.title: evaluating local viscoelastic properties of artery-mimicking phantoms using high-resolution flexural wavenumber analysis
papers.summary: The measurement of guided wave propagation is an effective approach for evaluating arterial wall stiffness. A more comprehensive characterization of viscoelastic material properties could yield more informative biomarkers; however, this additionally requires estimation of wave attenuation. Furthermore, spatially local estimation is necessary for localized pathologies, such as atherosclerotic plaques. To this end, we propose an original two-stage high-resolution method to recover local viscoelastic properties from guided waves in artery-like soft tubes. First, the local frequency-wavenumber dispersion relation including losses is estimated using a high-resolution complex wavenumber identification method. Second, assuming a fractional Kelvin-Voigt rheological model for the tube wall, we estimate the viscoelastic material parameters by fitting the dispersion relation computed with a spectral element method to this estimate. We experimentally validate the proposed approach on flexural wave propagation along water-filled soft tubes, measured with a high-speed camera coupled with digital image correlation. Owing to the high resolution of the method, the axial modulus variation of a graded phantom is recovered. Finally, a Cram\'er-Rao analysis indicates that the complex wavenumber estimator operates near its theoretical limit, and reveals why local attenuation is intrinsically difficult to recover.

papers.title: Superstability of micrometer viscous jets surrounded by weakly-elastic viscous shells
papers.summary: Our experiments demonstrate the strong stabilizing effect of a viscoelastic shell on flow-focused viscous jets. The results suggest that stabilization occurs when the polymer viscosity, $\eta_p$, exceeds a critical threshold, provided the extensional relaxation time, $\lambda$, is large enough to allow the polymer molecules to undergo the coil-stretch transition. Under these conditions, substantial extensional viscoelastic stresses develop as the liquid accelerates. Since both $\eta_p$ and $\lambda$ increase with shell viscosity, the polymer concentration required to stabilize the viscous jet decreases accordingly. Remarkably, moderately to highly viscous jets can be stabilized with very small polymer concentrations, for which no beads-on-a-string (BOAS) instability is observed.

papers.title: Finite-size scaling of spin-wave scattering and enhancement in magnonic Fabry-P\'erot nanoresonators
papers.summary: Magnonic neural networks require compact resonant nodes that scatter spin waves efficiently, concentrate spin-wave energy and can be reconfigured. Hybrid magnonic Fabry-P\'erot resonators, formed by a ferromagnetic-metal stripe dipolar-coupled to a yttrium iron garnet (YIG) film, provide low-loss and programmable control of spin-wave transmission, but have so far been studied only for stripes that are long compared with the spin-wave wavelength. Here we use micromagnetic simulations to determine how the response of a 200-nm-wide CoFeB stripe on a 55-nm-thick YIG film evolves as the stripe length is reduced from infinity to 640 nm. An infinitely long stripe acts as a one-dimensional cavity that opens a transmission gap at the first-order resonance (1.70 GHz and 1.47 GHz for the parallel and antiparallel magnetic configuration) and enhances the out-of-plane precession amplitude in the YIG film by factors of about 5 and 12, without distorting the transmitted wavefront. For lengths of a few micrometers, backward-volume spin waves emitted from the stripe ends modulate the precession along the stripe and fragment the reflected and transmitted wavefronts. Below about 1.2 micrometer, the resonator scatters incident spin waves over the entire isofrequency contour of the film, with caustic beams that are most pronounced in the antiparallel configuration. In this regime the parallel configuration supports weakly enhanced quantized modes, whereas the antiparallel configuration supports a single mode with an out-of-plane enhancement of about 15. The width, thickness and shape of the stripe tune this mode by 50-100 MHz, and its strong enhancement lowers the onset of nonlinear frequency shift and fold-over to incident amplitudes of a few percent of the saturation magnetization. Sub-micrometer magnonic resonators are therefore promising reconfigurable nonlinear nodes for magnonic networks.

papers.title: Simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation for stochastic reaction networks
papers.summary: Uncovering stochastic reaction networks from data is central to single-cell biology. Simulation-based inference has evolved into a flexible paradigm for this purpose, circumventing the computational intractability of the likelihood. Notably, approximate Bayesian computation performs this inference by carrying out extensive Gillespie simulations, usually at a high computational cost. Here, we propose a simulation-free approximate Bayesian computation (SFABC) framework that avoids both simulation and explicit likelihood solutions of the network dynamics. Instead, SFABC exploits the Chemical Master Equation to formulate a tractable convex optimization with ensuing constraints, which are then used to accept sampled parameters consistent with the observed data. The resulting posterior approximation comes with theoretical guarantees: it can be tightened systematically, and it provably converges to the exact Bayesian posterior distributions. Using synthetic benchmarks, we show that SFABC matches the accuracy of standard simulation-based algorithms at a substantially reduced computational cost. We then showcase the applicability of SFABC to experimental systems biology by analyzing gene transcription bursting kinetics from snapshot, time-resolved, and cell-cycle-resolved single-cell data.

papers.title: Two-Dimensional Quantum Droplets in a Mixture of Bose-Einstein Condensates
papers.summary: Quantum droplets represent a striking manifestation of beyond-mean-field physics, with properties that depend sensitively on dimensionality. Although quantum droplets have been experimentally realized in one and three dimensions, their realization in two dimensions has remained elusive. Here, we observe the formation of a two-dimensional (2D) quantum droplet in a quasi-2D geometry by transferring the single-component Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs) into a spin mixture in the Lee-Huang-Yang (LHY) regime, where the LHY effect evidently deviates from its three-dimensional form. We find that, in our scheme, 2D quantum droplets are more stable and exhibit longer lifetimes than previously reported quantum droplets. By instead transferring the initial BECs into another single-spin state with a negative scattering length, we generate 2D Townes solitons. A comparison between the two types of self-bound states shows that, whereas 2D Townes solitons are stable only near a critical atom number determined by the scattering length, 2D quantum droplets remain well-defined and self-bound over a much broader parameter range. These realizations of quantum droplets and Townes solitons in two dimensions provide new insights into self-bound states and open new avenues for exploring nonlinear dynamics in quantum liquids.

papers.title: End-to-End Optimization of Partial Fault Tolerance in Neutral-Atom Arrays
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant (FT) quantum computation offers a pathway to quantum advantage, but its realization is hindered by its significant overhead. The partially FT "STAR" architecture reduces the cost of universal computation at the price of relaxing FT requirements for non-Clifford operations, increasing exposure to hardware noise. Therefore, maximizing its performance and applicability demands careful co-design with the underlying hardware. In this work we investigate the co-design of the STAR architecture with neutral-atom platforms, connecting the underlying atomic physics to logical error modeling and application-level performance. At the physical level, we identify a favorable noise bias in $^{171}\mathrm{Yb}$ Rydberg gates, and show how it can be enhanced through error-selective pulse optimization. At the logical level, we identify an intrinsic error suppression mechanism, yielding vanishing logical coherent noise in leading order. Detailed circuit-level simulations of surface code implementations show more than an order of magnitude reduction in logical error relative to previous estimates. As a concrete target application, we focus on the Fermi-Hubbard model with periodic boundaries, for which we design a simulation circuit particularly suited to early implementations. We quantify the resource tradeoff of partially and fully FT approaches to gate synthesis, with the former showing approximately an order of magnitude reduction in state-injection depth, and an even larger reduction in Clifford resources. Comparing with classical and fully FT approaches, we identify regimes where partial fault tolerance provides both lower overheads and lower error rates. In our estimates, this is accessible with moderate error rates $p\sim 10^{-3}$ and a few thousand qubits, underlining that for these types of problems, partial FT approaches provide a compelling pathway to early quantum advantage.

papers.title: Non-local Stabilization and Synchronization of Larmor Precession in Trapped Polariton Condensate Dimer
papers.summary: We demonstrate mutual synchronization of Larmor precessions between spatially separated, optically trapped polariton condensates. We identify the cross-condensate correlation g(2)1,2({\tau}) as a sensitive metric for condensate coupling. Synchronization of precessions in a condensate dimer is mediated by polariton outflow and resonantly depends on spectral overlap and precession winding. All-optical stirring of one site non-locally increases the pseudo-spin dephasing time of its static neighbor, prolonging phase-locking in a dimer by an order of magnitude. Our work establishes a scalable platform for studying non-equilibrium time-periodically driven systems and for high-speed spinoptronic networks.

papers.title: Vacancy and Helium-Cluster Thermomigration in Tungsten
papers.summary: Strong thermal gradients in tungsten plasma-facing components can bias the migration of irradiation-induced defects and thereby alter their redistribution, interaction, and retention. Here, we extend an atomistic jump-statistics framework previously developed for hydrogen to quantify the thermomigration of a single vacancy and interstitial He$_1$--He$_4$ clusters in body-centered-cubic tungsten. Non-equilibrium molecular-dynamics simulations performed over several thermal gradients are used to determine the directional jump ratio, while geometrically derived projected jump lengths convert the fitted directional-bias coefficient into the heat-of-transport coefficient $Q^*=\alpha kT^2$, where $k$ is the Boltzmann constant, $T$ the temperature, and $\alpha$ a constant. All investigated defects exhibit negative values of $\alpha$, corresponding to net migration toward the hot region. He$_4$ has the largest response, $\alpha=-2.2457\times10^{-2}$ K$^{-1}$, followed closely by the vacancy, whereas He$_3$ exhibits the weakest response despite its intermediate cluster size. Independent constant-temperature simulations over 1000--1600 K show that He$_3$ is also the least mobile cluster and has the largest effective migration energy, $E_m^{\mathrm{eff}}=0.271$ eV. In contrast, He$_4$ is more mobile than He$_3$ and has the smallest effective migration energy, 0.087 eV. Agreement between the He$_3$ concentration profile predicted from the jump statistics and that obtained from a long molecular-dynamics trajectory provides an independent validation of the method. These results show that thermomigration cannot be inferred from cluster size, diffusivity, or migration energy alone and provide defect-specific heat-of-transport parameters for higher-length-scale models of tungsten under fusion-relevant thermal gradients.

papers.title: Measurement-efficient energy estimator for quantum chemistry of photodynamic materials
papers.summary: Accurate modelling of chemical reaction rates requires precise correlated energy differences. Quantum computing offers a potential route to their determination, but extracting energies from quantum-prepared states can demand prohibitive sampling. We demonstrate measurement-efficient correlated energy estimation using an electronically challenging H$_2$DBB--Ru model derived from a Ru-functionalized hafnium metal-organic framework relevant to radiodynamic and photodynamic therapies. The mixed estimator combines a quantum-prepared target with sparse multiconfiguration references and recovers ground-state corrections using magnitude-only compute-uncompute measurements. Analytical variance estimates predict 1.6 mHa precision with a few hundred shots, about 100 times fewer than the single-determinant formulation and three orders of magnitude fewer than optimized Hamiltonian-term sampling. With approximate targets, it reaches comparable accuracy using simpler state preparation than direct expectation-value estimation. Emulator and trapped-ion experiments on Quantinuum Helios validate the approach up to (10,10), including a 50-qubit circuit combining AI-assisted state preparation with error detection, providing a measurement-efficient route to correlated energy differences for challenging chemical problems.

papers.title: Proximity Transient Absorption in van der Waals Heterostructures
papers.summary: Transient absorption spectroscopy is a widely used technique for investigating ultrafast electronic dynamics, where transient optical signals are generally interpreted as arising from excitations within the material hosting the probed optical transition. A distinct form of transient absorption spectroscopy, termed proximity transient absorption (PTA), is demonstrated, in which the probed optical transition and the monitored photoexcited carriers reside in different materials. Using graphene/hBN/WS$_2$ heterostructures, photoexcited carriers in graphene induce a strong transient optical response at the excitonic resonance of a WS$_2$ monolayer through Coulomb screening, even when the two layers remain electronically isolated by an atomically thin hBN spacer. The resulting signal follows the carrier dynamics of graphene rather than those of WS$_2$, demonstrating that the WS$_2$ exciton acts as an optical transducer of electronic processes in a neighboring material. The signal decreases systematically with increasing hBN thickness, confirming its proximity origin while remaining substantial for separations approaching 2 nm. PTA provides a noncontact approach for optically modulating one material using photoexcited carriers in another and enables probing of carrier dynamics in materials that are otherwise difficult to investigate directly. More broadly, PTA establishes a new modality of ultrafast spectroscopy and reveals that transient optical signals in van der Waals heterostructures can originate from excitations residing in spatially separated layers.

papers.title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
papers.summary: Legged locomotion on flowing ground ({\em e.g.} granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s ($\approx 60$ cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction $\phi$ and the limb frequency $\omega$, and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when $\phi$ becomes small enough and/or $\omega$ large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.

papers.title: The hidden spin-momentum locking and topological defects in unpolarized light fields
papers.summary: Electromagnetic waves characterized by intensity, phase, and polarization degrees of freedom are widely applied in data storage, encryption, and communications. However, these properties can be substantially affected by phase disorders and disturbances, whereas high-dimensional degrees of freedom including momentum and angular momentum of electromagnetic waves can offer new insights into their features and phenomena, for example topological characteristics and structures that are robust to these disturbances. Here, we discover and demonstrate theoretically and experimentally spin-momentum locking and topological defects in unpolarized light. The coherent spin is locked to the kinetic momentum except for a small coupling spin term, due to the simultaneous presence of transverse magnetic and electric components in unpolarized light. To cancel the coupling term, we employ a metal film acting as a polarizer to form some skyrmion-like spin textures at the metal/air interface. Using an in-house scanning optical microscopic system to image the out-of-plane spin density of the focused unpolarized vortex light, we obtained experimental results that coincide well with our theoretical predictions. The theory and technique promote the applications of topological defects in optical data storage, encryption, and decryption, and communications.

papers.title: Clustering coefficients for networks with higher order interactions
papers.summary: We introduce a clustering coefficient for nondirected and directed hypergraphs, which we call the quad clustering coefficient. We determine the average quad clustering coefficient and its distribution in real-world hypergraphs and compare its value with those of random hypergraphs drawn from the configuration model. We find that real-world hypergraphs exhibit a nonnegligible fraction of nodes with a maximal value of the quad clustering coefficient, while we do not find such nodes in random hypergraphs. Interestingly, these highly clustered nodes can have large degrees and can be incident to hyperedges of large cardinality. Moreover, highly clustered nodes are not observed in an analysis based on the pairwise clustering coefficient of the associated projected graph that has binary interactions, and hence higher order interactions are required to identify nodes with a large quad clustering coefficient.

papers.title: Nanoparticle arrays levitated in a cavity for quantum sensing
papers.summary: Levitated nanoparticles are being investigated as ultrasensitive quantum sensors of forces and accelerations, with applications ranging from fundamental physics phenomena such as dark matter or quantum gravity to real world applications. Attention is now turning to multiparticle regimes, and an important question is whether collective effects offer advantages for sensing. We investigate here the spectral characteristics of collective motion of $N $ trapped nanoparticles interacting via the optical mode of a cavity. We find the collective motion typically exhibit two generic spectral features: a broad spectral feature, the collective bright mode (CBM) which has been previously studied; but we find also a new structure of sharp peaks , the mechanical mode comb (MMC). We can describe all the detailed spectral features of the system, with a simple closed-form expression, by reducing the motion to a 1D generic collective mode which is non-Hermitian. We show that the MMC is more advantageous than the usual CBM for increased sensitivity in force sensing. We find that the mechanical comb can autonomously repair loss of `teeth' due to particle loss, a feature that may offer robustness in sensing.

papers.title: Intercity connectivity and urban innovation
papers.summary: Urban outputs, from economy to innovation, are known to grow as a power of a city's population. But, since large cities tend to be central in transportation and communication networks, the effects attributed to city size may be confounded with those of intercity connectivity. Here, we map intercity networks for the world's two largest economies (the United States and China) to explore whether a city's position in the networks of communication, human mobility, and scientific collaboration explains variance in a city's patenting activity that is unaccounted for by its population. We find evidence that models incorporating intercity connectivity outperform population-based models and exhibit stronger predictive power for patenting activity, particularly for technologies of more recent vintage (which we expect to be more complex or sophisticated). The effects of intercity connectivity are more robust in China, even after controlling for population, GDP, and education, but not in the United States once adjusted for GDP and education. This divergence suggests distinct urban network dynamics driving innovation in these regions. In China, models with social media and mobility networks explain more heterogeneity in the scaling of innovation, whereas in the United States, scientific collaboration plays a more significant role. These findings support the significance of a city's position within the intercity network in shaping its success in innovative activities.

papers.title: The cost of connectivity: Network tradeoffs in subway expansion and historic street preservation
papers.summary: As cities become increasingly interconnected, expanding regional mobility networks can come at the cost of local social networks. This study examines such tradeoffs in the case of Miaoqianzhijie, a historic street in Guangzhou, China, which was planned to be demolished for building a new interchange subway at Line 10. We introduce a network tradeoff framework that analyzes subway lines as spatial networks and his-toric streets as social networks within a single analytic frame. Empirically, we combine a participatory GIS-based social network survey with origin-destination (OD) flow analysis of Guangzhou's subway system. Our findings show that Miaoqianzhijie functions as a dense corridor of social infrastructure that support everyday routines, social ties, mutual aid, and symbolic place attachment for residents, workers, and frequent visitors. Our OD analysis found that Line 10's mobility benefits are unevenly distributed and the station closest to the demolition area sees only modest improve-ments. These findings reveal an asymmetric network tradeoff that highlights concentrated social connectivity losses versus diffuse and limited local mobility gains. This study contributes a case study and network-based methodology for representing such tradeoffs and highlights how these representations can inform more equitable planning debates around subway expansion and historic street preservation.

papers.title: SynradG4: A Geant4-Based Extension for Synchrotron Radiation Background Studies in the ePIC Detector at the Electron-Ion Collider
papers.summary: The Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will operate at high luminosity with multi-GeV, high-current electron beams, resulting in substantial synchrotron radiation (SR) emission in the electron storage ring (ESR). A detailed understanding of SR photon transport in the complex three-dimensional interaction region (IR) geometry is critical for estimating backgrounds in the ePIC detector and for developing effective shielding and masking strategies. This paper presents SynradG4, an EIC-specific extension of Geant4 for fast photon tracking in vacuum based on established models of SR reflection and rough-surface scattering. SynradG4 integrates the specular and diffuse photon reflection models of Synrad+ into the Geant4 geometry and field framework, while disabling all bulk matter interactions to achieve high-statistics transport through the 50-m-long IR vacuum system. The absorbed photons are then passed to a second-stage DD4hep simulation, in which electromagnetic processes such as photoabsorption, Compton scattering, Rayleigh scattering, and fluorescence are enabled for their propagation through the beam pipe and detector materials. SynradG4 is not intended to replace general SR simulation codes; rather, it complements them by providing the workflow and geometry integration capabilities needed for EIC-specific background studies. Benchmark tests show that SynradG4 reproduces Synrad+ to within about 1% for both specular and diffuse reflection, and that it agrees well with Synrad3D and with the native Geant4 X-ray reflection model for smooth surfaces. Using the full IR geometry and machine lattice, we present the first SR background estimates for the ePIC detector and evaluate the impact of potential SR masks.

papers.title: Rethinking Symmetry Principles and Partial Observables With Reference Frames
papers.summary: Dynamically uncoupled fields are a modelling device used in the literature on reference frames, classical and quantum. We argue that the device is not innocuous. First, uncoupled fields violate Earman's symmetry principle SP1---that every dynamical symmetry is a spacetime symmetry---and the violation, unlike the familiar Newtonian one, cannot be repaired by excising surplus spacetime structure: it arises from a deficit of dynamical structure, not an excess of spatiotemporal structure. This qualifies implicit assumptions of Earman's SP1, while leaving its diagnostic role intact. Second, uncoupled fields expose a lacuna in the partial/complete observables programme: only dynamically coupled fields can serve as bona-fide partial observables, so partial observability is derivative on complete observability. We then reinterpret the standard formalism for partial observables: qua measurable, a partial observable is a relational quantity expressed with respect to an uncoupled frame, and it remains gauge-variant. This reinterpretation vindicates Rovelli's claim that partial observables are individually measurable, against Thiemann and Adlam, and separates two properties easily conflated in the generally covariant formulations of theories: invariance under diffeomorphisms and invariance along the gauge flow.

papers.title: A New Theory of the Dark Photon and Its Preliminary Experimental Verification
papers.summary: The dark photon defined in this paper is fundamentally different from the dark photon in the traditional kinetic mixing framework. According to the principle of energy conservation, a complete moving photon is defined in this work as a binary composite entity consisting of a dark photon and a light-wave component. The dark photon embodies the particle nature of light, while the light-wave embodies the wave nature of light. When the light source is turned off or the light-wave component is absorbed by matter, the complete photon loses its light-wave component and transforms into a pure dark photon state. In conventional high-energy physics, dark photons from kinetic mixing scenarios exhibit no direct electromagnetic coupling and cannot be detected through experiments. In distinct contrast, the dark photon proposed in this work possesses intrinsic particle properties of light, enables direct electromagnetic interaction, and can induce the photoelectric effect upon incidence on a metal surface. Based on this self-consistent definition, a systematic theory of dark photons is established, which provides reasonable physical interpretations for several currently controversial optical phenomena. The experimental scheme in this paper is designed strictly based on the above theoretical premise. Preliminary tabletop experimental results verify the rationality and feasibility of the proposed dark photon theory.

papers.title: Comprehensive Analysis of Relative Pressure Estimation in Type B Aortic Dissection Utilizing 4D-Flow MRI
papers.summary: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) can estimate three-dimensional (3D) time-resolved blood velocity fields using 4D-flow MRI, providing rich relative pressure field information. Clinical alternatives---catheterization and Doppler echocardiography---provide one-dimensional pressure drops. While the accuracy of one-dimensional pressure drops from 4D-flow has been explored, the accuracy of 3D relative pressure field estimates requires further evaluation. This work analyzes three state-of-the-art relative pressure estimators: virtual Work-Energy Relative Pressure (vWERP), the Pressure Poisson Estimator (PPE), and the Stokes Estimator (STE). Spatiotemporal characteristics and noise sensitivity were determined in silico via comparison with CFD-derived relative pressure fields. Estimators were then validated using a type B aortic dissection (TBAD) flow phantom with varying tear geometry and twelve catheter pressure measurements. Finally, each estimator was evaluated across eight patient cases in a clinical feasibility analysis. Estimators were cross-compared and evaluated for coherence since no reference catheter pressure measurements were available. PPE outperformed STE in the in silico relative pressure analysis, while both outperformed vWERP in plane-to-plane assessment. High velocity gradients and low spatial resolution contributed most significantly to local variations in 3D relative pressure field errors. Low temporal resolution led to systematic underestimation of highly transient peak pressure events. In the flow phantom analysis, vWERP was the most accurate method, followed by STE and then PPE. Each relative pressure estimator was strongly correlated with ground truth relative pressure values, despite the tendency to underestimate peak relative pressure. Patient case results demonstrated that each relative pressure estimator could be feasibly integrated into a clinical workflow.

papers.title: Connected components in networks with higher-order interactions
papers.summary: We address the problem of defining connected components in hypergraphs, which are models for systems with higher-order interactions. For graphs with dyadic interactions, connected components are defined in terms of paths connecting nodes along the graph. However, defining connected components in hypergraphs is a more involved problem, as one needs to consider the higher-order nature of the interactions associated with the hyperedge. Higher-order interactions can be taken into consideration through a logic associated with the hyperedges, two examples being OR-logic and AND-logic; these logical operations can be considered two limiting cases corresponding to non-cooperative and fully cooperative interactions, respectively. In this paper we show how connected components can be defined in hypergraphs with OR or AND logic. While OR-logic and AND-logic provide the same connected components for nondirected hypergraphs, for directed hypergraphs the strongly connected component of AND-logic is a subset of the OR-logic strongly connected component. Interestingly, higher-order interactions change the general topological properties of connected components in directed hypergraphs. Notably, while for directed graphs the strongly connected component is the intersection of its in- and out-component, in hypergraphs with AND-logic the intersection of in- and out-component does not equal the strongly connected component. We develop a theory for the fraction of nodes that are part of the largest connected component and through comparison with real-world data we show that degree-cardinality correlations play a significant role.

papers.title: A mass invariant in a compressible turbulent medium
papers.summary: Predicting the measurable statistical properties of density fluctuations in a supersonic compressible turbulent flow is a major challenge in physics. In 1951, Chandrasekhar derived an invariant under the assumption of the statistical homogeneity and isotropy of the turbulent density field and stationarity of the background density. Recently, Jaupart & Chabrier (2021) extended this invariant to non-isotropic flows in a time-evolving background and showed that it has the dimension of a mass. This invariant $M_{\rm inv}$ is defined by $M_{\rm inv} = \mathbb{E}(\rho)\text{Var}\left(\frac{\rho}{\mathbb{E}(\rho)}\right)(l_{\rm c}^\rho)^3$ where $\rho$ is the density field and $l_{\rm c}^\rho$ is the correlation length. In this article, we perform numerical simulations of homogeneous and isotropic compressible turbulence to test the validity of this invariant in a medium subject to isotropic decaying turbulence. We study several input configurations, namely different Mach numbers, injection lengths of turbulence and equations of state. We confirm that $M_{\rm inv}$ remains constant during the decaying phase of turbulence. Furthermore, we develop a theoretical model of the density field statistics which predicts without any free parameter the evolution of the correlation length with the variance of the logdensity field beyond the assumption of the gaussian field for the logdensity. Noting that $M_{\rm inv}$ is independent of the Mach number, we show that this invariant can be used to relate the non-gaussian evolution of the logdensity probability distribution function to its variance with no free parameters.

papers.title: IRENE: a fluId layeR finitE-elemeNt softwarE
papers.summary: We present a finite-element software library, IRENE, which allows to solve numerically the dynamics of a viscous fluid layer embedded in three-dimensional space. Unlike finite-element libraries present in the literature, IRENE can handle two-dimensional open surfaces with a wide range of boundary conditions, and inter-surface obstacles with any shapes, and is built upon the user-friendly and versatile finite element computational software (FEniCS). Also, the library can describe a wide range of physical regimes--both low-Reynolds-number and inertia-dominated ones--capturing the complex coupling between in-plane flows, out-of-plane deformations, surface tension, and elastic response. We validate IRENE against known analytical and numerical results, and demonstrate its capabilities through physical examples. Overall, IRENE provides a versatile and efficient tool for understanding fluid-layer dynamics on multiple physical scales, from flows of lipidic membranes on a microscopic level, to fluid flows on a macroscopic scale, to atmospheric air flows on a planetary level.

papers.title: Hyperparameter Optimization in the Estimation of PDE and Delay-PDE models from data
papers.summary: We propose an improved method for estimating partial differential equations and delay partial differential equations from data, using Bayesian optimization and the Bayesian information criterion to automatically find suitable hyperparameters for the method itself or for the equations (such as a time-delay). We show that combining time integration into an established model estimation method increases robustness and yields predictive models. Allowing hyperparameters to be optimized as part of the model estimation results in a wider modelling scope. We demonstrate the method's performance on a number of synthetic benchmark problems of different complexity, representing different classes of physical behaviour. This includes the Allen-Cahn and Cahn-Hilliard models, as well as different reaction-diffusion systems without and with time-delay. The published version of this preprint can be found under this URL: https://iopscience.iop.org/article/10.1088/1367-2630/ae2e33 or the DOI: 10.1088/1367-2630/ae2e33

papers.title: A Targeted Quadrature Framework for Simulating Large-Scale 3D Anisotropic Electromagnetic Measurements
papers.summary: A new efficient and accurate method is presented for simulating frequency-domain borehole electromagnetic (EM) measurements acquired in the presence of three-dimensional (3D) variations of anisotropic subsurface conductivity. The method is based on solving the quasi-static Maxwell equations with a finite-volume discretization via goal-oriented block-quadrature reduced-order modeling. Discretization is performed with a Lebedev grid that enables accurate and conservative solutions in the presence of any form of anisotropic electrical conductivity. Likewise, the method makes use of a new effective-medium approximation to locally account for non-conformal boundaries and large contrasts in electrical conductivity, especially in the vicinity of EM sources and receivers. The finite-volume discretization yields a large symmetric linear system of equations, which is reduced to a set of smaller structured problems via block Lanczos recursion. The formulation also enables the efficient calculation of the adjoint solution, which is necessary for gradient-based inversion of the measurements to estimate the associated spatial distribution of electrical conductivity, i.e., to solve the inverse problem. The method is applied and verified for borehole ultra-deep azimuthal resistivity (UDAR) measurements commonly used in subsurface geosteering and well navigation. Efficiency, robustness, and scalability are demonstrated using synthetic UDAR data generated in a three-dimensional formation inspired by North Sea geology. The numerical results confirm suitability for integration into real-time UDAR processing frameworks.

papers.title: An Algebra Bundle for Non-Composable Coincidence Probabilities in Gamma-ray Spectroscopy
papers.summary: Understanding nuclear level schemes from the detection of emitted gamma-rays is, at its core, a combinatorial problem. The transition matrix formalism that treats nuclear decay as a Markov process is a well established treatment for the prediction of emitted and detected gamma-rays. However, with the path algebra being the underlying algebra of such matrix methods, the formalism is restricted to calculating probabilities only for composable paths through the decay. This paper presents a new algebra that allows for the calculations of non-composable coincidence probabilities offering a more complete formalism for the prediction of gamma-ray spectra. The aim of this \textit{coincidence algebra} is to provide a general treatment for predicting all full energy summing peaks for composable and non-composable transitions. Non-composable summing peaks often corrupt peaks of interest by creating doublets in the energy spectra. The coincidence algebra serves as a tool for investigating any possible doublets produced from full energy coincidence summing. This formalism is tested for the prediction of gamma-ray peaks in the electron capture of $^{133}$Ba and compared to the results a Geant4 simulation of the decay within the GRIFFIN spectrometer. It is also shown how the path algebra formalism may be useful for understanding uncertainty propagation in nuclear level schemes.

papers.title: From Poincare Invariance to Gauge Theories: Yang-Mills and General Relativity
papers.summary: This article is founded on two fundamental principles: the principle field equations introduced in Refs. \cite{S, S1, S2} and the Fock-Ivanenko covariant derivatives \cite{FI, F}. The former yields the equations of motion for free fields of arbitrary spin and helicity. In the massless case, it also dictates that Lorentz transformations for tensor fields acquire an additional term, which takes the form of a gauge transformation \cite{W, S1}. The latter principle, the Fock-Ivanenko derivative, introduces interactions based on the intrinsic and Poincare groups. This framework allows us to recover a complete Yang-Mills theory, as well as general relativity in the connection-based formulations of Palatini and Ashtekar, both of which are theories with local gauge symmetries. While the standard approach begins with the symmetries of a matter action, we will instead derive dynamics directly from Poincare invariance. This perspective reveals that for free fields, Lorentz invariance induces the gauge symmetry of massless tensors. A proper definition of these gauge transformations, in turn, requires the covariant derivatives provided by the Fock-Ivanenko approach. Considering matter fields, we derive the interacting Dirac equation in the presence of Yang-Mills and gravitational fields from its free counterpart.

papers.title: Optical Response in Spintronic Poisson Bolometers
papers.summary: Analog bolometers based on temperature-dependent phase-transition materials such as vanadium oxide (VOx) and barium titanate (BTO) represent the state of the art in uncooled infrared detectors. Recently, the first room-temperature spintronic Poisson bolometer based on magnetic tunnel junctions (MTJs) was proposed and demonstrated as a promising infrared detector. Unlike conventional bolometers, the spintronic Poisson bolometer operates in a probabilistic regime dominated by Poissonian noise, where the response is governed by resistance fluctuations arising from thermally activated magnetization transitions. Spontaneous transitions between two metastable magnetic states occur even in the absence of incident light, and the transition probability increases under illumination. In this work, we experimentally study the statistical properties of the optical response of the spintronic Poisson bolometer under illumination. We demonstrate that transitions in spintronic Poisson bolometers, both in the absence and presence of light, exhibit Poissonian behavior, with transition rates and interarrival times modulated by incident radiation. Under illumination, we observe a 153% increase in the count rate accompanied by a 70% reduction in interarrival time. These results establish spintronic Poisson bolometers as a promising platform for probabilistic, high-speed, and high-sensitivity infrared detection at room temperature.

papers.title: Non-Negativity, Non-Singularity and Energy Conservation of the Zonal Method with Non-Reciprocal Exchange Factors
papers.summary: This paper proves that the zonal balances of Hottel's method, written in power variables for a first-interaction exchange factor matrix $\mathbf{F}$, have a unique and non-negative solution for any combination of prescribed temperatures and prescribed source terms in which at least one element with prescribed temperature absorbs radiation, and that they conserve energy as an algebraic identity. The results hold for media ranging from transparent to absorbing, emitting and scattering, and for boundaries ranging from absorbing to reflecting. They require only that $\mathbf{F}$ be non-negative, row stochastic and irreducible: reciprocity is not needed, so the guarantees hold for Monte Carlo exchange factors as traced, without smoothing, which the symmetric notation of the zonal method does not make apparent. Both the non-singularity and the non-negativity follow from a single discrete minimum principle, and both have been machine-checked in Lean 4. To this end the balances are written as one linear system in the total radiant powers, $\mathbf{M}\mathbf{j} = \mathbf{h}$, assembled row by row from the prescribed temperatures and source terms, with a system matrix that inherits the sparsity of $\mathbf{F}$; the total exchange areas of Noble's matrix formulation are in general dense, and the two agree symbolically and numerically to machine precision. Validation is provided symbolically against the textbook closed-form solutions for infinite parallel plates and concentric cylinders, numerically against the results of Crosbie and Schrenker for pure and partial scattering, against an exact symmetry identity in a three-dimensional enclosure, and against the diffusion approximation in an optically thick problem with about $10^6$ elements, solved in about one minute.

papers.title: Quantum-Accurate Vibrational and Conformational Dynamics from Small Molecules to Proteins with Machine-Learned Force Fields
papers.summary: Biomolecular thermodynamics and spectroscopy depend on relative conformer energies, local curvatures, and collective dipole fluctuations on the potential-energy surface. Conventional molecular mechanics force fields enable large-scale simulations, but their fixed functional forms can misrepresent infrared intensities, mode character, and environment-dependent vibrational response. Here we assess general-purpose machine-learned force fields across small molecules, finite-temperature infrared spectra, gas-phase peptides, and monomeric, oligomeric, and solvated protein assemblies. To enable this analysis, we introduce QVib, a dataset of 293 molecules and 1365 conformers, together with peptide amide-band benchmarks and p53 oligomerization-domain models, to evaluate vibrational transferability from DFT references to experimental spectra. Across these systems, machine-learned force fields substantially improve over molecular mechanics in reproducing DFT-level forces, vibrational frequencies, densities of states, mode eigenvectors, conformational energetics, and experimental infrared spectra. Among models with explicit long-range electrostatics, SO3LR provides the most favourable accuracy-cost balance for the biomolecular systems considered. These results show that machine-learned force-field dynamics can recover collective, environment-dependent vibrational landscapes at near-DFT fidelity, enabling spectroscopically validated biomolecular simulations at force-field-like cost.

papers.title: A Level Set Method on Particle Flow Maps
papers.summary: Accurate interface tracking is central to numerical simulations involving moving boundaries, including multiphase flows, free-surface dynamics, phase-change problems, and other interface-driven processes in computational mechanics. Although level set methods provide a flexible implicit representation of evolving interfaces, their grid-based advection and reinitialization procedures often introduce numerical diffusion, volume loss, and degradation of thin or highly curved structures. This paper introduces a Particle Flow Map Level Set (PFM-LS) method that addresses these limitations by transporting interface geometry through particle-carried bidirectional flow maps. In contrast to particle level set methods that use particles mainly as corrective markers, PFM-LS uses particles as primary carriers of level-set values, gradients, and Hessians within a narrow band around the interface. The method combines long-range flow-map transport, high-order particle-grid reconstruction, adaptive particle control, and a hybrid particle-grid redistancing scheme to preserve both signed-distance consistency and sub-grid geometric features. Numerical benchmarks in two and three dimensions, including topology-change tests, chamfer and Hausdorff shape-error metrics, and coupling to an incompressible free-surface flow solver, show that PFM-LS achieves strong volume preservation, high shape fidelity, and near fourth-order convergence, outperforming a broad range of existing level set and reference-map-based methods.

papers.title: Purely equatorial lasing in spherical liquid crystal polymer microlasers with bipolar refractive index profile
papers.summary: Liquid crystal whispering gallery mode (WGM) microlasers show high sensitivity to external stimuli and distinct spectral features, rendering them ideally suited for various sensing applications. They also offer intrinsic anisotropic optical properties, which can be used to shape and manipulate light even inside spatially highly symmetric structures. Here, we report the fabrication of a spherical bipolar liquid crystal polymer microlaser that tightly confines the optical path of WGMs to the equatorial plane. By controlled anchoring of the liquid crystal mesogens followed by polymerization, a fixed refractive index profile is formed within the spherical microcavity. Consequently, only transverse electric (TE) modes oscillating in the equatorial plane experience the high extraordinary refractive index, allowing to confine lasing into a single plane. Furthermore, we observe a characteristic splitting into sub-modes. By combining hyperspectral imaging, optical modeling, and theoretical calculations, we show that the observed sub-modes originate from the lifting of the energy degeneracy of azimuthal WGMs. The unique ability to confine lasing into a single plane makes these spherical microlasers independent of the exact position of the pump beam, which allows consistent localized sensing especially in combination with fast point scanning microscopes or inside highly dynamic biological environments.

papers.title: On the Adversarial Robustness of Hydrological Models
papers.summary: The evaluation of hydrological models is essential for both model selection and reliability assessment. However, simply comparing predictions to observations is insufficient for understanding the global landscape of model behavior. This is especially true for many deep learning models, whose structures are complex. Further, in risk-averse operational settings, water managers require models that are trustworthy and provably safe, as non-robustness can put our critical infrastructure at risk. Motivated by the need to select reliable models for operational deployment, we introduce and explore adversarial robustness analysis in hydrological modeling, evaluating whether small, targeted perturbations to meteorological forcings induce substantial changes in simulated discharge. We compare physical-conceptual and deep learning-based hydrological models across 1,347 German catchments under perturbations of varying magnitudes, using the fast gradient sign method (FGSM). We find that, as expected, the FGSM perturbations systematically reduce KGE and increase MSE. However, catastrophic failure is rare and, surprisingly, LSTMs generally demonstrate greater robustness than HBV models. Further, changes in both the predicted hydrographs and the internal model states often respond approximately linearly (at least locally) as perturbation size increases, providing a compact summary of how errors grow under such perturbations. Similar patterns are also observed for random perturbations, suggesting that small input changes usually introduce approximately proportional changes in model output. Overall, these findings support further consideration of LSTMs for operational deployment (due both to their predictive power and robustness), and motivate future work on both characterizing model responses to input changes and improving robustness through architectural modifications and training design.
