papers.title: Impact of the equation of state on core collapse supernovae I: the low-$T/|W|$ instability
papers.summary: Rapidly rotating core-collapse supernovae are promising sources of multimessenger emission, as non-axisymmetric dynamics in the newly formed proto-neutron star can leave characteristic imprints on both gravitational waves and neutrinos. We present three-dimensional neutrino-magnetohydrodynamics simulations of the collapse of a rapidly rotating $35\,\mathrm{M}_\odot$ progenitor, performed with five different finite-temperature nuclear equations of state, to investigate how dense-matter physics affects the development of the low-$T/|W|$ instability and its associated multimessenger signatures. We find that the low-$T/|W|$ instability develops in all equation of state models considered, indicating that its occurrence is robust for this rapidly rotating progenitor. However, its onset time, dominant azimuthal structure, lifetime, and characteristic multimessenger frequencies vary among models, reflecting differences in the evolving proto-neutron star structure and rotation profile. The instability produces large-scale spiral modes that generate quasi-periodic gravitational wave emission and modulate the neutrino luminosities, especially along directions close to the equatorial plane. The dominant gravitational wave frequency associated with the instability correlates with the effective stiffness and compactness of the proto-neutron star: models with more compact/stiffer configurations emit at higher frequencies. This suggests that, in rapidly rotating core-collapse supernovae, the frequency of the low-$T/|W|$ instability-driven gravitational wave signal may provide a diagnostic of the dense-matter equation of state, complementary to the information carried by the neutrino signal.

papers.title: Ultraviolet diversity of Little Red Dots as a probe for direct-collapse black hole ages
papers.summary: Little Red Dots (LRDs) uncovered by the James Webb Space Telescope have been proposed as candidate galaxies hosting embedded accreting direct-collapse black holes (DCBHs), yet the relative ultraviolet (UV) emission of their host galaxy remains highly uncertain and diverse across the population. Using a large-scale cosmological hydrodynamical simulation from the \textsc{meli$\odot$ra} suite, we investigate the contribution of PopIII stars and accreting DCBHs in LRD candidates at $z>8.5$, in the rest-frame $0.2-0.6~\mu\mathrm{m}$ band. We find that the UV emission from the host galaxy evolves rapidly over the first $\sim 30~\mathrm{Myr}$ following DCBH formation, reflecting the build-up of stellar mass and metal enrichment. This evolution consists of a rapid transition from initially BH-dominated systems, with negligible stellar mass, low metallicity, and high accretion rates, to progressively more developed hosts in which rapid star formation enhances the UV output and metallicity increases. After $\sim 30~\mathrm{Myr}$, the stellar continuum typically overwhelms the accreting DCBH contribution, producing bluer colours and more extended stellar distributions. As a result, UV-bright LRDs are predicted to host older DCBHs, have higher gas-phase metallicities, lower BH-to-stellar mass ratios, and lower Eddington ratios. The short-lived nature of the LRD phase places strong constraints on their emergence over cosmic time. Overall, our results suggest that DCBH ages can be constrained from the host galaxy contribution to the UV-optical spectrum of LRDs, relative to that of the accreting DCBH, and support the picture in which a DCBH evolutionary sequence is systematically encoded in emission line properties, gas-phase metallicities, and accretion states.

papers.title: Intermediate States in Chaotic Triple Evolution and Applications to Black Hole Merger Statistics
papers.summary: Three-body interactions exhibit phases of strong chaotic evolution as well as hierarchical motion where one body separates from a binary and follows a hyperbolic or elliptic trajectory around it. The binaries produced during phases of hierarchical motion may lead to gravitational wave (GW) inspirals, but this depends on the outcomes of the chaotic states. In this paper we re-derive the elliptic outcome distribution using equilibrium statistical mechanics and explore it together with the hyperbolic distribution. When comparing to N-body simulations, we find that we can reduce the elliptic outcome model to one free parameter instead of the previously used two and that the predicted disintegration probabilities agree except for very low angular momentum triples. We then use both outcome distributions along with a star cluster model to design a Monte Carlo algorithm for repeated binary-single scatterings within dense star systems. We explore star cluster masses of $[10^5 - 10^7] M_{\odot}$, with the goal of quantifying observably eccentric merger (OEM) GWs, visible to instruments such as LIGO and Virgo. Assuming an OEM detection sensitivity of $f_{\rm min}=10 {\rm Hz}, e_{\rm min} = 0.1$, we find the elliptic OEMs are about $\sim (32 - 63)\%$ of the total elliptic mergers and that the total cluster mass greatly impacts the fraction of ejected binaries. The OEM to total merger fraction (OEM fraction) is found to be $(2.6 - 4.4)\%$. Considering the detection sensitivity that GW interferometers have today $(f_{\rm min} \simeq 34.4 {\rm Hz})$ we obtain the OEM fraction in the $(1.6 - 3.1)\%$ range.

papers.title: Something green beneath the surface: The dynamical nature of Fossil Structures in IllustrisTNG-100
papers.summary: Fossil structures (FS) have traditionally been considered dynamically relaxed end-products of group evolution, characterized by a large magnitude gap ($\Delta m_{1,2} \geq 2$). However, recent observations and simulations suggest this picture is incomplete. We investigate whether FS are dynamically relaxed systems and how their galaxy populations differ from non-fossil systems (non-FS), focusing on system dynamics and evolution of the galaxies inside them. Using \textsc{IllustrisTNG-100}, we select 182 structures ($M_{200} > 10^{13}\,M_{\odot}$) at $z = 0$, classifying them as FS/non-FS based on $\Delta m_{1,2}$ in the $r$-band. We track $\Delta m_{1,2}$ evolution over 9\,Gyr and analyze: (1) the emergence of $\Delta m_{1,2}$, (2) the fraction of quenched galaxies (sSFR $< 10^{-11}$\,yr$^{-1}$), (3) the distribution of galaxies in color--stellar mass space, and (4) the gas--BSG centroid shift as a dynamical proxy. The magnitude gap in FS is primarily driven by the absence of massive recent accretion: FS exhibit significantly lower BSG-to-satellite stellar mass ratios ($\mu^{\rm{FS}}{\star}$=0.17 vs. $\mu^{\rm{NFS}}{\star}$=0.39) for the most massive satellite accreted within the last 6\,Gyr. FS also host a more prominent red sequence and marginally higher quenched fractions than non-FS. Our findings indicate that while the magnitude gap effectively identifies systems that have ceased major mergers in the last 3-6 Gyr, it is a poor proxy for their current global dynamical state. Both FS and non-FS populations exhibit intermediate gas-BSG offsets ($D_{BSG-CM} \approx 0.15 R/R_{200}$), failing to reach full relaxation. This decoupling suggests that the magnitude gap traces the assembly history of massive components rather than the overall stability of the intra cluster medium.

papers.title: A cross-calibration approach for polarisation-sensitive detectors in CMB experiments: application to LiteBIRD's polarisation angle calibration
papers.summary: We present a cross-calibration algorithm that determines the relative calibration of detectors within the same frequency band of a CMB experiment. The method iteratively compares single-detector maps with frequency-band maps, and it can be applied to any calibration parameter that can be corrected through reprocessing of the instrument's data at the map level. This allows for validation and correction of calibration both before and after observations. We validate the pipeline by calibrating the polarisation angle of simulated sky maps from the upcoming \textit{LiteBIRD} experiment. The cross-calibration algorithm has been tested both in the case of random miscalibration of each individual detector and in the case of rotation of entire detector wafers. In both cases, the cross-calibration algorithm converges to the correct value and we are able to identify and correct relative miscalibrations in the polarisation angle of each detector with arcminute precision. Absolute calibration can then be addressed either through ground-based measurements, or through the $E$-$B$ nulling technique. To assess compliance with \textit{LiteBIRD}'s systematics budget, we propagate the residual miscalibration uncertainties through component separation and tensor-to-scalar ratio ($r$) estimation pipelines using both parametric (\texttt{FgBuster}) and blind (\texttt{HILC}) methods. In both cases, the induced bias on $r$ remains well below the \textit{LiteBIRD} maximum budget for systematics of $\delta r < 6.5\times10^{-6}$. This confirms that the cross-calibration method presented is suited for use in modern high-precision CMB experiments.

papers.title: JWST Characterization of Earth Quasi-Satellite (469219) Kamo`oalewa
papers.summary: Near-Earth asteroid (469219) Kamo`oalewa is a uniquely stable quasi-satellite of the Earth and a target of the Tianwen-2 spacecraft mission. Here we report observations taken with JWST's NIRSpec instrument in integral field unit (IFU) mode in February 2026. The JWST reflectance spectrum is notably less red (more neutral) from $1.0-2.5$ $\mu m$ than previous ground-based spectrophotometric observations. New observations made with LBT in April 2026, observed and processed similarly to the 2021 observations, find $zJ$ colors in agreement with JWST. Kamo`oalewa's infrared colors appear more similar to typical silicate-rich asteroids and unlike the reddened, space-weathered lunar-like silicates suggested by previous observations. In agreement with the ground-based spectrum, we detect a faint silicate absorption feature at $0.93\pm 0.01$ $\mu m$. We do not detect a 2.0 $\mu m$ silicate absorption. Models of Kamo`oalewa's faint thermal emission (beginning near 4.5 $\mu m$) find a mean diameter of $D=18\pm2\mathrm{m}$ and best-fit visible albedo $p_V = 0.59^{+0.25}_{-0.17}$, with models as low as $p_V = 0.36$ providing adequate model fits. This combination of color, albedo, and absorption bands is similar to oldhamite-bearing enstatite-rich compositions. Kamo`oalewa's brightness variations over the course of the JWST program provides independent confirmation of its rotation period of 27.9 minutes, with an axis ratio $\sim1.4$ ($D\sim15-21$ m).

papers.title: A comprehensive Gaia DR3 study of the open cluster NGC 6134: Bayesian distances, present-day mass function, mass segregation, and structural decomposition
papers.summary: Open clusters are key laboratories for studying the formation and dynamical evolution of stellar populations. We present a comprehensive characterization of the intermediate-age open cluster NGC 6134 using Gaia DR3 astrometry and photometry. Adopting the 890-member Hierarchical Density-Based Spatial Clustering of Applications with Noise (HDBSCAN) membership catalog, we determine the cluster distance and individual member distances with the Bayesian hierarchical code Kalkayotl under a King spatial prior, derive the fundamental parameters with the automated isochrone-fitting code ASteCA, quantify mass segregation, and decompose the projected spatial distribution into structural components. We obtain a Bayesian cluster distance of $1070.8^{+21.0}_{-19.0}$ pc (mode and 68\% credible interval), consistent with the ASteCA value ($d = 1064.4 \pm 15.2$ pc), with member distances peaking at $1071.2 \pm 2.5$ pc. ASteCA yields $\mathrm{[Fe/H]} = 0.08 \pm 0.06$, $\log(t) = 9.14 \pm 0.01$, and $A_\mathrm{V} = 1.03 \pm 0.05$ mag. The present-day mass function (PDMF) follows a broken power law with slopes $\Gamma_A = -2.10^{+0.10}_{-0.10}$ and $\Gamma_B = 1.59^{+0.14}_{-0.14}$ and break mass $M_c = 0.95^{+0.02}_{-0.02}\ M_\odot$, with a negative low-mass slope and a high-mass slope steeper than the canonical Salpeter value ($\Gamma = 1.35$), consistent with the preferential loss of the most massive stars through stellar evolution rather than with dynamical depletion. The observed mass segregation is consistent with an origin in long-term dynamical evolution. The cluster comprises a core, a diffuse halo, and a coherent plane-of-sky elongated feature that is unlikely to arise from noise based on a size-matched isotropic null test, and that lies beyond the radius at which masses are available. The observed main-sequence gap is closely linked to the cluster's binary fraction.

papers.title: Debris Disc Substructures Induced by Secular Planetary Perturbations
papers.summary: Observations of debris discs have the potential to provide valuable information about massive planets perturbing them gravitationally. In this work, we explore the evolution of the azimuthally-averaged (or axisymmetric) surface density (ASD) --- a characteristic routinely derived from observations --- in a disc that is secularly perturbed by an inner planet. We develop a detailed analytical understanding of ASD evolution and verify it using a novel numerical framework {\sc debrispy}, which we make publicly available. With these tools we show that in a secularly evolving disc ASD develops a set of sharp features --- sharp peaks at eccentricity nulls and finite discontinuities at caustic points where particle periastra or apoastra pile up --- marching out through the disc as it ages. We probe the dependence of these features on planetary eccentricity, ratio of the free to forced particle eccentricity, and underlying radial mass distribution, showing in particular that more eccentric planets produce more prominent ASD features. Convolution with the PSF of realistic observations (as well as the non-zero random free eccentricity of debris) smooths out these features, but they can still be detectable in high-resolution observations. The radial locations of secular ASD peaks follow a particular, well-defined pattern, which should unambiguously point to their secular nature in observations. We illustrate how both detection and non-detection of such secular features in observed discs can be used (in combination with other constraints) to measure or constrain key parameters of perturbing planets (even those not yet detected) --- mass, semi-major axis and eccentricity.

papers.title: When X-ray Features Fail to Identify Intrinsic Emitters: Label Noise and Luminosity Overlap in Machine Learning Classification of AGN and Star-forming Galaxies
papers.summary: Previously, we found that adding an X-ray flux feature to a Random Forest classifier of active galactic nuclei (AGN) and star-forming galaxies (SFGs) coincided with a decrease in classification accuracy from 97.51% to 89.26%, a counterintuitive result given the prevailing theory that X-rays are a reliable AGN diagnostic. We investigate this discrepancy through both astrophysical and machine learning lenses. On the astrophysical side, we show that the X-ray luminosities of AGN and SFGs in the sample substantially overlap across the canonical $10^{42}$ erg/s threshold, reflecting the moderate luminosity characteristic of an optically-selected sample and the contribution of high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) to SFG emission. On the machine learning side, we argue that BPT-derived training labels carry instance-dependent label noise concentrated near the BPT demarcation line, where X-ray data would be most useful as a discriminator. We show that objects misclassified in 5-fold cross-validation cluster near the Kewley demarcation curve, with a median distance of 0.123 dex versus 0.743 dex for correctly classified objects (Kolmogorov-Smirnov $D = 0.745,\; p = 1.67\times 10^{-9}$). A controlled cross-validation decomposition shows that the previously reported decrease reflects predominantly sample selection: on a fixed sample, adding the X-ray feature leaves class-resolved metrics unchanged, and its permutation importance is consistent with zero across resampled splits. The classifier therefore makes negligible use of a physically informative feature, consistent with training labels coupled to the optical features. We conclude that future classifiers operating on optically-selected samples should employ independent label sources or noise-robust training methods.

papers.title: Morphological Bias: How Ellipticals and Spirals Trace the Cosmic Web Differently
papers.summary: We present a data-driven measurement of galaxy bias and scale-dependent relative bias for elliptical and spiral galaxies using angular auto- and cross-power spectra from DES and DESI Legacy Imaging Surveys DR8. We introduce the cross-tracer clustering ratio (CTCR), the ratio of auto- to cross-power spectra, which isolates the relative clustering of morphological tracers as a function of angular multipole $\ell$. Across both surveys, ellipticals are more strongly clustered than spirals; the cleanest constraints come from DESI, where the two redshift distributions are well matched. The difference is scale dependent: the relative bias is near unity on large scales ($\ell \lesssim 50$) and rises toward smaller scales, reaching $2.9$--$4.0\sigma$ per bin at $\ell = 200$ with an inverse-variance-weighted amplitude $\Delta b = +0.56 \pm 0.06$. A complementary linear-bias analysis confirms that ellipticals are positively biased relative to the matter field, while spirals are consistent with weak bias or anti-bias. The results are robust to two covariance estimators, contamination tests, luminosity splits, and comparisons with two N-body mock catalogs. Throughout, we present the CTCR as an \emph{effective} clustering ratio that is an upper bound on the physical bias ratio, adopting an assumption-light strategy appropriate for a first measurement; the joint multi-spectrum decomposition required to extract the physical bias ratio is identified as future work. These findings provide empirical evidence that galaxy morphology imprints both the amplitude and scale dependence of galaxy bias, and establish the CTCR as a useful observable for testing halo occupation and assembly-bias models with future imaging surveys.

papers.title: The stability of radially anisotropic rotating stellar systems with a central density cusp
papers.summary: We investigate the interplay between radial velocity anisotropy and internal rotation in self-gravitating systems characterised by initial spherical symmetry and a moderate density cusp. We study the stability properties of such configurations to disentangle the impact of anisotropy, rotation, and density structure on the formation of triaxial stellar systems. We perform a set of collisionless $N$-body simulations starting from initial equilibria with a phase space distribution function of the class introduced by Osipkov and Merritt, modified to impose a net global angular momentum with the Lynden-Bell daemon protocol. We analyse the growth of the density and phase space distribution modes, as well as the axial ratios and triaxiality index of the final configurations. We find that internal rotation has a mitigating effect on the strength of the radial orbit instability in radially anisotropic models with \mbox{Fridman-Polyachenko-Shukhman} anisotropy index close to the consistency limit, while it slightly enhances the onset of the instability in marginally stable models. From the analysis of the growth rate of the density modes, we also find that an inner bar, which for maximally rotating initial conditions declines after its initial growth, is formed even in systems with initial profiles with a central density cusp.

papers.title: Influence of local and global solar magnetic fields on medium-term forecasting of the number and parameters of coronal mass ejections
papers.summary: It has been shown that both the frequency and parameters of coronal mass ejections (CMEs) increased as solar cycles 23-25 approached their maxima and decreased toward their minima. However, significant differences were identified in the cyclic evolution of strong versus weak CMEs. Unlike weak CMEs, powerful, high-speed CMEs, characterized by large angular widths and substantial mass and energy, follow the cyclic evolution of active regions. During periods when the sector structure of the global magnetic field (GMF) dominates, the latitudinal distribution of CMEs becomes more uniform, and their frequency and parameter values increase, particularly during the declining phase of solar activity. A method based on combining GMF parameter data and Wolf numbers has been proposed for the medium-term forecasting of the frequency and parameters of strong and weak CMEs in cycle 26. A comparison of predicted and observed CME parameters for cycle 25 shows good agreement.

papers.title: NAPTIME: A Neural-Process Framework for Rubin Alert Classification
papers.summary: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory Legacy Survey of Space and Time will produce a high-volume stream of irregularly sampled multiband alerts for which spectroscopic confirmation will be available only for a small minority of sources. Tidal disruption events are rare phenomena that provide a direct probe of dormant massive black holes, but their light curves can be confused with nuclear variability and other transient subclasses. We present NAPTIME (Neural Astrophysical Photometric Transient Identification and Modeling Engine), a neural-process framework for photometric transient classification under sparse and partial observational context. NAPTIME models irregular multiband light curves directly, combining probabilistic light-curve reconstruction with classification and optional host-galaxy context, as well as photometric-redshift information. We evaluate on two simulated benchmarks: ELAsTiCC2, our primary Rubin-like broad-classification benchmark, and MALLORN, a photometry-only TDE-focused benchmark. On the 15-family ELAsTiCC2 task, the metadata-aware model reaches macro $\mathrm{F1} = 0.903$ and macro area under the receiver operating characteristic curve ($\mathrm{AUROC}$) $= 0.991$, while a matched photometry-only variant reaches 0.874 and 0.986. Viewed as a TDE-versus-rest ranking model, the classifier yields TDE average precision 0.985 with metadata and 0.979 without. Metadata is most valuable in the low-context regime. Using only the earliest 10\% of retained photometric measurements, macro F1 is $\sim$0.42 with metadata and $\sim$0.34 without it. On MALLORN, NAPTIME reaches macro $\mathrm{F1} = 0.693$ and macro $\mathrm{AUROC} = 0.958$. These results show that neural processes provide a practical probabilistic framework for Rubin-like transient classification and remain effective for TDE-focused candidate recovery.

papers.title: Probing an Intermediate-Mass Black Hole Companion of Sagittarius A* with Pulsar Timing
papers.summary: An intermediate-mass black hole (IMBH) hidden in our Galactic Center (GC) may explain the puzzling observations of the stellar distribution around Sagittarius A* (Sgr A*), the supermassive black hole (SMBH) in the GC. Future observations with the next-generation radio telescopes, such as the SKA, are promising to discover pulsars orbiting around Sgr A*, and thus provide the possibility of constraining the hidden IMBH with pulsar timing. We study the detectability of a third-body, the IMBH, in the pulsar-SMBH system based on radio timing observation. We find that the pulsar-SMBH system is very sensitive to such a third-body perturbation and can be used to put stringent constraints on the existence of the IMBH. Even under strong perturbations caused by the complex GC astrophysical environments, timing observation will still complement the existing observational constraints.

papers.title: Magnetic pressure anisotropy in ultra-dense white dwarfs: Landau quantization and neutronization effects
papers.summary: Strong magnetic fields modify the thermodynamics of white dwarf (WD) matter by quantizing the transverse motion of degenerate electrons into Landau levels and splitting the pressure into components parallel and perpendicular to the magnetic field. We investigate how this microscopic pressure anisotropy affects ultra-dense WD sequences when Coulomb lattice contributions, electron capture thresholds, neutron drip limits, and nuclear composition are treated consistently in the equation of state (EoS). The stellar equilibrium structure is obtained by solving an anisotropic extension of the Tolman--Oppenheimer--Volkoff (TOV) equations, where $P_r = P_\parallel$ and $P_t = P_\perp$ denote the radial and tangential pressures, respectively. We compare the post-electron-capture branches with their corresponding pre-capture sequences for pure $^{12}\rm{C}$, $^{16}\rm{O}$, $^{20}\rm{Ne}$, and $^{24}\rm{Mg}$ compositions, as well as for fixed 50/50 C/O, Ne/O, and Mg/Ne mixtures. The EoS predicts $P_\perp < P_\parallel$ in density ranges where only a few Landau levels are occupied. Consequently, pressure anisotropy shifts the stellar sequences toward smaller radii, with only minor changes in the maximum masses. We also find that post-capture configurations cannot be interpreted from the mass--radius plane alone, since the corresponding $M(\rho_c)$ curves reveal unstable portions after the maximum mass is reached. Our results show that strong magnetic fields significantly reduce the radii of low-mass WDs, yielding better agreement with the observational data available in the Montreal White Dwarf Database and suggesting that future high-precision observations of massive magnetic WDs could help assess the role of magnetic pressure anisotropy in determining their masses and radii.

papers.title: The impact of recombination during tidal disruption events
papers.summary: During a tidal disruption event, the resulting debris stream cools down adiabatically due to the tidal stretching. As the temperature drops, the gas is expected to undergo chemical processes, which can release thermal energy into the stream, potentially affecting the subsequent gas evolution. For the first time, we investigate in detail this effect and its dynamical impact on the early-time evolution of the stream by making use of three dimensional hydrodynamic simulations coupled with a realistic equation of state. We find that a few days after disruption, the energy injected by hydrogen recombination and molecular hydrogen formation causes the stream thickness to grow much more rapidly. In the bound debris, this effect stops the stream's confinement by self-gravity before the gas reaches apocentre. As a result, the maximum stream thickness increases by a factor that ranges from a few, for the most bound gas, to a few tens for the near-parabolic gas, reaching $\approx 30 \, R_{\star} $ around the peak of the mass fallback rate. We discuss how this accelerated stream expansion may affect the subsequent evolution of the gas, estimate the luminosity powered by recombination in the unbound debris, and evaluate the potential influence of non-ideal magneto-hydrodynamic effects. By characterizing the thermodynamic and hydrodynamic properties of the stream before its return near pericentre, our results provide physically motivated initial conditions to self-consistently model the later stages of tidal disruption events, offering a promising pathway to unveiling the physical origins of their observed emission.

papers.title: A deep learning algorithm for black hole spin estimation using hot-spot secondary images
papers.summary: Sagittarius A* exhibits frequent flaring activity across the electromagnetic spectrum that is often associated with a localized region of strong emission known as a hot spot. We aim to train a deep learning model to provide a link between key parameters of this phenomenon - hot-spot emission radius, and black hole inclination and spin - to the observed angle difference between the primary and secondary image ($\Delta PA$) that present and future interferometric arrays could resolve. Using the general relativistic radiative transfer code IPOLE, we generated a library of $\sim100.000$ models with varying system parameters and computed the position angle difference on the image plane between the primary and secondary images of the hot spot. We explore equatorial and non-equatorial circular orbits and evaluate our models against approximate observational constraints, including partial-orbit visibility and observational errors. Our algorithm STIHOS shows remarkable accuracy in calculating spin and inclination from the majority of the observational tests we perform ($\sigma_{a_*}=0.04,\,\sigma_i=2^{\circ}$), even in extreme conditions where only half of the orbit is visible. The off-equatorial estimation provides softer constraints in the absence of prior information. Our results demonstrate the importance of hot-spot observations for spacetime estimations. Given the increasing efforts to detect the photon-ring, our framework could prove valuable in interpreting the first observations of lensed emission.

papers.title: A giant magnetic eruption from the asymptotic giant branch star Mira A
papers.summary: Mass loss during the advanced evolutionary stages of low- and intermediate-mass stars is traditionally attributed to dust-driven winds, whereas the influence of magnetic fields remains poorly constrained. However, recent observations show massive directional mass ejections from the nearby asymptotic giant branch (AGB) star Mira~A that appear not to be driven by radiation pressure on the dust. We observationally investigate whether magnetic fields are responsible for the mass loss ejections from Mira A. We obtained full-polarisation ALMA observations of the SiO $v=1$, $J=5\rightarrow4$ maser transition at 215 GHz with angular resolutions of 1.5-2.6 au. The observations reveal a highly magnetized loop-like mass ejection traced by strongly polarised SiO masers extending to approximately eight stellar radii. The morphology, polarisation pattern, energetics, and kinematics indicate a magnetically driven eruption analogous to a stellar coronal mass ejection. The observations demonstrate that magnetic eruptions can dominate mass loss from evolved stars and imply that magnetic fields must become an integral component of future models of AGB, and potentially other cool giant, winds.

papers.title: Molecular and Atomic Gas Associated with the Gamma Ray Supernova Remnant RCW 103
papers.summary: We present a study of the interstellar molecular and atomic gas associated with the gamma-ray supernova remnant (SNR) RCW 103 using the Mopra $^{12}$CO($J$ = 1-0), Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array $^{13}$CO($J$ = 1-0), and the Australia Telescope Compact Array & Parkes HI data. We find that CO clouds in the velocity range from $-58.7$ to $-43.5$ km s$^{-1}$ show a clear spatial correspondence with the X-ray shell of RCW 103, particularly extending from the northwestern to the southeastern regions. The position-velocity diagram of the CO emission reveals an expanding gas motion with an expansion velocity of $\Delta V \sim$$7.5$ km s$^{-1}$, which may have been produced by shock waves and/or stellar winds from the progenitor system. We estimate the total cosmic-ray proton energy to be $\sim$$3.0^{+1.1}_{-0.6} \times 10^{47}$ erg, adopting a total interstellar proton density of $\sim$$810$ cm$^{-3}$. This value is more than an order of magnitude lower than those inferred for other gamma-ray emitting SNRs of comparable age. Given that a substantial amount of dense gas remains within the interior of RCW 103, where thermal X-ray emission is dominant, our results possibly suggest that a significant fraction of the shock energy may have been converted into thermal energy via gas heating, thereby reducing the efficiency of cosmic-ray acceleration.

papers.title: The Impact of Errors in the Shape Function of Rotating Neutron Stars in the Oblate Schwarzschild Approximation
papers.summary: Measurements of thermal X-ray flux emitted by neutron stars can constrain their radii and the equation of state of cold dense matter. Accurate flux modeling of rapidly rotating neutron stars requires an approximation for their oblate surface shape, usually given by a shape function. We examine the accuracy of five shape functions by comparing them against numerical relativistic stellar surfaces for seven representative equations of state over a broad range of compactness and spin. We characterize their errors in the surface radius and their derivative with respect to colatitude, test the extent of quasi-universality, and propagate these errors into the differential solid angle d{\Omega}, a geometric factor underlying the observed flux, under the oblate Schwarzschild approximation. We find that the shape functions produce distinct error patterns associated with their forms and parameter ranges. These errors remain structured in compactness, spin, and colatitude. Simple polynomial corrections substantially reduce the radius errors of several shape functions, with most corrected errors within approximately 0.5%. We show that errors in d{\Omega} may be understood as coming from an area contribution, which scales with twice the relative radius error, and a projection contribution controlled primarily by the error in the surface derivative. The projection contribution grows towards the limb, where small surface errors can produce much larger local errors in d{\Omega}. We provide a set of guidelines for the construction of improved quasi-universal shape functions that can be used in future radius estimation efforts. Our recommendations include that both the shape and its derivative be modeled accurately, that more accurate predictions of the polar radius be developed, and that the shape function be calibrated over the same compactness-spin range that is to be tested.

papers.title: Calibration of the Next Generation Palomar Spectrograph as a Stellar Speedometer
papers.summary: We calibrate the Next Generation Palomar Spectrograph (NGPS) for precision stellar radial-velocity (RV) measurements using repeated observations of 24 Gaia-ESO RV standards spanning $G=11$-$18$. Because NGPS is mounted at the Hale telescope's Cassegrain focus, changes in instrumental flexure produce wavelength-solution shifts of tens of km s$^{-1}$, with substantial time and wavelength dependence. We develop a pipeline that measures these shifts directly from each science exposure, using telluric absorption features in the R and I channels and the [O I] 5577 \r{A} sky-emission line in the G channel. This approach eliminates the need for frequent on-sky arc calibrations. The resulting wavelength-dependent flexure corrections reduce the median absolute discrepancy relative to Gaia-ESO RVs from tens of km s$^{-1}$ to 1.6 km s$^{-1}$. Telluric absorption provides substantially more reliable flexure calibration than sky emission lines, which do not track point-source illumination of the slit. The I channel, which contains both many telluric lines and strong photospheric lines across a range of spectral types, generally yields the most stable RVs. The achieved precision remains above the photon-noise limit, indicating that NGPS RV performance is currently limited by calibration and modeling systematics. These results demonstrate that NGPS is well-suited for accurate and precise stellar RV measurements across a wide range of astrophysical studies.

papers.title: Consistency and precision of very long baseline interferometry source coordinate time series
papers.summary: Coordinate time series of extragalactic radio sources from very long baseline interferometry observations are widely used to evaluate source positional stability, select stable sources for celestial reference frames, assess reference-frame axis stability, and investigate source-related astrometric variability. Their external consistency, realistic errors, and relation to processing strategies and analysis configurations remain to be investigated. We aim to compare coordinate time series solutions from different analysis centers and investigate how processing strategies and configurations contribute to their differences. We collected eight solutions from seven analysis centers and selected 496 common sources after data selection, reference-frame alignment, and extraction of common observing sessions. Inter-solution differences were characterized with pairwise positional offsets and correlation analysis, and realistic positional errors with the N-cornered-hat (NCH) method and bootstrap resampling. Most solutions have median weighted root mean square (WRMS) values of a few hundred microarcseconds $(\mathrm{\mu as})$, and the median NCH-derived precision is about 200-300 $\mathrm{\mu as}$ in right ascension and 250-400 $\mathrm{\mu as}$ in declination. Solutions with similar strategies, software, or source constraints show higher consistency, with more similar WRMS values, stronger correlations, and closer precision estimates. Consistency is affected not only by the global or independent mode distinction but also by detailed analysis configuration. NCH-derived precision depends on declination, being poorer in the southern sky, and stabilizes with more observing sessions. Processing strategies and configurations introduce marginal differences; solutions remain generally consistent. Inter-solution comparisons independently estimate realistic stochastic errors beyond formal errors.

papers.title: Error Propagation from Integral Moments and Spectral Derivatives of Stokes Profiles to Magnetic Observables
papers.summary: We aim to derive convenient analytic estimations of magnetic inference errors, which can be used to inform and facilitate the creation of the science-traceability matrix of a polarimetric instrument. In order to do this, we study the general problem of the propagation of Poissonian noise in polarized light signals to derived data products of the Stokes profiles, namely integral moments of arbitrary orders and spectral derivatives of the intensity. In particular, we derive the errors on the longitudinal and transversal projections of the magnetic field inferred from the weak-field approximation (WFA) of the Zeeman effect. The propagated errors on magnetic inference are traced back to the signal- to-noise ratio (SNR) of the observations. The results can be used to quantify the contributions of different environmental and instrumental conditions (spectral line width, spectral resolution, line spread function, stray light) to the overall error on the inferred quantities. Our tests indicate that the integral-moment method of inference is comparable to the local derivative in a predictable way.

papers.title: Re-interpreting the GRS 1915+105 observations within the variable TADAF scenario
papers.summary: The Galactic microquasar GRS 1915+105 is one of the most interesting X-ray binary systems, exhibiting an exceptionally diverse range of observational phenomena. It displays the most complicated and variable X-ray light curves and carries superluminal radio jets. Its X-ray and radio fluxes change on very different timescales, from seconds to minutes to days and even longer. In recent years, its jet has also displayed large position angle shifts. We find that most of the observational phenomena can be well explained within our newly developed variable turbulent ADAF (TADAF) model. The accretion disk is composed of an outer thin disk and an unstable inner TADAF torus whose size is variable. The previously suggested 'disappearance' and regain of the inner disk is understood as the transition between the thick TADAF and the thin disk. Some types of QPOs are understood in terms of the radius change of the TADAF torus. The jet position angle shift is understood as the direct sideways frame-dragging on the jet by the Lense-Thirring effect from a tilted, spinning black hole. The slower the outshooting jet, the larger the angle shift. We note that such an effect also applies to other sources, such as V404 Cygni and the AGN M87. This mechanism may also be applicable to the famous 'precessing' jet in SS 433.

papers.title: Chondrule size averaging in two and three dimensions
papers.summary: Chondrule sizes are an important discriminant of chondrite groups and chondrule formation theories. Yet most studies report 2D sizes without attempting the somewhat tedious corrections to 3D proposed in the past literature. I show here that 3D size averages can be simply calculated directly from 2D averages of appropriate powers of sizes (and vice-versa), without having to reconstruct 3D distributions, although explicit formulas to that end are also provided. This illuminates the comparison between 3D and 2D arithmetic size averages, which are confirmed to be little different for the published datasets. Yet I suggest another type of average, the "sphere-weighted average" (i.e. weighted by the chondrule equal-volume sphere area), a measure of the surface/volume ratio of the chondrule population, which is more robust against omission of small chondrules. While larger than the arithmetic averages, it is best in line with previous literature estimates based on less exhaustive surveys of chondrules.

papers.title: Towards breaking the degeneracy between stellar ages and unresolved multiplicity
papers.summary: Stellar age is the central desirable parameter we need to disentangle different Galactic formation scenarios. Nevertheless, no stellar age dating method is completely model-independent. Even in the best-case scenarios, present-day stellar age estimates are only precise to $\sim7\%$ and accurate to $\sim10-15\%$. A main drawback of state-of-the-art stellar parameter inference codes like {\tt StarHorse} is that they do not take into account unresolved stellar multiplicity. Especially in the case of nearly equal-mass binaries or higher-order systems on the main sequence, properly taking into account unresolved multiplicity is imperative for the next generation of stellar surveys. Simulation-based inference (SBI) is a robust and flexible approach for dealing with complex models where traditional likelihood-based methods become unfeasible. Here we sketch how SBI can be used to obtain precise stellar ages, masses, binary mass ratios, and other stellar parameters from spectroscopic, photometric, and astrometric measurements.

papers.title: The Structure in the Structure Function of Black Hole Light Curves
papers.summary: Of the two black holes, M87$^\ast$ and Sgr~A$^\ast$, for which event-horizon-scale imaging is currently achievable, only Sgr~A$^\ast$ at our Galactic Center exhibits sub-hour variability, making light curve observations of the inner accretion flow especially valuable for time-domain studies of the spacetime and the surrounding plasma. Observed light curves are often sampled with variable cadence, so a structure function is often used to quantify their variability properties. In this work, we assemble a heterogeneous Sgr~A$^\ast$ light curve data set from discrete observations acquired over $\sim12$ years at 230 GHz, with different instruments, durations, and cadences, and study its structure function in three frameworks. First, we consider analytic predictions for the features of structure functions of stationary random processes with Fourier spectra dictated by the Mat\'ern covariance. We then study the structure functions resulting from lensed movies of synthetic optically thin accretion flows approximated with Mat\'ern covariance in both space and time, and identify which features in the structure function can be attributed to the black-hole geometry. Lastly, we examine the structure functions of a library of $72$ general relativistic magnetohydrodynamic simulations. We find that, in general, magnetically arrested disk (MAD) models produce smoother structure functions with steeper slopes than standard and normal evolution (SANE) counterparts. On time scales of $5-15$ minutes, the observed structure function slope of Sgr~A$^\ast$ more closely aligns with the MAD trend, while both simulation types are generally more variable than the data on all sub-hour timescales.

papers.title: 3D Global Climate Simulations of Synthetic Mars Warming
papers.summary: Artificial warming via engineered aerosols presents a novel pathway to bypass volatile scarcity on modern Mars. Utilizing the Generic Planetary Climate Model, we evaluate the physical feasibility of aerosol-induced terraforming over a full Martian year (669 Sols). Unlike previous approaches that added aerosols to background dust or assumed continuous nanoparticle injection, we simulate the complete substitution of natural dust with a single-injection profile of radiatively active aluminium nanoparticles without continuous dumping. This tests whether initial infrared greenhouse forcing can overcome the severe ice-albedo cooling induced by a massive regional water-ice sheet ($3400 \text{ kg/m}^2$) localized in the Hellas Basin. Comparing this scenario against an unperturbed control run, we analyze surface temperature dynamics, sublimation fluxes, and water vapour concentration. Our 3D global climate simulations quantify the radiative-dynamical feedback thresholds and determine whether engineered aerosol forcing can trigger a self-sustaining water-vapour greenhouse effect or remains fundamentally limited by regional ice-albedo suppression in Hellas.

papers.title: Galactic Outflows and Star-Formation Quenching: A JWST Perspective
papers.summary: Outflows driven by active galactic nuclei (AGN) are widely considered a key mechanism for regulating and quenching star formation in massive galaxies. However, direct observational evidence linking outflows to quenching has remained elusive for decades. This article reviews recent findings for massive galaxies at cosmic noon ($z\sim 2$), based on sensitive James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations tracing both star formation histories (through Balmer absorption lines) and neutral outflows (through blueshifted NaID absorption). Neutral outflows are found in $\sim$ 25 - 50% of massive ($\log(M_*/M_\odot)>$ 10) galaxies, independent of star formation rate. Outflows from star-forming galaxies are consistent with being powered by star-formation and/or AGN activity, whereas outflows from quiescent systems are generally attributed to current or previous AGN activity. There is growing evidence that recent rapid quenching of star-formation is associated with powerful AGN-driven outflows with mass loading factors $\eta \gtrsim$ 1 - 10. The neutral gas dominates the outflow mass budget but in most cases its velocity is below the halo escape velocity, indicating that this gas may form part of a galactic fountain. Detections of neutral gas inflows and residual cold gas reservoirs in quiescent galaxies suggest that other feedback mechanisms such as AGN heating are required to keep galaxies quenched over long timescales. We highlight the potential of multiphase outflow measurements to constrain feedback models, describe the main systematic uncertainties in mass outflow rate measurements, and discuss how the $z\sim 2$ results inform our understanding of the formation of the earliest massive quiescent galaxies.

papers.title: The dawn of the first galaxies
papers.summary: Understanding how the first galaxies assembled their stellar mass at cosmic dawn is a central frontier of modern astrophysics. JWST has now revealed an unexpected population of ultraviolet-bright galaxies at z>10, whose intense emission points towards a rapid stellar mass growth that challenges current models of early galaxy assembly. Yet, the cold gas fueling this growth remains hidden: current ALMA sensitivity restricts routine detection to only the brightest ionized-gas tracers such as [OIII] 88$\mu$m, while [CII] 158$\mu$m, a key coolant and gas-mass proxy of the neutral interstellar medium (ISM), is undetected beyond $z\sim8$. This leaves fundamental questions unanswered: how quickly primeval galaxies gathered cold gas and turned it into stars; what physical conditions (density, temperature, radiation field) characterized their ISM; how fast metals and dust built up; and how feedback regulated early gas assembly. Only a transformational sub-millimeter facility like ALMA2040 can address these questions, enabling systematic surveys of [CII] in the first galaxies and providing a representative census of gas fractions and depletion times. A simulated galaxy at $z=11.3$ shows that ALMA2040 not only will detect, but also spatially resolve its merging cold-gas structure in [CII] on $\sim$200 pc scales in 5 hours (below 100 pc in 10 hours). ALMA2040 will also spectrally resolve multiple lines simultaneously, akin to integral-field spectroscopy, providing the key diagnostics needed to break density-metallicity-radiation-field degeneracies and map the multi-phase ISM of z>10 galaxies. The combination of dramatically increased line sensitivity and wide instantaneous bandwidth will push the search for the first galaxies out to the earliest cosmic times, with [OIII] detectable up to $z\sim20$. ALMA2040 will thus be transformative for understanding how the first galaxies assembled at cosmic dawn.

papers.title: Neutrino production at the extreme vicinity of supermassive black hole in NGC 1068
papers.summary: The identification of NGC~1068 as an extragalactic high-energy neutrino source raises the question of the physical conditions required for neutrino production. Motivated by the newly updated IceCube data (down to $\sim 0.2 \,\rm TeV$) for NGC 1068, we present a statistical, model-independent inference primarily constrained by the multi-messenger observations. We calculate neutrino production from hadronic channels (including hadronuclear and photomeson processes) and the accompanying cascade gamma rays, and then employ the Latin hypercube sampling (LHS) method to explore the parameter space comprehensively, constrained by observational data. According to our results, the emission region is tightly limited: $R \gtrsim 10\,R_{\rm s}$ is excluded at $\sim 5\sigma$, and $R \gtrsim 6\,R_{\rm s}$ at $\sim 3\sigma$, where $R_{\rm s}$ is Schwarzschild radius of supermassive black hole (SMBH). Furthermore, reproducing $\gtrsim 80\%$ of the observed neutrino flux further restricts the emission to $R \lesssim 3R_{\rm s}$. Finally, we explore the possible particle acceleration mechanisms and find that stochastic acceleration naturally satisfies all constraints, whereas alternative mechanisms require extreme, fine-tuning parameters. We therefore identify stochastic acceleration as the most viable origin of the neutrino emission from NGC~1068.

papers.title: Improving Slow-Roll Estimates in Starobinsky Inflation Using an Analytic Hubble Parameter
papers.summary: Inflationary observables are naturally formulated in terms of the Hubble-flow hierarchy. Because exact background solutions are often unavailable, the Hubble-flow parameters are commonly approximated using potential slow-roll (PSR) quantities constructed from derivatives of the inflationary potential. We revisit the accuracy of this replacement for Starobinsky inflation by mapping analytic Jordan-frame background variables to their Einstein-frame counterparts and deriving the Hubble-flow parameters directly. The leading analytic background is an exact solution of a controlled deformation of the Starobinsky action. Linearizing the pure Starobinsky equation about this background yields a closed-form perturbative correction. Using the same first-order spectral expressions throughout, the perturbatively corrected background tracks the numerical evolution of the first two Hubble-flow parameters more accurately than the next-to-leading-order (NLO) PSR approximation over the common domain in which the NLO expressions remain physical. Moreover, the NLO estimate of \(\widetilde{\epsilon}_1\) reaches a maximum value of approximately \(0.114\), subsequently decreases, and therefore cannot determine the end of inflation from \(\widetilde{\epsilon}_1=1\). For the Planck 2018 central value \(n_s=0.9649\), the perturbatively corrected background gives \(\widetilde{N}_*\simeq55.60\), compared with \(55.72\) for the converged numerical background and \(56.98\) for the conventional large-\(\widetilde{N}_*\) estimate. For the adopted ACT DR6 combined-data value \(n_s=0.974\), it gives \(\widetilde{N}_*\simeq75.43\), compared with the conventional value \(76.92\). The analytic construction therefore provides a self-consistent endpoint and a first-order estimate of the e-fold number that closely reproduces the converged numerical result.

papers.title: Relative Jump Distance: a diagnostic for Nested Sampling
papers.summary: Nested sampling is widely used in astrophysics and cosmology to reliably infer model parameters and compare models within a Bayesian framework. To address models with many parameters, Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) random walks are used within nested sampling to advance a live point population. Diagnostics for nested sampling inference are essential to verify that trustworthy astrophysical conclusions can be drawn. We develop a diagnostic to identify poorly mixed random walks that do not meet the requirements of nested sampling. The distance from the start to the end of the random walk, the jump distance, is compared to the typical neighbour distance between live points, to obtain a relative jump distance (RJD). A robust estimate of a typical neighbour Mahalanobis distance is obtained with the MLFriends algorithm. In mock and real-world inference applications such as inferring the distance to GW170817, we observe the relative jump distance. We propose the geometric mean and fraction of RJD>1 as new summary diagnostics. To evaluate the sensitivity of the new diagnostics, problematic runs are identified by comparison with reruns using much longer MCMC chains. Trustworthy inference runs are consistently associated with above 1.1, while problematic runs can fall below these thresholds. The RJD is more sensitive than previous tests based on the live point insertion order. The RJD diagnostic is proposed as a widely applicable diagnostic to verify inference with nested sampling. It is implemented in the UltraNest package in version 4.1.

papers.title: Probing Compact Binary Coalescences in the Decihertz GW Band with IndIGO-D
papers.summary: We present an astrophysical science-case study of IndIGO-D, a decihertz gravitational-wave mission concept, focusing on compact binary sources across the 0.1-10 Hz band bridging LISA and next-generation ground-based interferometers. For these science projections, we consider three spacecraft forming an L-shaped interferometer in a heliocentric orbit, with two orthogonal 1000 km arms sharing a common vertex. We calculate the time-dependent antenna response of this geometry, including modulation produced by the orbital motion of the constellation. We treat the strain-sensitivity curve supplied by the IndIGO-D collaboration as an input. For the assumed sensitivity, we estimate a BNS detection rate of $\sim76$-$767\,{\rm yr}^{-1}$. We compute horizon distances for different source classes and find that intermediate-mass black-hole binaries with masses $10^2$-$10^3\,M_\odot$ are detectable throughout their formation history, complementing the reach of LISA and terrestrial detectors. Binary neutron star systems are observable to a horizon redshift of $z\lesssim0.3$, allowing continuous multi-band coverage with Voyager-class interferometers from the decihertz regime to merger. A Bayesian parameter-estimation study of a GW170817-like binary shows that the sky localization area improves from $\sim21\,{\rm deg}^2$ at one month, $\sim1\,{\rm deg}^2$ at one week, down to $0.3\,{\rm deg}^2$ at six hours pre-merger. These sky areas are readily tiled by the Rubin Observatory, whose $9.6\,{\rm deg}^2$ field of view and r-band depth enable high-cadence, repeated coverage of GW170817-like kilonovae at this distance and beyond. IndIGO-D bridges the gap between millihertz and terrestrial observations, enabling early warnings on timescales from months to hours and enhancing the prospects for multi-band and multi-messenger discoveries. papers.title: Gravitational Wave Propagation in K-essence Cosmology: Theory and Observational Constraints
papers.summary: Gravitational waves (GWs) provide a powerful, theory-independent probe of the dynamical structure of spacetime and the cosmological background. We investigate the propagation of linearized tensor modes in k-essence cosmology, where the dark sector is described by a non-canonical scalar field. Working in the high-frequency (short-wavelength) limit on a Friedmann-Lema\^{\i}tre-Robertson-Walker background and restricting to the transverse-traceless sector, we obtain a modified evolution equation in which the GW speed remains strictly luminal (compatible with GW170817), while the background field $\bar{\phi}$ generates a time-dependent effective mass term $m_{\rm eff}$. This background-induced mass alters the dispersion relation without introducing extra propagating degrees of freedom, producing an accumulated, frequency-dependent phase shift over cosmological distances. We show that $m_{\rm eff}$ is uniquely determined by background cosmological parameters and can be expressed as a redshift-dependent function $m_{\rm eff}(z)$, providing a direct connection between GW observables and scalar-field dynamics. The GW luminosity distance stays identical to the electromagnetic one, preserving standard-siren consistency. We confront the model with a joint Bayesian analysis combining cosmic chronometers, BAO, Pantheon+SH0ES, and standard-siren measurements from GWTC-2.1/3/4, and assess performance using $\chi^2$, $\chi^2_{\rm red}$, AIC, BIC, and DIC. The reconstruction is consistent with current data, reproduces the late-time expansion history, and provides data-driven constraints on the redshift evolution of $m_{\rm eff}(z)$.

papers.title: SPLIT: Loosely-coherent inference of long-inspiral gravitational-wave sources for robustness against modeling and data outliers
papers.summary: The Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA) will detect gravitational waves (GWs) from dozens of extreme- and intermediate-mass-ratio inspirals (EMRIs/IMRIs). These sources will stay in-band for months to years, offering extraordinary scientific potential. However, their fully phase-coherent analysis standard in current pipelines imposes stringent waveform accuracy requirements; failing to model the signal over such long durations can result in significant systematic biases. To address this, we formulate a robust Bayesian inference framework that segments the data into blocks, infers each block coherently, and recombines the results using loosely-coherent phase information. By restricting full phase-tracking to much shorter block durations, this approach prevents significant accumulation of phase errors. We implement this methodology in \textsc{SPLIT} (Segmented Posteriors for Long-Inspiral Templates), a GPU-accelerated Python package. Applying \textsc{SPLIT} to an environment-rich injection, we demonstrate that while a fully-coherent vacuum-GR analysis incurs a maximum 1D systematic bias of $\approx 4.8\sigma$ from the truth, the shorter integration window of our loosely-coherent approach restricts such biases to $\lesssim 0.5\sigma$. Overall, despite a fractional loss of optimal signal-to-noise ratio, the substantial improvement in parameter accuracy offered by our method presents a highly advantageous trade-off for LISA and other future GW detectors.

papers.title: scCTM: Continuous Thought Machine Reconstruction of Glioma Cell Fate Dynamics Attractor Landscapes and Algorithmic Perturbation Signatures
papers.summary: Cell fate plasticity dynamics in glioma ecosystems is usually inferred from static single-cell snapshots, leaving a gap between manifold geometry, predictive modelling, and mechanistic intervention ranking. We developed scCTM, a complexity theory and machine learning framework that combines the Sakana AI Continuous Thought Machine (CTM) with autoencoding, a continuous actor-critic policy over synchronization-derived latent states for predicting single-cell fate dynamics. We also incorporated integrated-gradient and decoder-weight explainability, network science, empirical Waddington-like landscape (attractor) reconstruction, and post-hoc Block Decomposition Method (BDM) perturbation analysis. The complexity framework was evaluated in two malignant cell secondary analyses: GSE210567 stem-like versus differentiated H3K27M cells (18,490 cells) and longitudinal H3K27M initial versus recurrent disease trajectory (20,000 cells) from Sussman et al. (2026) as a ML binary classification problem. CTM-AE achieved AUROC values of $0.99$ in both datasets. CTM-RL preserved classification almost exactly but did not improve reconstruction. Out-of-fold CTM-RL latent states produced potential basins across PCA, UMAP, and PHATE embeddings. BDM edge perturbation analysis further identified recurrent high-impact network interactions, including epigenetic/chromatin-associated signatures involving ARID1B and developmental or neuronal-state genes such as AUTS2, CTNND2, DPP6, NRXN1, and CADM2. These in silico findings support CTM synchronization as an interpretable latent-state representation and predictive forecasting of cell fate dynamics, as well as BDM perturbation signatures as a complementary in silico intervention ranking layer for systems medicine.

papers.title: gpuGEM: GPU-based linear optimisation of genome-scale metabolic models
papers.summary: Summary: Genome-scale metabolic models increasingly challenge CPU linear-programming solvers in repeated-optimisation workflows. We present gpuGEM, an open-source Python library for GPU-based GEM optimisation using NVIDIA cuOpt, with size-adaptive settings validated against HiGHS and Gurobi. Across a ten-model benchmark suite spanning four orders of magnitude in problem size, gpuGEM achieved speed-ups of 1.1x to 94x relative to the faster of the HiGHS dual-simplex and interior-point methods for each model. gpuGEM also outperformed Gurobi on three of ten models, with speed-ups of 1.6x to 2.5x. In a candidate-gene prioritisation workflow, gpuGEM reduced end-to-end query time from 41 s to 21 s. Availability and Implementation: gpuGEM is released under the MIT licence at https://github.com/Digital-Metabolic-Twin-Centre/gpuGEM and on PyPI (pip install gpugem). An archived release(v0.1.2) is available at https://zenodo.org/records/23422813. gpuGEM requires an NVIDIA GPU, Python 3.11 or later, CUDA 12 and cuOpt 26.6 or later. cuOpt requires a GPU with Volta architecture or newer (compute capability 7.0 or newer). papers.title: LiveCoMS Roundtable: Discussing Markov state models after two decades of development v1.0
papers.summary: Markov state models (MSMs) play a central role in the analysis of molecular dynamics (MD) simulations for biomolecules, and MSM methodologies have been under continual development since their introduction to the field in the early 2000s. MSMs take MD trajectory data as input and produce a more compact, i.e., coarse-grained, and interpretable representation of the system in terms of conformational states and quantitative observables such as the equilibrium populations of states and the timescales of interconverting between states. Numerous strategies and considerable mathematical formalism have been developed to improve coarse-graining in both time and space to enable the most reliable representation of the underlying biomolecular dynamics. Nevertheless, there remains considerable discussion in the literature regarding best practices and MSM limitations, as well as proposals to abandon or extend the first-order Markovian framework in common use. This Roundtable article gathers together diverse opinions from $> 10$ authors active in MSM development, and by design, each author or author group offers a separate contribution. No consensus view is provided. Instead, the article is meant to be a guide for readers wishing to be exposed to a wide set of expert perspectives.

papers.title: Spaceflight-associated Motion Sickness in Commercial Crew Astronauts
papers.summary: Spaceflight-associated motion sickness, including space motion sickness (SMS) and terrestrial readaptation motion sickness (TRMS), has presented as the most operationally limiting effect on the human in the days following a gravity transition. Published data suggest that astronaut head movements provoke symptoms, but those studies rarely controlled for them. Most previous studies use postflight retrospective reporting and have not quantified temporal dynamics or persistence of symptoms; no study has published motion sickness in a cohort of commercial flyers. Here, we comprehensively evaluate SMS and TRMS within commercial flyers (N=8; 4F, 4M) for the first time, across two commercial missions of short duration (Polaris Dawn and Fram2). Utilizing a standard reporting methodology, we find an 87.5% incidence of SMS, which persisted for at least three days on orbit in 25% of crewmembers. The symptoms included vomiting in 62.5% of crewmembers. Regarding TRMS, incidence was 50%, severity was significantly lower than SMS (p = 0.007), and it tended to persist for a shorter duration than SMS for these short-duration flights. These findings establish a systematic baseline for spaceflight-associated motion sickness, informing its operational impact and salience as human spaceflight missions expand in accessibility and scope.

papers.title: Longitudinal fMRI reveals multi-network reconfiguration and a recurrent frontoparietal shift across rest and task states during adult aging
papers.summary: Functional connectivity changes across adult aging, but most evidence is cross-sectional, and covariance-based connectivity depends on blood oxygenation level dependent (BOLD) fluctuation amplitude. Covariance decline can reflect changing fluctuation amplitude, and its interpretation may depend on whether normalization uses signal amplitude or includes estimated noise. It is also unclear which longitudinal changes recur across brain states. We analyzed 852 adults (baseline age 36-89 years) from the Aging Adult Brain Connectome with repeated functional MRI (fMRI) during rest, inhibitory control, associative memory, and visual-motor processing (2,220 sessions; median follow-up 5.5 years). Baseline age and elapsed follow-up were modeled separately. Ten cortical networks were tested jointly across states, and covariance was normalized either by released signal amplitude or by a candidate total amplitude reconstructed from released signal and noise amplitudes. Native common covariance declined by 7-11% per 5 years, while signal pair amplitude declined by 9% on average across states, significantly more than estimated noise pair amplitude. Under signal normalization, the relative balance among networks reconfigured over follow-up and differed across states, and the frontoparietal network shifted positively relative to the other nine networks in all four states, by 5-8% per 5 years. The estimated common trajectory was near zero under signal normalization but declined by 4-7% per 5 years under candidate total normalization. The network reconfiguration and the positive frontoparietal-relative direction persisted under both. Within-person coupling between the frontoparietal shift and fluid cognition was not detected. Adult aging thus combines normalization-dependent overall change with a state-dependent redistribution among networks that includes a recurrent frontoparietal shift.

papers.title: Evidence-informed dynamic modelling and intervention prioritisation in diabetic bone marrow
papers.summary: Aims. Fragmented understanding of how diabetes disrupts interconnected bone marrow niches has hindered integrated strategies to restore function. Building on a previous static network, we developed a dynamic model to simulate intervention responses. Methods. The investigator and ChatGPT dialogued to extract evidence from a frozen corpus and develop the model. A Python implementation extended Boolean logic to three ordinal levels (0, 1 and 2) representing biological states and, where applicable, intervention strength. Under high metabolic stress, 15 interventions were assessed at three strengths and four with binary settings; 171 pairs were tested at maximal strength. A domain balanced score (0 to100) integrated favourable and adverse changes. Staged simulations assessed withdrawal; regulatory constraints on recovery after metabolic stress reduction were examined separately. Results. Endothelial reactive oxygen species (ROS) suppression achieved the highest score among 19 single interventions (24.2), improving three functional domains. Endothelial protein kinase B (Akt) augmentation scored 15.2 (two domains); oncostatin M (OSM) blockade and haematopoietic 66 kDa SHC transforming protein 1 (p66Shc) loss each scored 13.6 (two domains). ROS suppression combined with either OSM blockade or p66Shc loss scored 37.9, (five domains). No pair restored all functions under high stress. Benefits of ROS suppression, Akt augmentation and ROS and OSM blockade disappeared after withdrawal. Reducing metabolic stress led to variable scores (range 4.5 to 100), increasing mainly with restored endothelial function, followed by progenitor recovery and interruption of inflammatory and adipocyte stromal signalling. Conclusions. These simulations offer a rule based framework for investigating diabetic marrow recovery. Experimental studies must establish whether it can guide targeted therapy.

papers.title: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
papers.summary: Despite breakthroughs in AI-driven molecular generation, existing discovery pipelines operate largely in silico, with wet-lab feedback reserved for validation rather than iterative improvement. Whether large language model (LLM)-based reasoning agents can accelerate de novo discovery by iterating with lab data remains unproven. Here we use protein-binding aptamer design as a sandbox (1-2 week cycles, \$1-\$3 per candidate) to demonstrate a wet lab in a closed loop with AI systems. We tasked agentic pipelines with developing aptamer binders against $\alpha$-thrombin and myoglobin across three design-test-improve cycles ($\sim$1,000 candidates per round; $\sim$4,400 constructs). Statistically significant, bead-corrected on-target hit rates among new candidates rose across rounds from 0.0% in Round 1 to 26.0% in Round 2 and 42.1% in Round 3 on $\alpha$-thrombin (37.1% excluding literature motif descendants), and from 10.2% in Round 1 to 3.7% in Round 2 and 33.5% in Round 3 on myoglobin. Single-clone bead-binding titrations of eight full-length $\alpha$-thrombin candidates confirmed concordance with pooled sequencing enrichment (Pearson $r = 0.90$). In these assays, literature-derived motifs engineered by the agents to reduce off-target reactivity in the pooled screen reached apparent affinities of $K_D = 24.6$--$133$ nM, whereas de novo scaffolds showed low-micromolar binding ($K_D > 1\ \mu$M). We also report how our pipelines used myoglobin binding data to exploit the G-quadruplex binder space, diagnose cross-reactivity as on-target specificity dropped from 75.0% to 19.1%, and recover by developing strategies that restored specificity to 72.4%. We demonstrate that empirical lab data is more valuable than existing computational proxies, showing how iterative experimental feedback enables AI agents to diagnose assay artifacts and refine molecular designs across rounds.

papers.title: Accurate quantification of protein concentrations and state populations by 2D 1H-N Q-BEST NMR
papers.summary: We introduce 2D Q-BEST NMR as a quantitative approach for determining protein concentrations and relative state populations from a set of three 1 H-15 N correlation spectra. The BEST methodology ensures short overall experimental times and highest sensitivity. The method was validated using ubiquitin as a model system, where a precision of approximately 15-20% was achieved at the level of individual cross-peaks. This precision can be further improved by averaging corrected intensities of well-resolved resonances corresponding to the same protein state. The approach was subsequently applied to the quantification of protein concentrations across multiple samples and to the determination of conformational state populations in proteins exhibiting intrinsic or ligand-induced heterogeneity. In both cases, 2D Q-BEST NMR provides accurate and robust quantification of NMR-visible species, demonstrating its utility as a general spectroscopic tool for quantitative biomolecular NMR analysis.

papers.title: The resource cost of cooperative invasion
papers.summary: A contact network can favor cooperation by sheltering a lineage until its descendants compete with defectors as a group. We determine the contact strengths, invasion times and measurement effort needed to realize this advantage at fixed population size. Individuals reproduce according to averaged cooperation payoffs, and offspring replace neighbors through contacts of equal weight in both directions. Contact contrast is the ratio of strongest to weakest contact. Under weak selection on a six-site path, the least contrast needed to favor a single cooperator over the reverse invasion by a defector grows as $656\epsilon^{-2}$ for uniformly placed mutants and $4050\epsilon^{-3}$ for mutations in newborn offspring, as the benefit-cost ratio $b/c=1+\epsilon$ approaches one. The extra power arises because rare replacement protects a site while suppressing mutation arrival there. Global bounds force two weakly coupled groups and exact mirror symmetry of the least-contrast contacts for sufficiently small $\epsilon$. Under uniform introduction, additional contrast shortens the leading mean time to extinction or fixation in the absence of selection, from $12/\epsilon$ toward $6/\epsilon$ reproduction attempts, and eventually breaks the mirror symmetry of the fastest design. Estimating the uniform-introduction advantage from fixation outcomes of independent completed invasions defines a third optimum. Within the six-site family with mirror-symmetric, strongly separated contacts, we optimize contacts and selection strength with reproduction weighted linearly or exponentially by payoff. At fixed relative precision, with contrast a fixed factor above its minimum, the leading summed trial duration grows as $\epsilon^{-3}$. Efficient measurement accepts a smaller advantage in exchange for shorter trials. The cheapest, fastest and most efficiently measured networks therefore differ.

papers.title: PyGPLA: A Python Package for Generalized Phase Locking Analysis
papers.summary: Spike-field couplings measure the links between neuronal spiking and local field potential (LFP) and provide a tool to study how neural populations coordinate activity across spatial and temporal scales. While modern high-density electrophysiology enables the simultaneous recording of numerous LFP channels and neuronal units, this massive scale poses significant statistical and computational challenges for conventional pairwise coupling analyses. The number of channel-unit comparisons grows rapidly, and a coherent population-level structure can be obscured by high-dimensional coupling matrices. Generalized Phase Locking Analysis (GPLA) addresses this challenge by organizing spike-triggered LFP phase information into a complex coupling matrix and extracting dominant low-rank modes. These modes summarize whether a population is coupled to the field, which channels and units contribute to the coupling, and how their relative phases are organized. Here, we present PyGPLA, an open-source Python package implementing GPLA for high-density electrophysiological recordings. Designed for straightforward integration into existing neural data analysis pipelines, PyGPLA supports multivariate spike-LFP coupling analysis, from coupling estimation and interpretation to significance assessment using analytical and surrogate-based tests.

papers.title: Affective Valence as the Interoceptive Rate of Change of Jacobian Scale
papers.summary: Affect is widely held to depend on interoception. This paper proposes that valence is the rate at which interoception moves a self-sustaining system's responsiveness relative to its terminal set (roughly, death). Responsiveness is formalised as the scale of the system's Jacobian and interoception as its internal inputs: receptors, signals and forecasts of its energy reserve. Changes in responsiveness that bypass interoception, such as brain damage, are not felt. Language models have no valence because they are not self-sustaining. The chain rule splits valence over the system's parts and the causes that affect its internal inputs. With the log scale, these splits account for need-dependent pleasure, diffuse hunger and localised pain, negativity bias, and relief when a threat fails to arrive. In a minimal model of a body: (1) Blocking the reserve signal leaves depletion unfelt, and driving it produces hunger with an undepleted reserve. (2) Removing receptors or their gain, or driving receptors, reproduces congenital insensitivity to pain, asymbolia and phantom pain. (3) A receptor gain learned to sustain the body signals local damage to the whole body, so an injury hurts in proportion to its cost. (4) If the reserve also modulates the gain, the body learns to suppress pain due to receptors as energy runs low. (5) When it learns to maximise its own scale, it becomes a wirehead. The account explains when changes are felt, where they are felt, and when feelings mislead.
