papers.title: 2-Adic Tree Embeddings: A Modeling and Optimization Framework for Computational Phylogenetics
papers.summary: Phylogenetic inference is a fundamental problem in computational biology, with applications ranging from epidemiology and oncology to developmental biology and comparative genomics. Many major phylogenetic problems are NP-hard; consequently, existing methods often explore tree space using local search or MCMC based on a limited repertoire of combinatorial rearrangements. However, the size and ruggedness of tree space make it difficult for such heuristics to reliably reach optimal or near-optimal solutions. Recently, there has been growing interest in alternative approaches that embed trees into numerical spaces and apply numerical optimization techniques. However, such methods are still limited in practical applicability. We propose a new approach to phylogenetic inference based on embeddings of trees into the non-Archimedean space of $2$-adic numbers. The hierarchical organization of $2$-adic space naturally encodes tree topologies, while its rich topological, algebraic, and measure-theoretic structure provides a natural foundation for a coherent theory of tree calculus and optimization. Here, we introduce 2-adic tree embedding, establish their basic topological, probabilistic, and algebraic properties, and show that they support natural representations of tree distributions, algebraic operations, and broad classes of tree rearrangements extending standard operations such as NNI, SPR, and TBR. Building on these results, we introduce a general local search framework in which tree neighborhoods are generated by parametric families of $2$-adic polynomials. We show that even infinitely many transformations induce only quadratically many distinct neighboring trees, which can be generated in polynomial time. These results suggest a new mathematically rigorous and flexible approach to representing and exploring tree space.

papers.title: Global stability of Michaelis-Menten networks
papers.summary: In a very nice paper, Blanchini, Breda, Giordano and Liessi studied networks of species coupled through Michaelis-Menten interactions. Under standard assumptions of strong connectedness and non-degeneracy, they show that there is a unique equilibrium, which is (locally) asymptotically stable. This note shows that global stability, which was stated there as an open problem, holds as well. In fact, whenever a positive equilibrium exists, it attracts every solution with positive initial condition, with no connectedness or non-degeneracy hypothesis at all; those assumptions are needed only in order to guarantee existence and to cover solutions starting on the boundary of the orthant. The key is to note that the system is contractive with respect to the Thompson part metric.

papers.title: panvram: GPU-resident random access to a human pangenome cohort
papers.summary: Repeatedly sampling short sequence windows from a human pangenome requires an access representation as well as compression. panvram stores each assembly as a reference-relative block archive and pools these archives on a GPU. For 558 haplotype assemblies, the default q4k representation occupies 16.642 GB of persistent pools including the decoded reference; a packed-reference, compact-directory representation occupies 11.634 GB. These quantities are not peak application memory. In the C1 experiment, default and fully compact forms delivered 743,271 and 736,762 windows/s; a separate public Colab run delivered 741,931 and 680,760 windows/s. All are batch API measurements and must not be pooled as repeated trials of an identical environment. Full-decoding checks compared reconstructed FASTA checksums with the manifest. On the CPU, the M6 shuffled-window workload at the same cohort cardinality reported 26 requests/s for AGC and 145,222 requests/s for refrel3 q4k. This comparison concerns one-thread requests of 4 KiB on the recorded warm-cache workload, not all genome-access patterns. AGC provides the smaller incremental archive: 5.40 MB/assembly versus 13.04 MB/assembly for refrel3 q16k, with different exclusions; the size pair is not the same refrel3 configuration as the q4k timing pair. We derive an expected-work expression for fixed independent granules and distinguish it from an empirical median-latency predictor. Cohort-scale counter and DRAM measurements motivate a locality hypothesis, but do not establish a causal per-miss latency or independently reproduce a model-failure verdict. The window-cost verdict at N=558 is published with its harness and raw timings.

papers.title: HP-GSBS: Accelerating greedy state boundary search with reusable interval statistics
papers.summary: Greedy State Boundary Search (GSBS) identifies transitions between relatively stable neural activity patterns, but repeated candidate evaluation makes large analyses expensive. HP-GSBS is an open-source Python package that reorganizes the search around reusable interval contributions and correlation statistics. Streaming candidate reduction and local refinement further reduce repeated work; CPU, PyTorch CUDA and Triton backends share sequential segmentation decisions. Across seven controlled workloads with two realizations each, median same-input speedups range from 154 to 1730 times. All 168 optimized executions reproduce original boundaries and selected state counts, with maximum absolute t-distance difference $1.88\times10^{-11}$. Four frozen EEG recordings provide complementary validation, including a complete input-to-segmentation application example. Batch processing, versioned result persistence and optional low-memory execution support recording collections and longer inputs. By removing redundant computation, HP-GSBS makes established neural-state segmentation faster while preserving its scientific outputs.

papers.title: Distributions of metric $n$-point invariants and applications to molecular evolution
papers.summary: Datasets often arise as samples from a metric measure space whose geometry reflects the data-generating process. We introduce metric $n$-point invariants, defined as functions of the pairwise distances of $n$-point configurations, to study the geometry of such spaces. This provides a unified framework for existing concepts, such as the pairwise distance itself, the Gromov product, and Vietoris-Rips persistence diagrams. The distribution of a metric $n$-point invariant $F$ over random $n$-point configurations can be used to extract geometric information from the space and is obtained as the pushforward of Gromov's $n$-th curvature measure $\mu_n$ along $F$. Our main result is an explicit bound for the expected $p$-Wasserstein distance between $\mu_n$ and the empirical curvature measure $\hat{\mu}_{n}$ of finitely many sampled $n$-point configurations, and carries over to the associated distributions of Lipschitz metric $n$-point invariants. From this we derive the sample size needed to achieve a prescribed accuracy and level of confidence in the approximation of the curvature measure. As an application, we use metric $n$-point invariants to study molecular evolution. We describe how site-wise nucleotide frequencies shape the corresponding distributions in Jukes-Cantor and Halpern-Bruno substitution models, and analyse five million SARS-CoV-2 genomes, revealing increasingly common failures of the four-point condition, constrained nucleotide accessibility consistent with the biased mutation spectrum, and rare cycles in persistent homology reflecting recurrent mutations across lineages. These findings demonstrate the potential of our sampling-based approach to the geometry of data as a scalable, phylogeny-free tool for detecting and quantifying evolutionary structure in large genomic datasets.

papers.title: Application of Single-cell Deep Learning in Elucidating the Mapping Relationship Between Visceral and Body Surface Inflammatory Patterns
papers.summary: The subcutaneous fascia (scFascia) is a widely distributed connective tissue, yet its contribution to systemic responses during visceral inflammation remains insufficiently defined. In the rat model of Salmonella-induced dysentery, scRNA-seq of scFascia combined with deep neural network (DNN)-based nonlinear feature discovery revealed transcriptional alterations indicative of Warburg-like reprogramming in macrophages (MPs), accompanied by reduced activity of the citrate cycle. CD34+/PDGFR{\alpha}+ telocytes (CPTCs) regulated MP differentiation and proliferation through Wnt/Fgf signaling, suggesting a pathological communication pattern between scFascia and visceral organs, termed the fascia-visceral inflammatory crosstalk pattern (FVICP). PySCENIC analysis showed increased activity of transcription factors Fosl1, Nfkb2, and Atf4, modulated by CPTC signaling to MPs, leading to downregulation of aerobic respiration and upregulation of the cell cycle, DNA replication, and transcription. Co-culture assays demonstrated that CPTCs suppressed the pro-inflammatory activity of MPs by transcriptionally downregulating TLR4 and CPT1A while upregulating ATF4, and enhanced anti-inflammatory potential via post-transcriptional MTOR upregulation. These findings highlight the role of scFascia in immunomodulation and metabolic reprogramming during visceral inflammation, emphasizing its contribution to systemic homeostasis.

papers.title: Invading activity fronts or near-critical clusters may stabilize vulnerable excitable systems against stochastic trajectories terminating in an absorbing state
papers.summary: Stochastic chemical reaction or population dynamics in finite systems often terminates in an absorbing state. Yet in large spatially extended systems, the time to reach the absorbing configuration (e.g., species extinction or fixation) becomes exceedingly long. Tuning control parameters may effectively diminish the survival probability, rendering active states (species coexistence) susceptible to stochastic extinction events. In inhomogeneous settings, where a vulnerable subsystem is diffusively coupled to an adjacent stable patch, the former is re-activated through influx from the interfaces, provided the vulnerable region either sustains spreading activity fronts or near-critical large active clusters. Either dynamical structure resets the system to correlated initial conditions favorable for survival. We demonstrate this generic elimination of finite-size extinction instabilities via immigration flux in stochastic predator-prey, cyclic competition, and epidemic spreading models.

papers.title: Dynamic response phenotypes and model discrimination in systems and synthetic biology
papers.summary: Biological systems encode function not primarily in steady states, but in the structure of transient responses elicited by time-varying stimuli. Overshoots, biphasic dynamics, adaptation kinetics, fold-change detection, entrainment, and cumulative exposure effects often determine phenotypic outcomes, yet are poorly captured by classical steady-state or dose-response analyses. This paper develops an input-output perspective on such "dynamic phenotypes," emphasizing how qualitative features of transient behavior constrain underlying network architectures independently of detailed parameter values. A central theme is the role of sign structure and interconnection logic, particularly the contrast between monotone systems and architectures containing antagonistic pathways. We show how incoherent feedforward (IFF) motifs provide a simple and recurrent mechanism for generating non-monotonic and adaptive responses across multiple levels of biological organization, from molecular signaling to immune regulation and population dynamics. Conversely, monotonicity imposes sharp impossibility results that can be used to falsify entire classes of models from transient data alone. Beyond step inputs, we highlight how periodic forcing, ramps, and integral-type readouts such as cumulative dose responses offer powerful experimental probes that reveal otherwise hidden structure, separate competing motifs, and expose invariances such as fold-change detection. Throughout, we illustrate how control-theoretic concepts, including monotonicity, equivariance, and input-output analysis, can be used not as engineering metaphors, but as precise mathematical tools for biological model discrimination. Thus we argue for a shift in emphasis from asymptotic behavior to transient and input-driven dynamics as a primary lens for understanding, testing, and reverse-engineering biological networks.

papers.title: CPTCs Drive Somatic-Visceral Communication via the Wnt Axis in Somatic Mechanotherapy: A Single-Cell Deep Learning Study
papers.summary: Somatic mechanical stimulation (e.g., acupuncture) exerts systemic immunomodulatory effects, yet the cellular bridge translating peripheral physical force into visceral repair remains elusive. Here, employing a custom interpretable deep learning framework (CARSS) on single-cell RNA sequencing data, we identify CD34+PDGFR{\alpha}+ telocytes (CPTCs) as the primary mechanosensors in both fascia and colon during bacterial colitis. We show that somatic mechanotherapy triggers an AP-1/Hsp70-dependent transcriptional program in fascial CPTCs, inducing systemic Wnt elevation, which elicits a "transcriptional resonance" in colonic CPTCs, reprogramming their communication network from an inflammatory amplifier to a Wnt-driven regenerative hub. Mechanistically, this axis activates epithelial \b{eta}-catenin/Myc signaling, suppressing apoptosis and restoring barrier integrity independent of immune cells. Our findings define a CPTC-Driven Mechano-Resonance Axis, where CPTCs serve as synchronized relay stations that convert somatic mechanical stimulation into systemic regenerative microenvironments.

papers.title: Direct RNA sequence design under codon constraints using expressive tensor-based secondary structure models
papers.summary: Nucleic acid sequence design via codon optimization is a fundamental task with applications across synthetic biology, mRNA therapeutics, and vaccine design. Given a target protein, it is a major open challenge to navigate the combinatorially large design space of codon sequences mapping to its amino acid sequence. Computational approaches generally seek to optimize simple objectives based on the codon sequence, possibly together with more complicated contributions based on secondary structure analysis. In this work, we demonstrate a direct and efficient algorithm to sample sequences from a suitable Boltzmann distribution defined in terms of the codon sequence and a fully detailed secondary structure free energy model, as well as related algorithms for exact computation of statistical quantities such as free energies, base pairing probabilities, and base and codon marginals. These algorithms draw upon a recently developed tensor-based formulation of secondary structure thermodynamics and demonstrate, for the first time, that global sequence design can be accomplished with respect to a highly accurate free energy model. Moreover, the algorithms can leverage any available CPU and GPU resources in parallel for massive computational speedups.

papers.title: Consensus-level substitution rates are distinct from the virion-level rate
papers.summary: Estimating viral substitution rates is central to evolutionary epidemiology, and recent interest in within-host evolution has sharpened the question of what such rates measure. I distinguish two classes of evolutionary rate estimand that are rarely separated in phylogenetic analysis: the virion-level substitution rate (VLSR), a molecular quantity counting mutational events along lineages, and consensus-level substitution rates (CLSRs), population-summary quantities counting allele frequency threshold crossings from below. CLSRs are indexed by the consensus-generation rule. The VLSR and CLSRs are both biologically meaningful, but not interchangeable. Because the consensus-generation rule defines a given CLSR, it should be reported routinely. This reflection should help analysts make more informed methodological choices when working with sets of virus sequences.

papers.title: Evaluating Conformal Reliability of Pathway-Level Transcriptomic Signatures Under Cross-Cohort Shift in Sepsis Mortality Prediction
papers.summary: Blood transcriptomic profiling enables prognostic modeling by capturing the host immune response at the molecular level. Yet, the within-cohort evaluation strategies employed by many transcriptomic models inadequately reflect deployment across independent hospitals. Outside deployment scenarios introduce a cohort shift that can substantially degrade predictive performance and reliability of uncertainty estimates. We present a framework for evaluating transcriptomic sepsis mortality prediction under realistic cross-cohort deployment, systematically comparing gene-level, pathway-level and hybrid molecular representations. Four publicly available whole-blood transcriptomic cohorts consisting of 936 patients and 248 mortality events were harmonized into a shared 7,660-gene feature space and evaluated under leave-one-cohort-out validation using logistic regression, random forests, XGBoost and LightGBM. Beyond AUROC and AUPRC, model behavior was evaluated via conformal prediction, calibration analysis, selective prediction and the proposed Pathway Stability Index. Gene-level and hybrid representations were found to generally achieve the strongest discriminative performance, whereas pathway-level representations exhibited greater robustness across model families, more reliable uncertainty behavior under cross-cohort shift and stable molecular signatures enriched for immune and host-defense processes identified through Gene Ontology and KEGG enrichment analyses. These findings demonstrate that molecular representation influences not only predictive discrimination but also calibration, uncertainty reliability, biological coherence and transferability under external validation.

papers.title: Orchestra: Corroboration-Based Regulatory Candidate Discovery via Composed Bioinformatics MCP Agents

papers.title: A theory of plasticity: capacity for change as inverse configurational constraint
papers.summary: Plasticity is invoked across the sciences to explain how systems can change, yet it is inferred from the very change it is meant to explain. A system may have many alternatives, realize none and still be plastic. Another may be driven far toward its only alternative, but the magnitude of that change does not establish its plasticity. What matters for plasticity is not how far the system moves but how strongly its present configuration constrains alternatives. Here I propose that plasticity, understood as a prospective property, is inverse configurational constraint: a system is plastic to the extent that its present configuration weakly constrains displacement toward alternatives within a declared representation. For systems sharing a functional partition, structural representation, and normalized architecture, increasing plasticity lowers every positive finite structural barrier separating the current state from its alternatives. With a fixed accessibility criterion, the accessible repertoire can expand but cannot shrink. In network representations, aggregate coupling is identified as configurational constraint, whose inverse defines plasticity. Barrier reduction and repertoire nesting are consequences, not components, of the definition. This connects two research traditions: quantifying connectivity without interpreting it as plasticity, and treating plasticity as a capacity for change without a prospective operational measure.

papers.title: An Open-Source Web-Based Viewer for Disseminating Image-Derived Models
papers.summary: Patient-specific 3-dimensional (3D) models are increasingly central to planning surgery and catheter-based intervention in children with congenital heart disease (CHD), whose anatomy is often atypical and variable. These models inform care only when the surgeons and interventional cardiologists who make treatment decisions can rotate, crop, and measure them directly. Desktop modeling applications require local installation, capable hardware, and training. Commercial web-based viewers are portable but closed, and, in our experience, cannot display volume rendering, time-resolved (e.g., 4-dimensional) data, or the custom workflows centers build for CHD. Because CHD populations are small and heterogeneous, such workflows are unlikely to be prioritized commercially, and end users have no means to add them. To address these limitations, we developed the SlicerHeart Viewer, an open-source module that presents a simplified interface to a complete 3D Slicer/SlicerHeart session running on a server. Clinicians access models created by clinical modeling services from any device through a web browser. Because 3D Slicer runs underneath, volume rendering, time-resolved data, and any SlicerHeart workflow, including those developed for CHD, are available without modification. The module is independent of the hosting environment; we chose internal servers behind institutional single sign-on, and a cloud-hosted option is in development. Over one year at a single pediatric center, nearly all of 82 modeled cases were shared through the Viewer with clinicians from five specialties, with cases loading in 5 to 10 seconds. The approach is not specific to CHD and is deployable at other centers.

papers.title: Asymmetric Entanglement-Assisted Quantum Locally Recoverable Codes
papers.summary: Locally recoverable codes (LRCs) permit reconstruction of a lost coordinate from a small subset of the remaining coordinates, a property that is a fundamental coding technique for distributed storage and, more recently, for fault-tolerant quantum memories and distributed storage systems. Existing constructions of quantum locally recoverable codes (qLRCs) and their entanglement-assisted generalizations (EA-qLRCs) impose a single locality parameter $r$ governing recovery from both bit-flip ($X$-type) and phase-flip ($Z$-type) errors, even though physical noise is rarely symmetric between the two. We introduce entanglement-assisted quantum locally recoverable codes (EA-qLRC) with \emph{asymmetric locality} $\{r_X,r_Z\}$, in which $X$-type and $Z$-type errors are corrected from recovery sets of size at most $r_X+1$ and $r_Z+1$, respectively. We extend a stabilizer sufficient condition for this property and, in particular, the CSS framework, where asymmetric locality corresponds to separate locality conditions on the two classical codes $\mathcal C_1$ and $\mathcal C_2$ underlying the construction. From this characterization we derive Singleton-, Griesmer-, Plotkin-, sphere-packing-, and Cadambe\textendash Mazumdar-like bounds for CSS-type asymmetric EA-qLRCs (AEA-qLRCs) built from Proposition~\ref{CSS-EA-qLRC-Asym}, and we characterize exactly when a pure CSS-type AEA-qLRC built from a pair of classical LRCs attains the Singleton-like bound with equality.

papers.title: Designing Robust Quantum Gates
papers.summary: For given control channels, quantum control theory determines whether quantum gates can be realized, but not their resilience to errors. We address this problem by establishing existence criteria for robust gate implementation in $d$-level systems. Our criteria reveal that implementability of all gates is not enough: a universal family of robust gates exists if and only if the driven Hamiltonians share no common symmetry. When these criteria hold, we can make gates resilient to any combination of static perturbations, uniform Hamiltonian rescaling, perturbations at a finite set of selected frequencies, and perturbations with arbitrary selected waveforms. We can impose robustness conditions broadly with limited information about errors, e.g., against any static perturbations; we can also tailor these conditions to the platform, e.g., against environment-induced noise with dominant spectral peaks, requiring no spectral details beyond the peak frequencies. We numerically construct explicit protocols for robust gates, reducing average gate infidelity by approximately two to seven orders of magnitude under Hamiltonian perturbations and environment-induced noise. Together, our existence criteria and numerical constructions provide practical guidance for evaluating the potential of quantum platforms and designing robust quantum gates.

papers.title: Operational Meaning of the Mandelstam-Tamm Time Scale in a Spin-1/2 Clock
papers.summary: Georgiev's analysis of a freely precessing spin correctly emphasizes that the Mandelstam-Tamm quantity $\Delta T=\Delta\hat A/|d\langle\hat A\rangle/d t|$ is not the variance of a time operator. He concludes, however, that its divergence near the extrema of the clock signal is devoid of physical meaning and that $\Delta T$ does not disclose how well the system measures the passage of time. For the same projective $\hat\sigma_x$ readout, we show that $\Delta T$ equals the inverse square root of the classical Fisher information in one binary outcome at regular operating points. Its divergence at submaximal-coherence extrema therefore identifies a loss of local sensitivity in the selected readout, not an infinite variance of physical time; a complementary $\hat\sigma_y$ measurement remains informative. This interpretation also separates Georgiev's exactly known tick--tock period from the statistical precision with which a tick can be located. It preserves his warning against a time-operator interpretation while qualifying his stronger conclusion that the Mandelstam--Tamm scale lacks physical content.

papers.title: Quantum error correction well below the color code threshold
papers.summary: Quantum error correction enables scalable fault-tolerant quantum computation by suppressing logical errors exponentially with code distance once physical error rates fall below a critical threshold. Here we demonstrate below-threshold operation of triangular color codes with distances $d=3,5,$ and $7$ on Quantinuum's Helios trapped-ion quantum processor. Leveraging both circuit- and hardware- level leakage reduction schemes, we achieve logical error rates as low as $5_{-2}^{+4}\times 10^{-6}$, and demonstrate error suppression by over an order of magnitude, $\Lambda=12_{-2}^{+3}$, with each successive increase in code distance. Moreover, we demonstrate below threshold scaling of error rates for Clifford two-qubit randomized benchmarking circuits when encoded in $d=3,5$ color codes, achieving logical error rate of $7^{+3}_{-3}\times 10^{-5}$ per logical two-qubit Clifford at distance $5$ with a suppression factor of $\Lambda=9_{-3}^{+8}$. We compare logical performance for existing near-optimal algorithmic decoders, and both convolutional neural network and transformer-based neural network decoders capable of real-time decoding an order of magnitude faster than the syndrome extraction rate. These results approach the logical error rates required for megaquop-scale quantum computation and indicate that scaled trapped-ion processors could reach application-relevant performance with substantially smaller code blocks than indicated by previous results in other qubit modalities.

papers.title: Performance of a Hot Rb Vapour-Based Portable Quantum Memory
papers.summary: Quantum repeaters will be paramount to the success of the future quantum internet. Presently however, the losses incurred in fibre communications are unsustainable when fragile quantum states are transmitted over long distances. The most effective repeater nodes will require incorporation of a minimum of two quantum memory units (QMems) for successful operation. Therefore a network composed of numerous nodes will ideally require scalable repeaters that contain QMems that are portable, robust and do not require a high amount of overhead. Here we investigate the performance of a commercial QMem based on a warm vapour of Rb atoms. Specifically, we characterize the coherence time, absolute efficiency, signal to noise ratio and bit error ratio of this device over a range of vapour temperatures that are readily controllable. For our system, we place these performance metrics into the same conventions as those established for current optical communication protocols. Development of QMem systems meeting these benchmarks will be a vital step for seamless integration of QMems systems into present-day communication architectures.

papers.title: Translation-Invariant Pure States with Exotic Half-Chain Factors
papers.summary: We construct translation-invariant pure quasifree fermionic states on the one-dimensional lattice whose half-chain von Neumann algebras are hyperfinite factors of type $\mathrm{II}_\infty$ or $\mathrm{III}_\lambda$ for any $0<\lambda\leq 1$. Via the Jordan-Wigner-Araki transformation, these yield translation-invariant pure spin-chain states with the same half-chain factors, demonstrating that such factors need not be of type I or III. Each state is the unique ground state of a gapless, translation-invariant parent Hamiltonian with superpolynomially decaying interactions. For any fixed factor type, the interval entanglement entropy can exhibit widely varying growth rates, from arbitrarily slow divergence to nearly power-law growth, showing that entropy scaling does not determine the factor type. In contrast, we prove that gauge-invariant quadratic Hamiltonians with finitely many flavours and exponentially decaying hopping exhibit a dichotomy: their ground states either satisfy an area law with a type I half-chain factor, or have logarithmic entropy growth with a type $\mathrm{III}_1$ factor. The counterexample was discovered with AI assistance.

papers.title: Trajectree - A quantum trajectory-based quantum circuit simulator
papers.summary: We introduce Trajectree, a quantum trajectory-based quantum circuit simulator that uses a novel, state-saving partial execution of the quantum circuits to simulate broad and deep noisy quantum circuits efficiently. Trajectree can efficiently generate a large number of Monte Carlo samples by saving partially executed trajectories. We conduct extensive performance analysis of the Trajectree approach, proving the utility of the trajectory saving scheme for simulations of open quantum systems. Using this architecture, we show that Trajectree can simulate standard benchmark noisy circuits over five times faster than Google's QSim, a part of the Cirq package. We also analyze Trajectree's performance for simulating quantum optical systems relevant to communication and computing applications. We demonstrate applications of the optical backend to simulate three optical experiments: CHSH Bell test, entanglement swapping, and optical CNOT gate. This shows Trajectree's potential for simulating noisy qudit and optical systems efficiently.

papers.title: Nonlocality as a Benchmarking Tool for Quantum Processors
papers.summary: Benchmarking quantum processors is a central task in every roadmap aimed at quantum advantage. Here, we discuss a benchmarking protocol based on the violation of the Svetlichny inequality, which is designed to simulate genuine multipartite nonlocality. We compare it with Mermin's inequality, and present the results of applying this framework to two different quantum processing units -the superconducting system Garnet (from IQM) and the ion-trap system Marmot (from AQT), testing different families of quantum circuits for three to five qubits under identical experimental conditions. We also run simultaneous triplet tests across the full register, including a comparison between GHZ and linear cluster states, to probe how Svetlichny-inequality violations depend on qubit location and calibration. Our results demonstrate that tests based on genuine multipartite nonlocality provide a powerful tool to characterize the collective performance of quantum devices and to guide their calibration and optimization.

papers.title: Optimal robust single-qubit gates in superconducting quantum processors
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum computing requires high-fidelity quantum gates that are resilient to control errors and device imperfections. Here, we develop energy-optimal control pulses for single-qubit gates that are simultaneously robust against frequency detuning and waveform inhomogeneities while also suppressing leakage outside the computational subspace. Combining the optimized pulse envelopes with an adaptive control scheme, we experimentally demonstrate optimal robust gates on a superconducting quantum processor. For a gate duration of 90ns, we achieve fidelities above 99.9% for the X gate and 99.6% for Hadamard-type gates. For the X gate, we maintain fidelities above 99.5% for simultaneous drive-amplitude variations up to 20% and qubit detuning up to 4 MHz. This robustness outperforms that of conventional Gaussian pulses by an order of magnitude, without much difference in peak gate fidelity. These results establish a route towards robust single-qubit control in large-scale quantum processors, advancing the development of fault-tolerant quantum computing.

papers.title: Generalized Svetlichny Inequalities as a Cross-Platform Benchmark for Quantum Processors
papers.summary: A cross-platform benchmark should be device-independent yet sensitive to imperfections accumulated during execution. Building on prior work, we formulate and validate a protocol through demonstrations based on generalized Svetlichny inequality violations (a simulation, rather than a loophole-free certification, of multipartite nonlocality) for larger subsystem sizes. We apply it unchanged to three processors, the trapped-ion Marmot and IBEX Q1 (both manufactured by AQT) and the superconducting Euro-Q-Exa System 1 (IQM), using identical GHZ-state circuits with fixed theoretical measurement settings from N=2 to N=10 qubits. Both trapped-ion processors sustain violations up to ten qubits, while the superconducting processor loses them beyond six qubits under unmitigated (raw) conditions; readout-error mitigation recovers violations up to eight qubits, with a substantial fraction of the degradation attributable to measurement imperfections. These processors provide a heterogeneous testbed for validating the protocol's cross-platform applicability and discriminating power, demonstrating its practicality as a common framework for assessing collective quantum performance.

papers.title: Quantum-Classical Iterative Refinement for the Pressure-Poisson Equation on NISQ Hardware
papers.summary: We present a hybrid quantum-classical iterative refinement for the pressure-Poisson equation of the incompressible Navier-Stokes projection method on noisy quantum hardware. Rather than solving the pressure equation once per time step, we solve it repeatedly for the normalized residual and scale each quantum direction by a least-squares fit to the physical residual. As a result, the error of the quantum solve enters as a contraction factor $\sin\theta_k$ of the residual rather than as an error floor. This removes the requirement of a state infidelity below $10^{-7}$ that was estimated for single-solve schemes. With a boundary-consistent staggered (MAC) discretization, the pressure residual equals the velocity divergence left after projection up to the factor $\Delta t/\rho$. On the IBM processor ibm_cleveland, a four-qubit ($16\times16$) problem reached a relative residual below $10^{-7}$ within eight to ten corrections in all 20 runs of a pre-registered experiment, whereas a single solve with a comparable number of shots stopped at 0.33-0.59. In a six-qubit ($64\times64$) pilot, all three runs reached the same tolerance in 13 corrections. On the IonQ Forte processor, a manufactured-solution benchmark reached $5.6\times10^{-8}$ in nine corrections, with a pressure error of $4.9\times10^{-8}$. Finally, we carried out the variational training itself on ibm_cleveland, so that every sampled value of the cost function was obtained from hardware measurements. The residual fell to $5.6\times10^{-4}$ in seven corrections, below the pre-specified tolerance of $10^{-3}$, at the rate predicted by a noise model and with 24 min of QPU time.

papers.title: FTWeave: Composing Logical Execution, Real-Time Decoding, and Magic-State Supply in Tightly Integrated Quantum-Classical Systems
papers.summary: Fault-tolerant quantum applications depend on both decoded measurement information and a continuing supply of magic states. While an operation waits for either, its logical data require protection that produces more syndrome data and decoding work. Architects must provision the quantum and classical parts of the machine together, before complete systems are available to measure. FTWeave is a system-level simulator for this architectural exploration. It accepts OpenQASM 2/3 circuits, CUDA-Q Logical compiler artifacts, Stim circuits, and provider-derived physical inputs through adapters that preserve operation and measurement dependencies. Users bind these inputs to quantum resources, classical processors, memory, communication, and factory configurations. One event timeline determines application progress, resource ownership, and continuing protection. This supplies the system model needed to connect circuit and decoder evidence to application performance. Controlled demand studies and complete multiplier and Ising circuits show why the coupling changes provisioning decisions. A fixed-work approximation predicts a 3.55x multiplier speedup from additional factories where the coupled model gives almost none. Explicit ownership also changes useful capacity: increasing decoder workers alone has no benefit in a storage-constrained case, while increasing workers and feedback entries together gives 4.93x speedup. Selected color and hypergraph-product code mappings take 53-90% longer under decoder service variability, despite an unchanged mean. These comparisons identify useful resource combinations and distinguish protection work from the elapsed lifetime of quantum data.

papers.title: Local response theory of multiparameter sudden-quench quantum Otto engines
papers.summary: Multiparameter quantum Otto engines raise an optimization problem absent in single-parameter cycles: which small quench vector maximizes the quadratic approximation to the exact output work in a multidimensional control space? We show that the local quadratic work decomposes into a thermal-bias gain and a quadratic response cost, whose competition determines the quench vector that maximizes the local quadratic work at a prescribed quench amplitude. We illustrate the theory in a minimal two-level working medium, where radial and transverse quenches play distinct roles, and in a finite interacting XYZ spin chain, where the resulting quench vector is determined by the balance between thermal-bias and response cost. Our results provide a practical local criterion for designing small multiparameter quenches in sudden-quench quantum Otto engines.

papers.title: Exact Quantum Query Complexity of the Five-Bit Symmetric Boolean Function $\Exact^5_{3,4}$
papers.summary: Let \(f = \text{EXACT}^5_{3,4}\) be the Boolean function that equals 1 exactly on inputs of Hamming weight 3 or 4. Earlier numerical studies reported success probabilities close to one using three queries, but the existence of an exact three-query algorithm had remained unresolved. This paper settles this problem by proving that the exact quantum query complexity of \(f\) is \(4\). For the lower bound, we express every three-query algorithm through layer-by-layer Gram matrices of low-degree Fourier coefficients. We then construct a fixed rational dual certificate whose slack matrices are all positive definite. This certificate separates the necessary Gram-matrix region from the exact-output condition and therefore rules out every exact algorithm using at most three queries in the stated model. The positivity verification reduces to five small rational matrices and Sylvester's criterion. For the upper bound, we invoke the previously known four-query algorithm for the seven-bit function \(\text{EXACT}^7_{3,4}\) and apply the standard padding reduction. To quantify the near-exact behavior, we use the same certificate to derive a valid, though not claimed tight, lower bound \(\frac{25600}{43779488192449}>0\) on the worst-case error of every algorithm using at most three queries. This positive error gap is compatible with the near-unit success probabilities reported in earlier numerical studies, which do not establish exact computation.

papers.title: Ergotropy of nonequilibrium steady states beyond the full secular approximation
papers.summary: Understanding the generation and activation of ergotropy, the maximum work extractable by cyclic unitary operations, is central to quantum battery research. Positive-temperature thermal states are passive, whereas nonequilibrium environments can sustain nonpassive steady states with nonzero ergotropy. However, the full secular approximation commonly used in Lindblad descriptions can suppress steady-state coherence and obscure its contribution to ergotropy. Using a Bloch-Redfield master equation beyond the full secular approximation, we investigate the ergotropy of the nonequilibrium steady state (NESS) of two exchange-coupled qubits connected to independent thermal reservoirs. The NESS ergotropy of two qubits with the same frequency is entirely coherent and grows quadratically with temperature bias near equilibrium. In contrast, detuned qubits can exhibit incoherent ergotropy. We derive an exact analytical criterion for its activation and show that activation requires the hotter reservoir to be coupled to the qubit with the higher bare frequency. Comparing NESSs obtained with and without full secularization reveals quantitative and qualitative differences in ergotropy that reflect changes in both its coherent and incoherent contributions. The results clarify the mechanisms of NESS ergotropy activation and demonstrate the importance of retaining steady-state coherence beyond the full secular approximation when characterizing stationary work resources.

papers.title: Concatenated continuous-drive protection of exchange-based spin-qubit gates
papers.summary: Exchange-based two-qubit gates in semiconductor spin qubits are sensitive to low-frequency detuning noise and control errors. Here, we extend concatenated continuous driving (CCD), implemented by phase modulation of a global microwave drive, to exchange-based SWAP and $\sqrt{\mathrm{SWAP}}$ operations between double-dressed spin qubits and investigate its effectiveness for protecting two-qubit gates. We find that CCD retains strong protection against quasistatic common-mode detuning errors while substantially improving robustness against Rabi-frequency errors and qubit-to-qubit Rabi-frequency mismatch compared with conventional continuous dressing. By contrast, the gate fidelity is impacted by differential detuning errors. By modeling partially correlated quasistatic detuning noise, we further show that the noise-averaged gate fidelity depends strongly on the spatial correlation of the qubit-frequency fluctuations, with positive correlations enhancing CCD protection by suppressing the differential-noise component. These results identify the symmetry and spatial correlation of qubit-frequency noise as key factors governing continuous-drive protection in coupled spin-qubit systems.

papers.title: Collective Strong Quantum Mpemba Effect in Accelerated Quantum Detectors
papers.summary: Collective coupling to the Minkowski vacuum allows uniformly accelerated quantum detectors to exhibit a strong quantum Mpemba effect, in which a state initially farther from equilibrium relaxes faster than a closer one. We establish the existence of this effect for every fixed finite number of detectors $N\geq 2$ at sufficiently small transverse separation within the pointlike secular master equation. The mechanism originates from two reflection sectors whose populations are conserved by the leading collective dynamics. Weak intersector transfer at finite separation generates an isolated, parametrically slow relaxation mode. A simple family of initial states permits its leading-order cancellation by matching the equilibrium sector populations, while a corrected preparation eliminates the slow-mode amplitude exactly. We construct a reference state that establishes a genuine reversal of trace-distance ordering. Numerical calculations and local-rate-preserving controls identify the collective origin of the effect, while spatially smeared detector calculations support its persistence within the second-order secular framework. The same mechanism extends to detectors coupled to a common thermal field, with analytically distinct slow relaxation rates. Thus, strong Mpemba relaxation is not exclusive to acceleration but emerges from a more general interplay between collective dissipation, reflection-sector conservation, and weak symmetry-breaking transfer.

papers.title: Efficient Quantum Algorithm for Mixed-State Quantum Geometry
papers.summary: Mixed-state quantum geometry plays a fundamental role in quantum metrology, multiparameter estimation, and the characterization of quantum many-body systems. Yet, unlike its pure-state counterpart, accessing mixed-state geometry requires solving an ill-conditioned Lyapunov equation for the symmetric logarithmic derivative (SLD), posing a major challenge for resource-efficient quantum computation. Here we address the challenge and develop a novel quantum algorithmic framework for efficiently accessing the quantum Fisher information matrix (QFIM) and quantum geometric tensor (QGT) of mixed states. Our key insight is to uncover a previously unexplored connection between the positive semidefinite structure of density matrices and exponentially convergent Gauss-Laguerre quadrature, enabling an efficient integral-based construction of the SLD. A rigorous complexity analysis further establishes the resource efficiency of our algorithm, demonstrating logarithmic precision dependence and double-logarithmic ancillary-qubit overhead at fixed conditioning. Building on this construction, we achieve near-Heisenberg precision scaling for diagonal QFI estimation without quantum phase estimation and construct unified block encodings of the full QFIM and QGT under a bounded spectral-gap assumption. A complementary regularized algorithm extends efficient diagonal estimation to exponentially small spectral gaps under a bounded-response condition. Our results establish a resource-efficient route to coherent mixed-state quantum geometry, enabling its direct integration into quantum linear-algebra algorithms without classical reconstruction and opening new possibilities for quantum-enhanced multiparameter metrology.

papers.title: Adiabatic controlled-$Z$ gate for neutral atoms with F\"orster-enhanced Rydberg dressing
papers.summary: We study an adiabatic controlled-$Z$ (CZ) gate for neutral atoms in which dipole-dipole coupling between nearly degenerate Rydberg pair states enhances the interaction between dressed ground states. This coupling produces an avoided crossing in the two-atom dressed-state spectrum. Approaching the crossing enhances the dressed interaction, but also reduces the dressed-state gap and increases the Rydberg admixture. We identify a F\"orster-enhanced operating range in which the required conditional phase is accumulated with adiabatic return and small transient Rydberg population. We then analyze the finite-time dynamics of the two-qubit computational states under a smooth pulse. Reducing the dressing strength weakens the dressed interaction, so maintaining the target phase at the same pulse duration requires operation closer to the avoided crossing, where the Rydberg admixture increases. This dependence is then used to select the shortest gate at a fixed peak Rabi frequency in the F\"orster-enhanced operating range that accumulates the CZ phase with high Bell-state fidelity while keeping the Rydberg population small. Changing the F\"orster defect shifts the avoided crossing, while the gate parameters change only weakly. For a specific rubidium F\"orster channel, the selected gate corresponds to experimentally relevant laser coupling, pulse duration, and interatomic separation. We also estimate errors from the finite Rydberg lifetime and from weak excitation of a neighboring spectator atom. For the parameters considered, the spectator-induced error remains below the finite-lifetime contribution.

papers.title: Characterizing Local and Correlated Pauli Noise in Quantum Teleportation Circuits
papers.summary: We analytically characterize how the location and the local or correlated structure of stochastic Pauli errors affect a three-qubit coherent quantum-teleportation circuit. Independent local channels and a fully correlated two-qubit channel are inserted separately in six configurations. Propagating each Pauli-error realization through the Clifford circuit yields the effective channel on Bob's qubit and analytical expressions for the average and state-resolved fidelities. Under a common ordered-pair probability convention, the six configurations form three pairs that induce equivalent reduced channels on Bob. Within each pair, corresponding Pauli-error realizations have the same probabilities and produce the same effective Pauli operator on Bob's output state. The equivalence therefore holds for every input state within the stochastic Pauli models considered here, rather than only for the average fidelity. Correlated Z errors do not affect the output for the first pair; local X and Z errors exhibit complementary qubit sensitivity for the second; and correlated same-axis Pauli errors cancel for the third. These results classify the error response of the selected circuit configurations and show that it depends jointly on the error statistics, Pauli axis, and position within the protocol.

papers.title: Symmetry-breaking chelation enables room-temperature all-optical spin coherence readout of aqueous Cu(II) for chemoselective discrimination
papers.summary: Optical initialization and readout of molecular electron spins in water remains challenging for 3d transition-metal complexes. Their Laporte-forbidden d-d transitions yield weak transition dipole moments, so optical spin detection in aqueous Cu(II) previously required ~1 M concentrations. Here we overcome this constraint through symmetry-breaking chelation. Coordinating Cu(II) with EDTA imposes a non-centrosymmetric ligand field with enhanced metal-ligand covalency, relaxing Laporte restrictions and amplifying d-d transition dipole moments. This design enhances absorption and magnetic circular dichroism by 7.3- and 5.6-fold, enabling ultrafast spin readout down to 100 {\mu}M with an apparent dephasing time T2^*~0.54 ns. As a proof-of-concept for selective molecular-spin sensing, histidine addition extends T_2^* to ~0.8 ns in a concentration-dependent manner, whereas glycine produces no measurable effect. These results show that symmetry breaking provides a strategy to create molecular spin-photon interfaces, opening avenues toward all-optical, analyte-responsive quantum sensing in water.

papers.title: Chiral Floquet Selection of an Algebraic Rydberg Bound State in the Continuum
papers.summary: Bound states in the continuum (BICs) remain localized despite the presence of extended modes at the same energy. In driven systems with long-range couplings, the absence of radiation does not by itself determine how a bound state decays in space. We study a Hermitian Rydberg spin waveguide coupled to a four-site plaquette, where a winding drive phase combines rotation with time translation to forbid propagating guide channels in one symmetry sector. The resulting eigenstate remains embedded in the continuum of other sectors and carries an inverse-cube waveguide amplitude, with coherent contributions from direct plaquette--guide coupling and long-range guide propagation. Pair-state calculations determine the microscopic couplings in the axial geometry, while coherent Floquet mixing sets the weight of the dominant circulating plaquette mode. The bound state thus retains the spatial signature of the long-range coupling even when radiation is forbidden.

papers.title: Super Howe duality and rigidity of hybrid Fourier transforms
papers.summary: We characterize the hybrid Fourier transform on the Schwartz--Grassmann space $\caS(\bbR^m)\otimes\Lambda_{2n}$ by operator intertwining relations. Using the bosonic oscillator Howe decomposition and the fermionic Lefschetz decomposition, we describe the action of the hybrid Fourier transform on both tensor factors. We show that first-order covariance with respect to coordinate multiplication and differentiation determines the transform up to a scalar. For $m,n\ge1$, we prove that covariance under all even quadratic operators, together with any one nonzero mixed quadratic operator, determines the linear span of the hybrid Fourier transform and its inverse. This rigidity result is obtained by computing the ordinary commutants of the even and full quadratic oscillator actions of $\fosp(4n|2m)$. After a degree-scaling change of normalization, we make the hybrid Fourier transform unitary with respect to the occupation number inner product, and factor it into a bosonic oscillator rotation and (up to a scalar phase) an $SU(2)$ rotation in the fermionic Lefschetz representation. For $m=1$ and $n\ge2$, we show that full even quadratic covariance together with the parity-preserving cubic relation for $qQ_f$ determines the unitary transform up to a global phase and a fermion-parity phase. Finally we calculate the unitary conjugation formulas for Hubbard--Holstein Hamiltonian for a hybrid continuous-variable and discrete-variable quantum system.

papers.title: On the Complexity of Level-Synchronized Tree Automata for Quantum Circuit Verification
papers.summary: Reliable quantum computation requires methods for verifying quantum circuits. Level-synchronized tree automata (LSTAs) were recently introduced to represent sets of quantum states for this purpose. We study LSTAs along two axes relevant to verification: the complexity of their decision problems and the size of their representations under circuit operations. We prove that acyclic LSTAs have NP-complete nonemptiness and $\Pi_2^P$-complete language inclusion, and that general language inclusion is EXPSPACE-complete. We further prove inherent quadratic representation growth under individual quantum gates in a fixed qubit order, and give an adjacent-qubit reordering construction that preserves level synchronization. These results clarify the scope of applicability of the automata-theoretic toolbox for quantum circuit verification.

papers.title: Exact probability laws of random inner products: Dirichlet splines, overlaps, uncertainty, and Bargmann invariants
papers.summary: Inner products of random matrices and random quantum states---such as orbital inner products, expectation values, overlaps, and cyclic Bargmann invariants---are shown to follow from two underlying mechanisms: the diagonal of an induced random state is Dirichlet distributed, and the expectation value of a random pure state in a rank-one or two-by-two operator is a numerical shadow on an elliptical disk. For states induced by an environment of dimension $K$, the expectation value of any observable is a Curry--Schoenberg spline with each eigenvalue repeated $K$ times, and the vector of moments has an explicit density on a simplex; for a qutrit, the variance law is obtained in finite form. The overlap of two random qubit states attains its mode at its mean for every rotation-invariant ensemble, but for Hilbert--Schmidt qutrits the density at the mean has a strictly negative derivative, so mode and mean separate; for large environments, the centred overlap converges to a variance-gamma law rather than a Gaussian. For two noncommuting qubit observables, the joint law of the two standard deviations is derived for all $K$, and the probability of coming within a small distance of the optimal sum of variances scales as a power of that distance, with a different exponent when the Bloch axes are orthogonal. For three Haar-random qubit states, the exact density of the Bargmann invariant is given in terms of a complete elliptic integral, together with its local behaviour and elementary marginals. In every dimension, the probability that its real part is negative---certifying basis-independent coherence---is computed, along with all mixed moments. For cycles of arbitrary length, the invariant is shown to be driven by an exact three-parameter Markov chain, and the logarithm of its modulus obeys a law of large numbers and a central limit theorem.

papers.title: Simulation-Based Quantum Forensics for QKD: Machine Learning Attack Detection and Signature Extraction
papers.summary: Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) supports secure key establishment under ideal protocol assumptions, but practical systems remain exposed to implementation-level attacks against optical channels, detectors, and controller behavior. This study presents Quantum Forensic Log (QF-LOG), a simulation-based forensic framework for analyzing aggregated QKD operational logs rather than raw quantum states. QF-LOG uses four observable features: quantum bit error rate (QBER), photon count, latency in milliseconds, and abort flag. The framework classifies normal operation and three simulated attack-related conditions: partial intercept-resend, detector-blind, and fiber-tap. A physics-inspired Generator-A dataset with 5 million balanced records was constructed using explicit mathematical generation models for all four features. A transparent threshold baseline, logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost were evaluated on Generator-A. The full-feature learning models achieved macro F1-scores from 0.8211 to 0.8243 and outperformed the transparent two-feature comparator. Feature diagnostics showed that QBER contributed most, followed by latency in milliseconds and photon count, while no single feature reproduced the full feature set performance. Robustness was assessed on a separately generated Generator-B dataset of 5 million records that uses the same governing equations under shifted simulated operating parameters. Without retraining or tuning, their macro F1-scores decreased to values from 0.5645 to 0.5669. These findings show that QF-LOG can support interpretable forensic classification in a controlled synthetic setting, but stable internal evaluation does not establish reliability under changed simulated QKD operating conditions. The framework provides a documented basis for future evaluation across broader simulated settings and hardware-generated QKD logs.

papers.title: Spatial Discretization Error for Quantum Chemistry Simulation
papers.summary: Nonrelativistic quantum chemistry is based on the Schr\"odinger equation in continuous, unbounded space. Computational approaches on classical and quantum computers often truncate the spatial domain and introduce a finite-dimensional basis, reducing the continuum problem to a finite-dimensional one. There is therefore a fundamental question: to what extent does this approximation capture the original continuum problem? In this work, we develop a general Sobolev-Galerkin framework for estimating spatial discretization errors in quantum simulation with unbounded Hamiltonians. We apply this framework to many-body Coulomb systems and establish both periodization and Galerkin error estimates for wave-function dynamics and ground-state energies. For dynamics, the finite-basis projection error of the exact wave function does not capture the full basis-discretization error: an additional dynamical projection error enters our bound at a different rate, and we introduce an inner-product argument to control this contribution. Interestingly, the spatial convergence rates for wave-function dynamics and ground-state energies differ quantitatively. For ground-state energies, we establish a sharp $M^{-1}$ convergence rate at fixed cell size, where $M$ is the number of one-particle basis functions. We also show that a uniform $M^{-1}$ convergence rate is impossible for the corresponding real-time wave-function error with general $H^2$ initial data. The analysis relies on many-body Sobolev estimates with explicit polynomial dependence on system size. Combining these estimates with state-of-the-art quantum algorithms, we obtain, to our knowledge, the first rigorous end-to-end complexity bounds for quantum simulation of molecular and electronic dynamics with all spatial errors explicitly controlled. The number of basis functions is determined directly from the continuum problem, without regularization.

An exact finite-chain solution proves this rate inversion, and symmetry-resolved calculations confirm the criterion in larger spin-one chains, including nonintegrable exchange. The zero-temperature endpoint of a continuous Gibbs family can therefore be dynamically isolated by its exact exclusion from slow relaxation channels.

papers.title: Exact quantum Hamming-weight computation at optimal depth and minimum width
papers.summary: Hamming-weight computation and symmetric Boolean functions are basic primitives for quantum arithmetic and state preparation, where circuit depth and qubit overhead matter. We construct an exact circuit computing the Hamming weight of an $n$-qubit register with depth $O(\log n)$ and size $O(n\log n)$, using only the $n$ input qubits and $m=\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$ binary output qubits. The circuit uses arbitrary one-qubit gates and CNOTs with all-to-all connectivity. Both depth and total width are optimal. Our constructions combine tree structures and pipelining, temporarily using input qubits as workspace. We also give exact circuits for every symmetric Boolean function with the same depth and size bounds, using only $m$ ancillary qubits returned to zero. Finally, we apply the counter to exact preparation of balanced Dicke states for even $n$. With only $O(\log n)$ ancillary qubits, we obtain expected depth $O(\log^2 n)$ using measurements and classical feedforward, and depth $O(n^{1/4}\log n)$ using unitary gates alone.

papers.title: Failure of disjoint additivity under magnetic Gauss constraints
papers.summary: Under local magnetic Gauss constraints, vertex-disjoint regions can have commuting physical observable algebras that do not generate all observables on their union. We construct such counterexamples for every finite non-Abelian group on regular square tori, retaining the full magnetic physical space and original supports inside a fixed contractible disk. A peripheral projector selects inputs on which a joint transition preserves the constraints, while its loop factor alone fails the universal test over physical exterior completions. For a specified support family around a fixed eight-edge square loop, additivity fails if and only if the group is non-Abelian and each inner face is covered by at least one of its two prescribed peripheral edges. Leaving a face uncovered restores full additivity. For the same loop, additivity also holds with any region at vertex-set graph distance at least two. These results refute a recent group-double additivity proposition.

papers.title: Can Quantum Entanglement Increase the Capacity of a Classical Relay Channel?
papers.summary: We show positive and negative results on classical relay channels with entanglement assistance, revealing a sharp contrast between strictly causal and causal relay encoding. Namely, entanglement shared between the source and relay significantly increases the capacity of a classical zero-delay relay channel.

papers.title: Topological Quantum Gates on FCIs with Bounded Quantum Geometry

The cyclic structure entails mildly non-abelian braiding phases and otherwise matches the spectral flow exhibited by the FCI's hybrid Wannier states, with the metric bound equivalently a bound on the states' real-space spread. We give a classification of quantum gates in principle implementable on this topological order; among them we find the non-Clifford T-gate and the non-Clifford entangling CCZ-gate. This points to novel pathways to fault-tolerant quantum processes within the known orbital structure of FCIs, potentially informing experimental searches towards hardware for future topological quantum computers.

papers.title: Randomness Certification from Statistically Hiding Commitments
papers.summary: Randomness certification aims to guarantee that the output of an untrusted quantum device contains genuine randomness that remains unpredictable even given quantum side information held by an adversary. For a classical verifier interacting with a single quantum device, such a guarantee cannot rely on the physical separation underlying standard Bell tests and must instead follow from computational restrictions on the prover. Building on the framework of Computational Bell Inequalities, we distinguish classical and quantum virtual-input hiding, showing that the former suffices for proofs of quantumness, whereas the latter enables randomness certification against quantum side information. Our main technical contribution is to establish quantum virtual-input hiding for a commitment-based protocol derived from the proof of quantumness from one-way-functions by Morimae and Yamakawa. We show that statistical hiding together with ordinary computational binding against quantum polynomial-time senders suffices, without requiring stronger quantum binding notions such as sum-binding or collapse-binding. This yields a randomness-certification protocol from post-quantum statistically hiding bit commitments. In particular, existing constructions of such commitments from post-quantum one-way permutations imply that post-quantum one-way permutations suffice for randomness certification. We further instantiate our construction using quantum-secure trapdoor claw-free functions, obtaining an efficient classical verifier, and in the quantum random oracle model, obtaining randomness certification without additional computational assumptions but with an inefficient verifier. These instantiations separate the cryptographic properties sufficient for randomness certification from the additional structure required for efficient verification within our commitment-based framework.

papers.title: Quantum State Search with Classical Interactive Advice

The bound allows arbitrary classical interaction and unrestricted computation between queries. Our proof extends the lower bound of Aaronson and Kuperberg from a single classical proof to an arbitrary classical interaction. As a result, we obtain a quantum-oracle separation of UniqueQMA from QCIP with polynomially many classical messages. In particular, we give a unitary oracle $\mathcal{U}$ such that there exists a language $L\in\mathrm{UniqueQMA}^{\mathcal{U}}$ but $L\notin\mathrm{QCIP}^{\mathcal{U}}$. papers.title: Distributed Phase Tags: A Locality-Preserving Realification Compiler for Misty-State Quantum Programs
papers.summary: Complex amplitudes can be simulated over real Hilbert spaces by adjoining a two-dimensional real/imaginary degree of freedom. In a multipartite program, however, one globally shared phase tag is not a locality-preserving program transformation: every party would have to act on the same auxiliary system. We recast the distributed real simulation of multipartite quantum mechanics as a syntax-directed compiler into a real misty-state intermediate language. For $n$ parties we give explicit phase-reference codewords $|0\rangle_{P_n}$ and $|1\rangle_{P_n}$ on $n$ local tags and prove that the same real operator $J=XZ$ on any single tag realizes the logical action of multiplication by $i$. If a complex party-local gate is $A=A_R+iA_I$, its real translation is \[ \widehat A_j=A_R\otimes I+A_I\otimes J_j, \] which acts only on party $j$'s data and local phase tag. We prove an intertwining theorem for arbitrary finite party-local pure-state circuits, exact preservation of computational-basis measurement probabilities, preservation of the run-time interaction graph, and one-rebit-per-party overhead. For the canonical three-party GHZ program, the translation lies entirely inside the ordinary black-and-white misty gate fragment: controlled-$J$ replaces the complex phase operation, while the invariant $J_jJ_k|0\rangle_P=-|0\rangle_P$ transfers the required branch sign. This yields a short correctness proof for all four promised GHZ inputs and explains the earlier 64-path cancellation calculation at a single logical phase-code boundary. We distinguish this program realification problem from the weaker task of finding any real strategy with the same correlations, and state precisely which parts are known real-Hilbert-space simulation and which parts belong to the misty-language compilation layer developed here.

papers.title: Perturbation theory for quantum information quantities of Gaussian states
papers.summary: Many quantum-information tasks can benefit from Gaussian quantum resources, while their fundamental performance limits are characterized by quantum information quantities. However, a unified perturbation theory for these quantities directly within the Gaussian-state formalism has been lacking. We develop such a theory for the von Neumann entropy, quantum relative entropy, quantum Chernoff quantity, and quantum fidelity, using perturbations of the moments of a reference Gaussian state. Using general Fr\'echet-derivative identities, we derive compact second-order expressions for reference-state covariance matrices whose symplectic eigenvalues are all greater than $1/2$. We also show that the perturbative quantum Chernoff quantity is maximized at its symmetric point, yielding the quantum Chernoff exponent (QCE). We further show that symplectic eigenvalues equal to 1/2 can lead to slower asymptotic vanishing, potentially improving the corresponding fundamental performance limits. For reference-state covariance matrices containing symplectic eigenvalues both equal to and greater than 1/2, we identify sufficient conditions under which the former determine the leading covariance-matrix contributions, allowing the remaining modes to be traced out without changing the leading-order asymptotic scaling or the coefficient. Applying the framework to quantum illumination and incoherent-light sub-Rayleigh object discrimination, we recover known asymptotic QCEs directly within the Gaussian-state formalism. In the latter problem, the slower asymptotic vanishing explains the known quadratic scaling of the QCE with the source separation.

papers.title: Quantum computing for plasma physics in magnetic-confinement fusion
papers.summary: Plasma simulations for magnetic-confinement fusion (MCF) involve high-dimensional kinetic dynamics, strong nonlinear coupling, complex geometries, and multiscale spatiotemporal behavior, imposing severe computational bottlenecks. While quantum computing offers a potential alternative for accelerating plasma simulation problems, its practical advantage for fusion research has not yet been demonstrated. We review existing quantum computing studies across kinetic dynamics, wave interactions, equilibrium, and macroscopic stability, evaluating their hardware implementations and operational bottlenecks. Current studies remain largely restricted to linearized equations, reduced models, or isolated computational subroutines, leaving a substantial gap from realistic fusion simulations. We summarize key problem characteristics, including high dimensionality, structured dynamics, and measurement requirements, under which plasma applications are most likely to yield a quantum advantage. Guided by these considerations, we highlight potential approaches and present a roadmap toward practical quantum advantage of simulating plasma in MCF.

papers.title: How Quantum Is Light? Concepts, Measures, and Applications of Optical Quantumness
papers.summary: Quantum states are ultimately responsible for numerous counterintuitive phenomena that defy classical intuition. As the development of quantum technologies accelerates, our ability to harness these quantum resources becomes essential. This review addresses a fundamental question. How do we quantify the quantumness of a state, and which specific traits distinguish it from its classical counterparts? We examine quantumness through both theoretical and operational lenses, providing a clear framework for state characterization. Ultimately, we demonstrate that certifying quantumness is not just a theoretical exercise. It is a practical necessity for identifying, and realizing quantum advantage in real-world applications.

papers.title: Entanglement-enhanced Ramsey spectroscopy of broadband signals
papers.summary: The use of entanglement in sensing is often motivated by improved sensitivity arising from non-classical correlations among probes. For static signals, however, this quantum advantage in Ramsey spectroscopy with $N$ probes is known to be highly susceptible to dephasing, which severely limits the possible gain from entanglement. In contrast, we consider sensing of signals that vary in time. Considering the simplest example of dephasing by classical white noise, we show that entanglement allows a large increase in bandwidth when estimating the frequency components of a time-dependent signal. Without sacrificing any sensitivity, entanglement allows for an increase in bandwidth by a factor of $N$. Alternatively, when interrogation times are limited by the signal bandwidth rather than by dephasing, the average estimation uncertainty over a fixed bandwidth is reduced by a factor of $\sqrt{N}$ compared with separable states.

papers.title: Efficient Block Encodings for Ensembles of Molecular Hamiltonians
papers.summary: Accurately characterizing molecular properties and reactivity often requires electronic-structure calculations across an ensemble of molecular geometries. Quantum algorithms that process such ensembles coherently could address this challenge, but they require Hamiltonian block encoding circuits that combine advanced factorization techniques with sublinear scaling in ensemble size. Here, we introduce SVD-THC, which extends tensor hypercontraction to sets of Hamiltonians defined at different nuclear geometries through a singular value decomposition of the ensemble. We use SVD-THC to construct a single multiplexed block encoding circuit for all geometries in an ensemble. We then evaluate the approach on ensembles generated by varying internal rotational coordinates in 1-bromo-2-chloroethane as well as in glycine and alanine dipeptides, corresponding to established model systems for peptide conformational landscapes, with up to 5,184 geometries. Across several resolutions of the internal-coordinate grids, the Toffoli complexity of the resulting circuits grows only weakly with the number of geometries, changing by at most 12\% over grids that differ in size by up to 576$\times$. In an energy-thresholding circuit, this yields 35--200$\times$ fewer Toffoli gates than slicing together single-geometry block encodings. This approach could help make coherent processing of molecular geometry ensembles a useful primitive for fault-tolerant quantum computing.

papers.title: Conjugate measurement-induced evolution towards maximally mixed states in quadratic quantum systems
papers.summary: In an earlier work, we showed that, in the interaction-dominant setting, coupling the conjugate variables of a subsystem to distinct environment modes drives the subsystem to a maximally mixed state. By tracking the exact reduced Weyl characteristic and Wigner functions, we demonstrate that they lose their dependence on local phase-space coordinates on every fixed compact region. In free-particle model, this happens for all values of coupling, whereas in the harmonic oscillator model, it happens above a critical value of the coupling. Under a finite-volume and momentum regularization, this behavior corresponds to the reduced subsystem approaching a maximally mixed state.

papers.title: A Dual-Uplink Dual-Satellite Architecture for Entanglement Distribution
papers.summary: Satellite-based quantum links are a promising enabler of long-distance entanglement distribution, overcoming the exponential losses of optical fibers. In uplink architectures, entangled photons are generated at ground stations and transmitted to orbiting satellites, reducing space-segment complexity but introducing significant atmospheric and geometric losses. Single-satellite dual-uplink configurations are additionally limited by the requirement of simultaneous visibility between both ground stations and the satellite. In this work, we investigate a dual-uplink dual-satellite network architecture and compare its performance with the single-satellite scheme under identical physical assumptions. The proposed topology introduces an inter-satellite link (ISL) that decouples the ground-station separation from the atmospheric uplink geometry. A realistic channel model is employed, incorporating geometric attenuation, atmospheric turbulence, background noise, and Bell-state measurement efficiency. The overall success probability and practical fidelity are evaluated as functions of satellite altitude and ground-station separation. Our results show that while the single-satellite configuration is suitable for regional-scale networks, it becomes infeasible for large separations due to geometric constraints. The proposed dual-satellite architecture mitigates this limitation and significantly extends the achievable communication distance, representing a key step toward scalable quantum internet infrastructures.

papers.title: Multi-path Security in Quantum Networks with Trusted Nodes
papers.summary: Quantum communication networks promise information-theoretic security but this security collapses if intermediate relay nodes are compromised, a risk that grows sharply when compromised nodes cannot be identified. We address this twofold: first, we show that multi-path routing provides quantifiable protection against unidentified compromised nodes. Second, we provide a comprehensive statistical and graph-theoretic analysis of network and node security under compromise, covering full and partial node compromise, optimal placement of additional edges via an iterative method, and comparative hacking-probability analysis across network topologies. Together, these results identify the topology and multi-path routing strategy that most improves security for a given network. We apply this framework to quantum key distribution across multiple network topologies, demonstrating a scalable route to secure, reliable quantum communication under realistic, unidentified adversarial threats, without relying on quantum memory.
